muscles.name: Latissimus dorsi
muscles.sourceFaceFilter: Z-Anatomy FBX material index 1 only; Tendon material faces excluded to show the visible muscle belly instead of the thoracolumbar tendinous sheet.
muscles.sourceTransform: Converted from Z-Anatomy FBX meters into BodyParts3D-style millimeter coordinates; depth axis reflected and shifted so the latissimus dorsi muscle belly aligns with the posterior back mesh coordinate band.

muscles.name: Trapezius
muscles.displayName: Trapezius (imported upper, middle, and lower fibers)

movements.name: Ab Wheel Rollout
movements.variant: Kneeling ab-wheel rollout emphasizing trunk anti-extension while the shoulders flex overhead.
movements.description: Start kneeling with the wheel under the shoulders, brace the ribs down toward the pelvis, roll forward only as far as the trunk can stay controlled without sagging, then pull the wheel back under the shoulders while keeping the hips and ribs connected.

hypertrophy.rationale: Good abdominal loading, but the movement is usually limited by bracing skill and shoulder position more than simple local hypertrophy progression.

strength.rationale: Strong trunk anti-extension strength signal, but not a high-load whole-body strength anchor.

joint_resilience.rationale: Can build trunk and shoulder tolerance when range is controlled, but poor scaling can irritate the low back or shoulders.

athletic_transfer.rationale: Useful bracing transfer, but the kneeling rollout is not a gait, sprint, throw, or loaded carry pattern.

control.rationale: Very high motor-control demand from anti-extension, pelvic/rib position, shoulder flexion, and eccentric range control.

fatigue_efficiency.rationale: Efficient trunk stimulus when scaled well, but shoulder and low-back compensation can add unrelated fatigue.

setup.rationale: Requires only an ab wheel and floor space, with little adjustment.

ease.rationale: Hard to perform well because range, spinal position, shoulder control, and return mechanics are easy to lose.

progression.rationale: Progression is possible through range and reps, but load is indirect and hard to quantify.

support.rationale: Minimal external support; the user self-stabilizes trunk and shoulders throughout.

primary.name: Rectus abdominis
primary.evidenceShort: Power Wheel rollout studies show high rectus activation.
primary.evidence: Power Wheel rollout and similar abdominal-device EMG studies report high upper and lower rectus abdominis activation.

primary.name: External oblique
primary.evidenceShort: Rollout/Ab-Slide evidence shows high external-oblique activation.
primary.evidence: Abdominal rollout and Ab-Slide evidence supports external oblique as a high-activation trunk-control target.

secondary.name: Internal oblique
secondary.evidenceShort: Measured abdominal-device activation supports a meaningful role.
secondary.evidence: Power Wheel and Ab-Slide evidence reports high internal oblique activation across nontraditional abdominal exercises, supporting a secondary trunk-stability role.

support.name: Latissimus dorsi
support.evidenceShort: Shoulder-extension support measured in Power Wheel exercise family.
support.evidence: Power Wheel abdominal exercise evidence measured latissimus dorsi activity, consistent with shoulder and trunk support during rollouts.

evidence.verdict: Kneeling ab wheel rollout: rectus abdominis and external oblique primary; internal oblique secondary; latissimus dorsi support.
evidence.clinicalShort: EMG estimates acute excitation; it does not prove hypertrophy, mechanical tension, or injury risk.
evidence.limitsShort: Kneeling versus standing, rollout distance, spinal position, shoulder range, wheel design, and tempo change difficulty and emphasis.
evidence.summary: The ab wheel rollout is classified as a trunk anti-extension movement with high abdominal activation and meaningful shoulder-girdle support demand.
evidence.clinicalInterpretation: The movement should be scaled by range of motion because compensation can shift load from the abdominal wall to the lumbar spine or shoulders.
evidence.limitations: The strongest direct evidence uses Power Wheel or Ab-Slide equipment rather than every commercial wheel design. Standing rollouts should be a separate, harder variant.

studies.type: Traditional and nontraditional abdominal exercise EMG
studies.finding: Power Wheel roll-out, pike, and knee-up were among the highest abdominal-activation exercises and also activated extraneous musculature.
studies.citation: Escamilla RF, Babb E, DeWitt R, et al. Electromyographic analysis of traditional and nontraditional abdominal exercises: implications for rehabilitation and training. Physical Therapy. 2006;86(5):656-671.
studies.relevance: Direct Power Wheel rollout-family EMG evidence for rectus abdominis, obliques, latissimus dorsi, and interpretation limits.

studies.type: Ab-Slide and abdominal exercise EMG
studies.finding: Ab-Slide produced high rectus abdominis, external oblique, and internal oblique activation.
studies.citation: Youdas JW, Guck BR, Hebrink RC, Rugotzke JD, Madson TJ, Hollman JH. An electromyographic analysis of the Ab-Slide exercise, abdominal crunch, supine double leg thrust, and side bridge in healthy young adults. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2008;22(6):1939-1946. doi:10.1519/JSC.0b013e31818745bf.
studies.relevance: Close rollout-style abdominal-device evidence for abdominal wall activation.

movements.name: Bar Bench Press
movements.variant: Flat barbell bench press, treated as a free-weight horizontal pressing pattern.
movements.description: Lie flat with eyes under the racked bar, feet planted, shoulder blades set against the bench, and hands slightly wider than shoulder width; unrack by moving the bar over the shoulder joints with wrists stacked over elbows, lower under control toward the lower chest or sternum with elbows roughly 45-70 degrees from the torso, then press back up without losing shoulder position.

hypertrophy.rationale: Strong pectoralis and triceps loading, but the fixed bar path and powerlifting-style setup make it less purely hypertrophy-biased than freer or more targeted press options.

strength.rationale: Elite upper-body strength anchor because heavy bilateral loading, stable setup, and precise barbell increments map cleanly to force expression.

joint_resilience.rationale: Provides some shoulder and elbow exposure, but it is not primarily a joint-resilience drill and can be limiting for irritated shoulders when technique, range, or volume are poorly matched.

athletic_transfer.rationale: Low transfer to athletic coordination because the body is supine, bilateral, externally braced, and the movement path is narrow.

control.rationale: Requires bar path and bracing control, but balance, unilateral control, locomotion, and whole-body coordination demands are limited.

fatigue_efficiency.rationale: Useful pressing stimulus, but heavy barbell loading, warm-up sets, spotter/rack demands, and shoulder/triceps fatigue reduce stimulus-per-recovery efficiency.

setup.rationale: Requires a bench, rack, bar, plates, safety setup or spotter judgment, and repeatable rack height. It is common but not low-friction.

ease.rationale: The pattern is familiar, but safe repeatable execution requires bar path, scapular position, grip, arch, touch point, and unrack control.

progression.rationale: One of the cleanest progressive-overload movements because load, reps, range, and barbell increments are directly trackable.

support.rationale: The bench supports the torso, but the bar path is free and the lifter must stabilize shoulders, elbows, wrists, and trunk tension under heavy load.

primary.name: Pectoralis major
primary.evidenceShort: High activation in seated/horizontal press EMG.
primary.evidence: Surface electromyography studies of seated chest press and horizontal bench press variants consistently measure substantial pectoralis major activation during horizontal pressing.

secondary.name: Anterior deltoid
secondary.evidenceShort: Meaningful press assist; angle/path sensitive.
secondary.evidence: Anterior deltoid activity is repeatedly measured during horizontal pressing; its contribution varies with bench angle, grip, and handle path.

secondary.name: Triceps brachii
secondary.evidenceShort: Elbow-extension contributor; grip/path sensitive.
secondary.evidence: Triceps brachii contributes to elbow extension during pressing, with activation influenced by grip width and movement variant.

support.name: Serratus anterior
support.evidenceShort: Scapulothoracic support; not primary chest target.
support.evidence: Serratus anterior activity has been reported in bench press and chest press comparisons and is best classified here as scapulothoracic support rather than a primary hypertrophy target.

support.name: Rotator cuff
support.evidenceShort: Glenohumeral stabilization during pressing.
support.evidence: Bench press research demonstrates direction-specific rotator cuff recruitment consistent with glenohumeral stabilization during pressing.

evidence.verdict: Flat barbell horizontal press: pectoralis major primary; anterior deltoid and triceps secondary; serratus anterior and rotator cuff support.
evidence.clinicalShort: EMG estimates acute excitation, not hypertrophy, mechanical tension, adaptation, or injury risk.
evidence.limitsShort: Grip width, bar path, arch, bench angle, and equipment change emphasis; dumbbell and machine versions should be separate movements.
evidence.summary: The flat bar bench press is classified as a free-weight horizontal pressing exercise. The best available evidence supports pectoralis major as the primary target, with clinically meaningful anterior deltoid and triceps brachii contribution. Serratus anterior and rotator cuff involvement is classified as shoulder and scapulothoracic support rather than as a primary hypertrophy target.
evidence.clinicalInterpretation: Surface electromyography is useful for estimating acute muscle excitation during a specific exercise condition. It should not be interpreted as a direct measure of hypertrophy, mechanical tension, long-term adaptation, or injury risk.
evidence.limitations: Bar bench press mechanics differ by grip width, touch point, arch, range of motion, tempo, load, and bench angle. Machine and dumbbell pressing evidence is used only when it is biomechanically close to the flat barbell horizontal press pattern.

studies.type: Horizontal bench/chest press EMG
studies.shortCitation: Muyor et al., J Hum Kinet, 2023
studies.finding: Seated chest press/bench variants measured pec regions, anterior deltoid, and triceps.
studies.citation: Muyor JM, Rodriguez-Ridao D, Oliva-Lozano JM. Comparison of Muscle Activity between the Horizontal Bench Press and the Seated Chest Press Exercises Using Several Grips. Journal of Human Kinetics. 2023;87:23-34. doi:10.5114/jhk/161468.
studies.relevance: Directly compared seated chest press grips with horizontal bench press grips and measured pectoralis major regions, anterior deltoid, and triceps brachii.

studies.type: Systematic review of bench press EMG
studies.finding: Bench press EMG literature supports pec/triceps dominance and key interpretation limits.
studies.citation: Stastny P, Golas A, Blazek D, Maszczyk A, Wilk M, Pietraszewski P, Petr M, Uhlir P, Zajac A. A systematic review of surface electromyography analyses of the bench press movement task. PLOS ONE. 2017;12(2):e0171632. doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0171632.
studies.relevance: Summarizes bench press EMG evidence and supports pectoralis major and triceps brachii as dominant contributors in the movement family.

studies.type: Bench inclination EMG study
studies.finding: Bench angle shifts pec, anterior deltoid, and triceps activation.
studies.citation: Rodriguez-Ridao D, Antequera-Vique JA, Martin-Fuentes I, Muyor JM. Effect of Five Bench Inclinations on the Electromyographic Activity of the Pectoralis Major, Anterior Deltoid, and Triceps Brachii during the Bench Press Exercise. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. 2020;17(19):7339. doi:10.3390/ijerph17197339.
studies.relevance: Shows how bench angle changes pectoralis major, anterior deltoid, and triceps brachii activation in the close horizontal/incline pressing family.

studies.type: Rotator cuff recruitment study
studies.shortCitation: Wattanaprakornkul et al., J Electromyogr Kinesiol, 2011
studies.finding: Rotator cuff recruitment is direction-specific during bench press and row tasks.
studies.citation: Wattanaprakornkul D, Halaki M, Cathers I, Ginn KA. Direction-specific recruitment of rotator cuff muscles during bench press and row. Journal of Electromyography and Kinesiology. 2011;21(6):1041-1049. doi:10.1016/j.jelekin.2011.09.002.
studies.relevance: Supports rotator cuff involvement as direction-specific shoulder stabilization during bench press tasks.

studies.type: Chest press lever machine EMG and scapular kinematics
studies.finding: Chest press lever machine data includes pec, anterior deltoid, serratus, and scapular kinematics.
studies.citation: Borges E, Dalla H, Mastandrea L, Nunes S, Santarem J. Comparative evaluation of muscular activation and scapular kinematics in a chest press lever machine and a barbell bench press. Journal of Physical Education and Sport. 2019;19:912-916. doi:10.7752/jpes.2019.s3131.
studies.relevance: Compared a chest press lever machine with barbell bench press and measured pectoralis major, anterior deltoid, and serratus anterior with scapular kinematics.

movements.name: Barbell Back Squat
movements.variant: Free-weight bilateral barbell back squat with the bar supported on the upper back; treated separately from front squat, Smith machine, hack squat, safety-bar, goblet, and bodyweight squat variants.
movements.description: Set the bar securely across the upper back, brace the trunk, unrack with a stable stance, and descend by bending the hips, knees, and ankles while keeping the feet rooted and the knees tracking over the toes. Reach a controlled depth that preserves position, then drive the floor away and stand tall without losing the bar path or trunk brace.

hypertrophy.rationale: Strong quad and glute loading through large ranges, but systemic fatigue, technique limits, and bracing demands can cap target-muscle volume before local failure.

strength.rationale: Elite lower-body strength anchor because heavy bilateral free-weight loading, full-body bracing, and small barbell increments map cleanly to force expression.

joint_resilience.rationale: Useful progressive exposure for hips, knees, ankles, trunk, and connective tissue, but high joint forces and technique sensitivity require appropriate loading and depth selection.

athletic_transfer.rationale: High transfer potential from loaded triple extension, ground force production, trunk stiffness, and evidence showing stronger jump transfer than 45 degree leg press training.

control.rationale: High Motor Control demand from free bar path, bracing, depth, balance, knee tracking, hip motion, and maintaining the center of mass over the feet.

fatigue_efficiency.rationale: Excellent global stimulus but low isolation efficiency because heavy loading creates large systemic, spinal, bracing, and warm-up costs.

setup.rationale: Requires a rack, bar, plates, safeties or spotter judgment, space, warm-up sets, and repeatable rack height.

ease.rationale: Demanding to learn and repeat well because stance, depth, bracing, bar position, ankle mobility, hip motion, and bar path all matter.

progression.rationale: Load and reps are highly trackable with precise barbell increments, with deductions because depth and technique consistency affect comparability.

support.rationale: The rack only supports setup and rerack; during the lift the lifter stabilizes the bar, trunk, hips, knees, ankles, and balance.

primary.name: Quadriceps
primary.evidenceShort: Direct squat EMG and biomechanics support high knee-extensor demand.
primary.evidence: Back squat studies consistently measure substantial vastus lateralis, vastus medialis, and rectus femoris involvement, while biomechanical comparisons show large knee-extensor moments that increase with load and depth.

primary.name: Gluteus maximus
primary.evidenceShort: Depth-sensitive hip-extension target in back squats.
primary.evidence: Back squat EMG and modeling evidence show meaningful gluteus maximus involvement, with gluteal contribution increasing as squat depth and hip-extension demand increase.

secondary.name: Hamstrings
secondary.evidenceShort: Measured posterior-chain assistant, not the dominant squat target.
secondary.evidence: Back squat studies measure biceps femoris and semitendinosus activity, including greater semitendinosus activity than front squats in one maximal-load comparison, but hamstrings remain secondary because knee and hip actions partly oppose each other during squatting.

support.name: Trunk stabilizers
support.evidenceShort: Back squat trunk activation is load sensitive and higher than hack squat.
support.evidence: Back squat studies measure erector spinae and anterior trunk activation during squatting, and a back-versus-hack squat study showed higher trunk activation in the unsupported back squat despite lower absolute loads.

support.name: Gastrocnemius
support.evidenceShort: Ankle and knee support contributor during squat ascent.
support.evidence: Back squat EMG studies measure gastrocnemius activity and technique-sensitive changes, supporting a support role for ankle control and lower-limb coordination rather than a primary hypertrophy target.

evidence.verdict: Barbell back squat: quadriceps and gluteus maximus primary; hamstrings secondary; trunk stabilizers and gastrocnemius support.
evidence.clinicalShort: Surface EMG and inverse-dynamics estimates are condition-specific and do not directly measure hypertrophy, injury risk, or long-term programming value.
evidence.limitsShort: High-bar versus low-bar position, stance, depth, load, heel elevation, tempo, fatigue, mobility, and bracing strategy all change emphasis.
evidence.summary: The barbell back squat is classified as an unsupported free-weight lower-body compound lift. The evidence supports quadriceps and gluteus maximus as the main visible targets, hamstrings as meaningful secondary contributors, and trunk stabilizers plus gastrocnemius as support muscles for posture, bracing, ankle control, and force transfer.
evidence.clinicalInterpretation: EMG amplitude helps identify acute excitation in measured superficial muscles, while biomechanics studies estimate joint moments and relative effort from model assumptions. These sources support muscle roles but should not be read as direct hypertrophy rankings or injury predictions.
evidence.limitations: This entry covers a generic back squat rather than a separate high-bar, low-bar, powerlifting, Olympic-style, box, pause, or heel-elevated variant. The local anatomy registry does not currently include an adductor magnus or broad adductor-group mesh, so no visible adductor role was added despite evidence that deep squats can load hip adductors.

studies.type: Back versus front squat biomechanics and EMG
studies.finding: Back and front squats produced similar overall muscle recruitment, while back squats produced higher knee compressive forces and knee extensor moments.
studies.citation: Gullett JC, Tillman MD, Gutierrez GM, Chow JW. A biomechanical comparison of back and front squats in healthy trained individuals. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2009;23(1):284-292. doi:10.1519/JSC.0b013e31818546bb.
studies.relevance: Direct free-weight back and front squat comparison with force, motion, and surface EMG data in trained participants.

studies.type: Maximal front and back squat EMG and kinematics
studies.shortCitation: Yavuz et al., J Sports Sci, 2015
studies.finding: Back squats used more trunk lean and greater semitendinosus activity than front squats, while front squats showed greater vastus medialis activity.
studies.citation: Yavuz HU, Erdag D, Amca AM, Aritan S. Kinematic and EMG activities during front and back squat variations in maximum loads. Journal of Sports Sciences. 2015;33(10):1058-1066. doi:10.1080/02640414.2014.984240.
studies.relevance: Direct maximal-load front/back squat comparison measuring vasti, rectus femoris, semitendinosus, biceps femoris, gluteus maximus, and erector spinae.

studies.type: Back squat depth EMG
studies.finding: Gluteus maximus contribution increased from partial to parallel and full-depth back squats, while vasti and biceps femoris contributions did not change significantly across depths.
studies.citation: Caterisano A, Moss RF, Pellinger TK, Woodruff K, Lewis VC, Booth W, Khadra T. The effect of back squat depth on the EMG activity of 4 superficial hip and thigh muscles. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2002;16(3):428-432.
studies.relevance: Direct back squat depth study measuring vastus medialis, vastus lateralis, biceps femoris, and gluteus maximus in experienced lifters.

studies.type: Squat depth and load biomechanics
studies.finding: Relative muscular effort in squatting changed with depth and barbell load across hip, knee, and ankle extensors.
studies.citation: Bryanton MA, Kennedy MD, Carey JP, Chiu LZF. Effect of Squat Depth and Barbell Load on Relative Muscular Effort in Squatting. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2012;26(10):2820-2828. doi:10.1519/JSC.0b013e31826791a7.
studies.relevance: Biomechanics source for how depth and load alter knee, hip, and ankle extensor demands in back squatting.

studies.type: Parallel, full, and front squat EMG
studies.shortCitation: Contreras et al., J Appl Biomech, 2016
studies.finding: Parallel, full, and front squat variations measured gluteus maximus, biceps femoris, and vastus lateralis EMG amplitudes.
studies.citation: Contreras B, Vigotsky AD, Schoenfeld BJ, Beardsley C, McMaster DT, Reyneke JHT, Cronin JB. A Comparison of Gluteus Maximus, Biceps Femoris, and Vastus Lateralis Electromyography Amplitude in Parallel, Full, and Front Squat Variations in Resistance-Trained Females. Journal of Applied Biomechanics. 2016;32(1):16-22. doi:10.1123/jab.2015-0113.
studies.relevance: Direct squat-variation EMG source for gluteus maximus, biceps femoris, and vastus lateralis in trained participants.

studies.type: Back squat lower-body and trunk EMG
studies.finding: Back squats showed greater posterior trunk and lower-body muscle activity than overhead squats during the concentric phase, with lateral gastrocnemius measured.
studies.citation: Aspe RR, Swinton PA. Electromyographic and kinetic comparison of the back squat and overhead squat. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2014;28(10):2827-2836. doi:10.1519/JSC.0000000000000462.
studies.relevance: Direct loaded back squat EMG and kinetic source measuring lower-body muscles and trunk musculature.

studies.type: Squat and leg press biomechanics and EMG
studies.finding: Squats produced greater quadriceps and hamstrings activity than high- and low-foot leg press variants; technique changed gastrocnemius activity and knee forces.
studies.citation: Escamilla RF, Fleisig GS, Zheng N, Lander JE, Barrentine SW, Andrews JR, Bergemann BW, Moorman CT 3rd. Effects of technique variations on knee biomechanics during the squat and leg press. Medicine and Science in Sports and Exercise. 2001;33(9):1552-1566. doi:10.1097/00005768-200109000-00020.
studies.relevance: Direct squat and leg press comparison for lower-body muscle activity, knee loading, stance width, and foot placement effects.

studies.type: Back versus hack squat trunk EMG
studies.finding: Back squats produced higher trunk muscle activation than hack squats at matched relative loads.
studies.citation: Clark DR, Lambert MI, Hunter AM. Trunk Muscle Activation in the Back and Hack Squat at the Same Relative Loads. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2019;33 Suppl 1:S60-S69. doi:10.1519/JSC.0000000000002144.
studies.relevance: Direct source for trunk stabilization differences between unsupported back squat and supported hack squat.

studies.type: Back squat versus 45 degree leg press training transfer
studies.finding: Eight weeks of parallel squat training improved jump outcomes more than 45 degree leg press training.
studies.citation: Wirth K, Hartmann H, Sander A, Mickel C, Szilvas E, Keiner M. The Impact of Back Squat and Leg-Press Exercises on Maximal Strength and Speed-Strength Parameters. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2016;30(5):1205-1212. doi:10.1519/JSC.0000000000001228.
studies.relevance: Training-transfer source comparing back squat and 45 degree leg press effects on maximal and speed-strength outcomes.

movements.name: Barbell Front Squat
movements.variant: Free-weight bilateral front squat with the bar supported across the anterior shoulders; treated separately from back squat, goblet squat, zercher squat, Smith machine, and machine hack squat variants.
movements.description: Support the bar across the front of the shoulders with elbows lifted, brace the trunk, and stand with the feet rooted. Descend by bending the knees, hips, and ankles while keeping the torso tall and the bar over the midfoot, then drive up from the bottom without letting the elbows drop or the knees collapse inward.

hypertrophy.rationale: Strong quad-biased squat stimulus with meaningful glute loading, but front-rack position and breathing can limit load and volume before target muscles fail.

strength.rationale: Major lower-body strength movement, though absolute loading is usually lower and more position-limited than the back squat.

joint_resilience.rationale: Useful controlled knee, hip, ankle, and trunk exposure, with evidence suggesting lower knee compressive forces than back squats under tested conditions; wrist, shoulder, and thoracic mobility can be limiting.

athletic_transfer.rationale: High transfer potential from upright loaded squatting, bracing, clean-receiving carryover, and ground force production, with less maximal loading than back squat.

control.rationale: High Motor Control demand from front-rack position, upright torso, bar-over-midfoot control, depth, bracing, and knee tracking.

fatigue_efficiency.rationale: Strong lower-body stimulus, but front-rack breathing, trunk bracing, mobility limits, and systemic fatigue reduce local stimulus efficiency.

setup.rationale: Requires a rack, bar, plates, safeties or spotter judgment, and a repeatable front-rack setup.

ease.rationale: Harder to learn than many lower-body options because front-rack mobility, elbow position, upright torso, depth, and bracing all constrain execution.

progression.rationale: Barbell increments make load progression clear, but front-rack tolerance, thoracic position, and depth consistency can limit clean tracking.

support.rationale: Very little external support during the lift; the bar position increases self-stabilization demands through the torso and upper back.

primary.name: Quadriceps
primary.evidenceShort: Front squat EMG supports high knee-extensor involvement.
primary.evidence: Front/back squat comparisons show front squats maintain comparable overall recruitment to back squats and can produce higher vastus medialis activity, supporting quadriceps as the primary visible target.

secondary.name: Gluteus maximus
secondary.evidenceShort: Measured hip-extension contributor, but less front-squat dominant than quads.
secondary.evidence: Front squat studies measure gluteus maximus activity during loaded squatting, but the upright torso and front-loaded position make it a meaningful secondary role rather than the main generic target.

secondary.name: Hamstrings
secondary.evidenceShort: Measured assistant with less emphasis than back squat in maximal-load data.
secondary.evidence: Front/back squat EMG data measure biceps femoris and semitendinosus; semitendinosus activity was greater in the back squat in one maximal-load comparison, so hamstrings are secondary in the front squat.

support.name: Trunk stabilizers
support.evidenceShort: Front rack and upright squatting require trunk support.
support.evidence: Front/back squat studies measured erector spinae and trunk-related demands; the front-rack position requires bracing and torso control even when lower-body EMG is comparable to back squat variants.

evidence.verdict: Barbell front squat: quadriceps primary; gluteus maximus and hamstrings secondary; trunk stabilizers support.
evidence.clinicalShort: Surface EMG is not a direct measure of hypertrophy, joint safety, or transfer; front-rack mobility and technique can dominate real-world execution.
evidence.limitsShort: Grip style, elbow position, depth, stance, heel elevation, load, tempo, torso angle, and mobility constraints change emphasis.
evidence.summary: The barbell front squat is classified as an unsupported anterior-loaded squat. Current evidence supports a quadriceps-primary classification, with gluteus maximus and hamstrings as secondary contributors and trunk stabilizers as support for bracing and maintaining the upright front-rack posture.
evidence.clinicalInterpretation: EMG comparisons across squat variants are useful for identifying measured muscle excitation, but differences are sensitive to load prescription, normalization, squat depth, and participant skill. Kinetic findings should be interpreted as condition-specific joint loading rather than a universal claim that one squat is always safer.
evidence.limitations: This entry assumes a conventional barbell front squat and does not split clean grip versus cross-arm, heel-elevated, pause, Olympic-style, or maximal powerlifting-style variants. No separate visible upper-back or adductor role was added because the current evidence and local anatomy registry did not support a precise, useful app classification for those names.

studies.type: Back versus front squat biomechanics and EMG
studies.finding: Front squats were comparable to back squats in overall muscle recruitment and produced lower knee compressive forces and extensor moments under the tested conditions.
studies.citation: Gullett JC, Tillman MD, Gutierrez GM, Chow JW. A biomechanical comparison of back and front squats in healthy trained individuals. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2009;23(1):284-292. doi:10.1519/JSC.0b013e31818546bb.
studies.relevance: Direct front/back squat comparison with kinetics and muscle activity in trained participants.

studies.type: Maximal front and back squat EMG and kinematics
studies.shortCitation: Yavuz et al., J Sports Sci, 2015
studies.finding: Front squats showed greater vastus medialis activity, while back squats showed greater semitendinosus activity and more trunk lean.
studies.citation: Yavuz HU, Erdag D, Amca AM, Aritan S. Kinematic and EMG activities during front and back squat variations in maximum loads. Journal of Sports Sciences. 2015;33(10):1058-1066. doi:10.1080/02640414.2014.984240.
studies.relevance: Direct maximal-load front/back squat EMG source measuring quadriceps, hamstrings, gluteus maximus, and erector spinae.

studies.type: Squat variation EMG
studies.finding: Front, hack, and other squat variations were compared with EMG signals from thigh, hip, and trunk muscles.
studies.citation: Erdag D, Yavuz HU. Evaluation of Muscle Activities During Different Squat Variations Using Electromyography Signals. In: Ahram T, Karwowski W, Pickl S, Taiar R, editors. Human Systems Engineering and Design II. Advances in Intelligent Systems and Computing. 2019;1026:859-865. doi:10.1007/978-3-030-35249-3_114.
studies.relevance: Close direct squat-variant EMG source that includes front squat and hack squat patterns.

studies.type: Parallel, full, and front squat EMG
studies.shortCitation: Contreras et al., J Appl Biomech, 2016
studies.finding: Parallel, full, and front squat variations measured gluteus maximus, biceps femoris, and vastus lateralis EMG amplitudes.
studies.citation: Contreras B, Vigotsky AD, Schoenfeld BJ, Beardsley C, McMaster DT, Reyneke JHT, Cronin JB. A Comparison of Gluteus Maximus, Biceps Femoris, and Vastus Lateralis Electromyography Amplitude in Parallel, Full, and Front Squat Variations in Resistance-Trained Females. Journal of Applied Biomechanics. 2016;32(1):16-22. doi:10.1123/jab.2015-0113.
studies.relevance: Direct front squat variation EMG source for quadriceps, gluteus maximus, and biceps femoris.

movements.name: Barbell Hip Thrust
movements.variant: Free-weight hip thrust with the upper back on a bench and a loaded barbell across the hips.
movements.description: Sit with the upper back against a stable bench, roll a padded bar over the hips, plant the feet about shoulder-width with the shins near vertical at the top, brace the trunk, drive the hips upward until the torso and thighs are roughly in line, then lower under control without letting the ribs flare or the pelvis dump forward.

hypertrophy.rationale: Excellent glute hypertrophy tool because the external load is applied directly across hip extension and the evidence consistently shows high gluteus maximus activation.

strength.rationale: Strong hip-extension loading option, but the bar position, bench support, and shorter knee contribution make it less globally strength-representative than squats or deadlifts.

joint_resilience.rationale: Useful loaded hip-extension exposure with relatively low knee demand, but it is not a broad lower-body joint-capacity exercise.

athletic_transfer.rationale: Has plausible transfer to horizontal hip-extension tasks, but the supported supine posture limits direct carryover compared with upright, unilateral, or locomotor patterns.

control.rationale: Requires pelvic and trunk control, but balance and path demands are low because the upper back and feet create a stable base.

fatigue_efficiency.rationale: High local glute stimulus for moderate systemic cost, with some efficiency lost to bar setup, abdominal pressure, and heavy loading discomfort.

setup.rationale: Requires a bench, bar, plates, hip pad, floor space, and setup time to get the bar into position.

ease.rationale: Simple conceptually, but bench height, foot distance, pelvic position, rib control, and bar comfort make consistent execution moderately difficult.

progression.rationale: Load and reps are very trackable once setup is standardized, and the barbell allows small progressive jumps.

support.rationale: The bench supports the torso, but the user still controls bar position, pelvis, foot pressure, and trunk stiffness.

primary.name: Gluteus maximus
primary.evidenceShort: Hip-thrust EMG consistently places gluteus maximus as the dominant target.
primary.evidence: Barbell hip-thrust EMG and systematic review evidence support gluteus maximus as the primary hip-extension target, with greater or high activation versus common comparison exercises in multiple tested conditions.

secondary.name: Hamstrings
secondary.evidenceShort: Biceps femoris and hamstrings are repeatedly measured during hip thrusts.
secondary.evidence: Direct hip-thrust studies measure biceps femoris or broader hamstring activation. The role is meaningful but secondary because the movement is most consistently gluteus-maximus dominant.

support.name: Gluteus medius
support.evidenceShort: Measured as a stabilizing gluteal contributor in hip-thrust research.
support.evidence: Hip-thrust review evidence includes gluteus medius among muscles evaluated. It is classified as support because the standard bilateral barbell setup mainly demands sagittal-plane hip extension rather than frontal-plane hip control.

support.name: Quadriceps
support.evidenceShort: Vastus lateralis is measured, but knee-extension demand is limited.
support.evidence: Hip-thrust EMG and biomechanics studies include vastus lateralis or knee-extensor demand, but the movement remains hip-extension biased, so quadriceps are listed as support rather than a primary target.

evidence.verdict: Barbell hip thrust: gluteus maximus primary; hamstrings secondary; gluteus medius and quadriceps support.
evidence.clinicalShort: EMG estimates acute excitation; biomechanics estimate joint demand. Neither directly guarantees hypertrophy, injury risk, or individual progression.
evidence.limitsShort: Bench height, foot distance, pelvic tilt, bar position, range of motion, load, and pause style materially change emphasis.
evidence.summary: The barbell hip thrust is classified as a free-weight lower-body hip-extension movement. The evidence base supports a gluteus-maximus-dominant profile with meaningful hamstring contribution plus visible gluteus medius and quadriceps support demands.
evidence.clinicalInterpretation: Surface electromyography should be interpreted alongside joint action, external load, range of motion, and technique. The classification here treats the standard barbell hip thrust as a loaded bilateral exercise, not a bodyweight bridge or single-leg variation.
evidence.limitations: Machine, banded, American, single-leg, bodyweight bridge, and elevated-foot variants should be separate entries if the app needs variant-specific scoring. Trunk and lumbopelvic stabilization are acknowledged in the evidence but are not shown as a separate visible muscle-map target for this entry.

studies.type: Barbell hip thrust versus back squat EMG
studies.shortCitation: Contreras et al., J Appl Biomech, 2015
studies.finding: The barbell hip thrust produced greater upper/lower gluteus maximus and biceps femoris activity than the back squat in the tested condition, while vastus lateralis favored the squat.
studies.citation: Contreras B, Vigotsky AD, Schoenfeld BJ, Beardsley C, Cronin J. A Comparison of Gluteus Maximus, Biceps Femoris, and Vastus Lateralis Electromyographic Activity in the Back Squat and Barbell Hip Thrust Exercises. Journal of Applied Biomechanics. 2015;31(6):452-458. doi:10.1123/jab.2014-0301.
studies.relevance: Direct barbell hip-thrust EMG source for gluteus maximus, biceps femoris, and vastus lateralis roles.

studies.type: Barbell hip thrust systematic review
studies.finding: The review concluded that hip-thrust mechanics favor hip-extensor activation, with an excitation sequence led by gluteus maximus followed by erector spinae, hamstrings, and quadriceps femoris.
studies.citation: Krause Neto W, Vieira TL, Gama EF. Barbell Hip Thrust, Muscular Activation and Performance: A Systematic Review. Journal of Sports Science and Medicine. 2019;18(2):198-206.
studies.relevance: Synthesis source for overall muscle-role hierarchy and performance-transfer limits.

studies.type: Barbell hip thrust biomechanics
studies.finding: Biomechanical analysis of trained lifters at 70% 1RM characterized hip and knee extensor demand across the barbell hip thrust.
studies.citation: Brazil A, Needham L, Palmer JL, Bezodis IN. A comprehensive biomechanical analysis of the barbell hip thrust. PLOS ONE. 2021;16(3):e0249307. doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0249307.
studies.relevance: Direct biomechanical source for hip-extension loading, progression, and quadriceps support interpretation.

studies.type: Sprint-athlete hip thrust kinetics
studies.finding: In sprinters, barbell hip thrust produced large lumbosacral and hip extension moments compared with back squat and deadlift conditions.
studies.citation: Otsuka M, Honjo T, Nagano A, Isaka T. Kinetics in lumbosacral and lower-limb joints of sprinters during barbell hip thrust compared to deadlift and back squat. PLOS ONE. 2021;16(7):e0251418. doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0251418.
studies.relevance: Biomechanical source for lumbopelvic and hip-extension demand in trained sprinters.

studies.type: Machine versus barbell hip thrust EMG
studies.finding: Machine and free-weight hip thrusts showed similar gluteus maximus mean activation; the machine showed greater biceps femoris mean activation and lower vastus lateralis mean activation.
studies.citation: Petrizzo J, Lopez J, Gaeta A, Aquino M, Otto R, Wygand J. Machine Vs. Barbell Hip Thrust: Electromyographic, Biomechanical, And Ease Of Use Comparison: 2266. Medicine and Science in Sports and Exercise. 2023;55(9S):749. doi:10.1249/01.mss.0000986876.72568.fb.
studies.relevance: Direct comparison source for free-weight versus machine hip thrust muscle activation and ease-of-use scoring.

studies.type: Hip thrust and RFESS EMG
studies.finding: In trained females, hip thrust and rear-foot-elevated split squat conditions measured hip and knee extensor activation including gluteus maximus and hamstrings.
studies.citation: McCurdy K, Walker J, Kelly C, Polinski M. Hip and Knee Extensor Activation During the Hip Thrust and Rear-Foot-Elevated Split Squat in Trained Females. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2021;35(5):1201-1207. doi:10.1519/JSC.0000000000004035.
studies.relevance: Direct hip-thrust movement-family EMG source in trained women.

movements.name: Barbell Romanian Deadlift
movements.variant: Free-weight barbell Romanian deadlift started from standing, using a hip hinge with soft knees and the bar kept close to the legs.
movements.description: Stand tall with a loaded barbell in the hands, feet about hip width, knees softly unlocked, lats set, and ribs stacked over the pelvis. Push the hips back while keeping the bar close to the thighs and shins, lower until the hamstrings limit the hinge without rounding the back, then drive the hips forward to stand tall under control.

hypertrophy.rationale: High posterior-chain hypertrophy signal, especially for hamstrings and gluteus maximus, with useful loaded lengthened-position exposure.

strength.rationale: Strong hip-hinge loading option, though peak whole-body force and floor-start specificity are lower than a conventional deadlift.

joint_resilience.rationale: Provides controlled hamstring, hip, and trunk loading through a long range, but heavy hinges can be sensitive to lumbar position and hamstring tolerance.

athletic_transfer.rationale: Useful hinge and posterior-chain capacity can carry over to sprinting, jumping, and lifting tasks, but the movement is still bilateral and constrained.

control.rationale: Requires meaningful hip-hinge control, bracing, bar proximity, and hamstring-range awareness without a guided path.

fatigue_efficiency.rationale: Good local posterior-chain stimulus, but grip, spinal erector demand, and systemic fatigue reduce efficiency compared with more supported hamstring options.

setup.rationale: Requires a bar, plates, space, and warm-up sets, but the lift starts from standing and does not need a rack setup.

ease.rationale: The pattern is simple once learned, but many users need coaching to keep a true hinge, neutral trunk, close bar path, and appropriate knee bend.

progression.rationale: Barbell loading is trackable and granular, with small deductions because range of motion and hinge depth can drift as load increases.

support.rationale: The user controls the entire free-weight path, trunk position, grip, and balance with no external body support.

primary.name: Hamstrings
primary.evidenceShort: Direct RDL EMG supports high biceps femoris and semitendinosus demand.
primary.evidence: Direct Romanian deadlift studies measured biceps femoris and semitendinosus activity during loaded hinges, and the deadlift systematic review reports that the Romanian deadlift emphasizes hamstring activation relative to the erector spinae.

primary.name: Gluteus maximus
primary.evidenceShort: Hip-extension EMG shows substantial gluteus maximus involvement.
primary.evidence: Romanian deadlift studies directly measure gluteus maximus during heavy hip hinges. It is listed as primary because the standard barbell Romanian deadlift trains loaded hip extension alongside the hamstrings.

secondary.name: Erector spinae
secondary.evidenceShort: Measured trunk-extensor demand, but less target-dominant than hamstrings in RDL evidence.
secondary.evidence: Romanian deadlift EMG studies measure erector spinae activity, and back-extension comparison data show similar erector spinae activation across hip-extension exercises. It is classified as secondary because the RDL card is primarily a hip-hinge posterior-thigh and glute movement, not a lower-back isolation exercise.

support.name: Latissimus dorsi
support.evidenceShort: Measured in RDL variation research as part of free-bar stabilization.
support.evidence: RDL variation research measured latissimus dorsi along with posterior-chain muscles. For the standard barbell RDL, it is included as bar-path and shoulder-extension support rather than a primary pulling target.

support.name: Trapezius
support.evidenceShort: Measured upper-back stabilizer demand in RDL variation research.
support.evidence: RDL variation research measured middle trapezius while comparing traditional and landmine Romanian deadlifts. The role is classified as support because it helps maintain shoulder girdle and bar position during the hinge.

support.name: Gluteus medius
support.evidenceShort: Measured gluteal stabilizer during RDL variants.
support.evidence: Direct Romanian deadlift EMG measured gluteus medius along with gluteus maximus and hamstring muscles. It is included as hip-pelvis support in the bilateral hinge, not as the main target.

evidence.verdict: Barbell Romanian deadlift: hamstrings and gluteus maximus primary; erector spinae secondary; latissimus dorsi, trapezius, and gluteus medius support.
evidence.clinicalShort: EMG estimates acute excitation, not hypertrophy, mechanical tension, adaptation, pain risk, or injury probability.
evidence.limitsShort: Knee bend, bar distance, hip range, load, tempo, straps, fatigue, and whether the lifter starts from the floor or standing can shift muscle emphasis.
evidence.summary: The barbell Romanian deadlift is classified as a free-weight hip-hinge exercise. Direct EMG evidence supports hamstrings and gluteus maximus as the primary posterior-chain targets, with meaningful erector spinae demand for trunk position. Upper-back and hip-pelvis stabilizers are included only where they have direct RDL-family measurement support.
evidence.clinicalInterpretation: Surface electromyography should be interpreted as condition-specific muscle excitation. The ratings combine direct RDL studies, deadlift-family review evidence, and explicit judgment about loadability, setup, fatigue, and skill demand.
evidence.limitations: The app entry assumes a standard standing barbell RDL rather than a deficit RDL, stiff-leg deadlift, single-leg RDL, landmine RDL, dumbbell RDL, or floor-start deadlift. Surface EMG cannot resolve every hamstring head equally and does not directly measure long-term growth or tissue tolerance.

studies.type: Romanian deadlift variation EMG study
studies.finding: Competitive bodybuilders performed Romanian, step-Romanian, and stiff-leg deadlifts at 80% 1RM while gluteus maximus, gluteus medius, biceps femoris, semitendinosus, and erector spinae regions were measured.
studies.citation: Coratella G, Tornatore G, Longo S, Esposito F, Ce E. An Electromyographic Analysis of Romanian, Step-Romanian, and Stiff-Leg Deadlift: Implication for Resistance Training. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. 2022;19(3):1903. doi:10.3390/ijerph19031903.
studies.relevance: Direct barbell Romanian deadlift and close-variant EMG source for hamstrings, gluteus maximus, gluteus medius, and erector spinae.

studies.type: Conventional versus Romanian deadlift EMG and kinetics study
studies.shortCitation: Lee et al., J Exerc Sci Fit, 2018
studies.finding: Compared conventional and Romanian deadlifts using electromyographic and kinetic measures, supporting variant-specific interpretation of hamstring, gluteal, erector, and quadriceps demand.
studies.citation: Lee S, Schultz J, Timgren J, Staelgraeve K, Miller M, Liu Y. An electromyographic and kinetic comparison of conventional and Romanian deadlifts. Journal of Exercise Science & Fitness. 2018;16(3):87-93. doi:10.1016/j.jesf.2018.08.001.
studies.relevance: Directly compares the assigned Romanian deadlift with the conventional deadlift and informs the different muscle-role and rating profiles.

studies.type: Deadlift EMG systematic review
studies.finding: The review reported that Romanian deadlift evidence is associated with lower erector spinae activation than biceps femoris and semitendinosus, and that hamstring activation patterns vary across deadlift variants.
studies.citation: Martin-Fuentes I, Oliva-Lozano JM, Muyor JM. Electromyographic activity in deadlift exercise and its variants. A systematic review. PLOS ONE. 2020;15(2):e0229507. doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0229507.
studies.relevance: Systematic review context for deadlift-family EMG and the Romanian deadlift hamstring-versus-erector interpretation.

studies.type: Hip-extension exercise EMG comparison
studies.finding: In resistance-trained women, Romanian deadlift and 45-degree Roman chair back extension produced greater gluteus maximus activity than seated machine back extension; Romanian deadlift also exceeded seated machine back extension for biceps femoris.
studies.citation: Andersen V, Pedersen H, Fimland MS, Shaw M, Solstad TEJ, Stien N, Cumming KT, Saeterbakken AH. Comparison of Muscle Activity in Three Single-Joint, Hip Extension Exercises in Resistance-Trained Women. Journal of Sports Science and Medicine. 2021;20(2):181-187. doi:10.52082/jssm.2021.181.
studies.relevance: Directly includes the Romanian deadlift and compares gluteus maximus, biceps femoris, and erector spinae activation against close hip-extension exercises.

studies.type: Traditional versus landmine Romanian deadlift EMG study
studies.finding: Traditional and landmine Romanian deadlifts were compared at 8RM with EMG from middle trapezius, latissimus dorsi, erector spinae, gluteus maximus, and biceps femoris.
studies.citation: McCurdy KW, Koldenhoven RM. Comparison of Muscle Activation and Range of Motion between the Traditional and Landmine Romanian Deadlift. International Journal of Strength and Conditioning. 2025;5(1). doi:10.47206/ijsc.v5i1.370.
studies.relevance: Direct RDL-family evidence for upper-back and latissimus support roles plus gluteus maximus, biceps femoris, and erector spinae interpretation.

movements.name: Bicycle Crunch
movements.variant: Bodyweight floor bicycle crunch alternating trunk flexion and rotation toward the opposite knee with a cycling leg action.
movements.description: Lie on the floor with the hands lightly behind the head, lift the shoulders, and bring one knee toward the opposite elbow while the other leg extends. Alternate sides in a controlled rhythm, rotating from the ribs instead of pulling the neck, and keep the low back from arching as the legs switch.

hypertrophy.rationale: High abdominal EMG signal for a floor drill, but loading is bodyweight and hard to overload precisely.

strength.rationale: Low strength signal because the exercise is mostly bodyweight trunk flexion and rotation.

joint_resilience.rationale: Low resilience value because repeated spinal flexion and rotation are not broadly useful as a joint-loading anchor.

athletic_transfer.rationale: Some transfer to coordinated trunk rotation and limb timing, but no standing, loaded, or sport-specific force transfer.

control.rationale: Requires alternating trunk rotation, hip flexion, breathing, and low-back position control.

fatigue_efficiency.rationale: Low setup and low systemic fatigue with a strong local abdominal burn, though technique often degrades with speed.

setup.rationale: Requires only floor space.

ease.rationale: Easy to recognize but harder to repeat cleanly without neck pulling, rushing, or losing lumbar control.

progression.rationale: Progression is mostly reps and tempo; meaningful external loading is awkward.

support.rationale: The floor supports the body, though the alternating limbs require more self-control than a basic crunch.

primary.name: Rectus abdominis
primary.evidenceShort: Exact bicycle-maneuver EMG ranked rectus activity high.
primary.evidence: The San Diego State/ACE abdominal EMG report ranked the bicycle maneuver highest for rectus abdominis activity among the tested exercises, and peer-reviewed crunch-family EMG supports rectus abdominis involvement during floor trunk-flexion tasks.

primary.name: External oblique
primary.evidenceShort: Exact bicycle-maneuver report supports high oblique activity.
primary.evidence: The bicycle crunch combines trunk flexion with rotation toward the opposite knee; the exact San Diego State/ACE report ranked the bicycle maneuver near the top for grouped oblique activity, and peer-reviewed abdominal EMG supports external oblique activation in related floor core tasks.

primary.name: Internal oblique
primary.evidenceShort: Oblique and rotation evidence support a primary role.
primary.evidence: The exact bicycle report groups obliques, and peer-reviewed abdominal exercise EMG measures internal oblique activity during crunch and side-bridge tasks; the alternating trunk-rotation demand supports internal oblique as a primary visible target.

secondary.name: Iliopsoas
secondary.evidenceShort: Alternating hip flexion makes hip flexors assist.
secondary.evidence: This is a movement-mechanics inference supported by leg-raise and hip-flexor EMG: each bicycle-crunch repetition flexes one hip while the other leg extends, so iliopsoas assists the cycling leg action without being the main target.

evidence.verdict: Bicycle crunch: rectus abdominis, external oblique, and internal oblique primary; iliopsoas secondary; no separate support muscles listed.
evidence.clinicalShort: EMG estimates acute excitation, not hypertrophy, mechanical tension, adaptation, or injury risk.
evidence.limitsShort: Speed, range, leg height, neck pulling, and lumbar position strongly change the stimulus and fatigue cost.
evidence.summary: The bicycle crunch is classified as a floor trunk-flexion and rotation exercise. The exact San Diego State/ACE report supports high rectus abdominis and grouped oblique activity for the bicycle maneuver, while peer-reviewed abdominal EMG supports rectus and oblique roles in crunch-family work. Iliopsoas is included as a secondary hip-flexion assistant because the alternating leg action repeatedly flexes the hip.
evidence.clinicalInterpretation: Controlled reps with the shoulder blades lifted and rotation from the trunk keep the exercise abdominal. Faster reps may raise fatigue and coordination demand but make the muscle stimulus less precise.
evidence.limitations: The exact bicycle-maneuver evidence is a university/ACE research report rather than a peer-reviewed journal article, so it is paired with peer-reviewed abdominal and hip-flexor EMG sources. The ACE report groups obliques rather than separating internal and external oblique. Rectus femoris and other hip flexors were not listed because the local anatomy map does not expose all of those muscles as separate visible labels and the app classification is clearer with iliopsoas as the mapped hip-flexor role.

studies.type: San Diego State/ACE abdominal EMG report
studies.finding: The bicycle maneuver ranked highest for rectus abdominis activity and second for grouped oblique activity in a 13-exercise EMG comparison.
studies.citation: Francis P, Davis J. New Study Puts the Crunch on Ineffective Ab Exercises. ACE FitnessMatters. May/June 2001. San Diego State University Biomechanics Lab and American Council on Exercise.
studies.relevance: Exact bicycle-crunch report for rectus abdominis and grouped oblique activation.

studies.type: Commercial and common abdominal exercise EMG
studies.finding: Common abdominal exercise EMG measured rectus abdominis plus external and internal oblique activity in crunch-family tasks.
studies.citation: Escamilla RF, McTaggart MSC, Fricklas EJ, et al. An electromyographic analysis of commercial and common abdominal exercises: implications for rehabilitation and training. Journal of Orthopaedic and Sports Physical Therapy. 2006;36(2):45-57. doi:10.2519/jospt.2006.36.2.45.
studies.relevance: Peer-reviewed abdominal EMG support for rectus and oblique activation in related floor trunk-flexion tasks.

studies.type: Crunch and side-bridge abdominal EMG
studies.finding: Compared abdominal crunch, supine double leg thrust, side bridge, and Ab-Slide using rectus abdominis, external oblique, internal oblique, and rectus femoris EMG.
studies.citation: Youdas JW, Guck BR, Hebrink RC, Rugotzke JD, Madson TJ, Hollman JH. An electromyographic analysis of the Ab-Slide exercise, abdominal crunch, supine double leg thrust, and side bridge in healthy young adults. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2008;22(6):1939-1946. doi:10.1519/JSC.0b013e31818745bf.
studies.relevance: Close floor-core EMG source supporting rectus abdominis and oblique roles.

studies.type: Sit-up and leg-raise abdominal/lower-limb EMG
studies.shortCitation: Lee et al., J Phys Ther Sci, 2016
studies.finding: Compared abdominal and lower-limb muscle activity during sit-up and leg-raise tasks.
studies.citation: Lee DK, Kang MH, Lee TS, Oh JS. Comparison of muscular activities in the abdomen and lower limbs while performing sit-up and leg-raise. Journal of Physical Therapy Science. 2016;28(2):491-494. doi:10.1589/jpts.28.491.
studies.relevance: Close leg-raise source supporting hip-flexion assistance in the alternating leg action.

studies.type: Hip flexor EMG
studies.shortCitation: Czuppon et al., J Clin Med, 2024
studies.finding: Measured hip-flexor muscle activation during common rehabilitation and strength exercises.
studies.citation: Czuppon S, et al. Hip Flexor Muscle Activation During Common Rehabilitation and Strength Exercises. Journal of Clinical Medicine. 2024;13(21):6617. doi:10.3390/jcm13216617.
studies.relevance: Supports iliopsoas as the mapped hip-flexor assistant during repeated hip flexion.

movements.name: Box Jump
movements.variant: Standing two-leg box jump using a countermovement takeoff and controlled landing on a stable box.
movements.description: Stand facing a stable box with feet about hip to shoulder width, dip into a quick countermovement, swing the arms, and jump up by extending the hips, knees, and ankles together. Land quietly on the box with bent knees and hips, stand under control if needed, then step down before the next rep.

hypertrophy.rationale: Plyometric contacts are high intent but too brief and hard to progressively tension for meaningful hypertrophy compared with resistance exercises.

strength.rationale: Can support rate-of-force expression, but unloaded box jumps do not provide high-force progressive overload for maximal strength.

joint_resilience.rationale: Can build landing and tendon tolerance when dosed well, but poor box choice, fatigue, or uncontrolled landings quickly raise joint stress.

athletic_transfer.rationale: Excellent transfer signal for lower-body power, coordinated triple extension, landing control, and explosive intent.

control.rationale: Requires timing, arm swing coordination, takeoff stiffness, landing mechanics, and repeatable foot placement.

fatigue_efficiency.rationale: Low-rep jumps provide useful power practice with modest metabolic cost, but quality drops quickly when fatigue accumulates.

setup.rationale: Needs a stable box and clear landing area, but no loading changes or rack setup.

ease.rationale: Simple to understand but not easy for all users because jump confidence, landing depth, shin clearance, and step-down control matter.

progression.rationale: Progression by box height is noisy because higher boxes can reward hip-flexion clearance instead of more propulsive output.

support.rationale: The movement is unsupported in takeoff and landing, aside from the box as a landing target.

primary.name: Quadriceps
primary.evidenceShort: Plyometric EMG and jump biomechanics support high knee-extensor demand.
primary.evidence: Box-jump and jump-family studies measure quadriceps activity during plyometric jumping, and countermovement-jump biomechanics support a major knee-extension role in takeoff and landing control.

primary.name: Gluteus maximus
primary.evidenceShort: Jump takeoff requires forceful hip extension, supported by vertical-jump EMG.
primary.evidence: Exact box-jump performance studies emphasize propulsive output, while vertical-jump EMG and biomechanics support gluteus maximus as a major hip-extension contributor during takeoff and landing control.

primary.name: Gastrocnemius
primary.evidenceShort: Direct plyometric EMG measured gastrocnemius during box-jump style tasks.
primary.evidence: Plyometric intensity research measured gastrocnemius along with quadriceps and hamstrings across jump exercises, including box jumps. Ankle plantar-flexion demand is also consistent with countermovement-jump biomechanics.

secondary.name: Hamstrings
secondary.evidenceShort: Measured jump contributor with hip-extension and landing-control demand.
secondary.evidence: Plyometric and vertical-jump EMG studies measure hamstrings during jump takeoff or landing tasks. They are classified as secondary because quadriceps, gluteus maximus, and gastrocnemius better represent the primary propulsive profile.

evidence.verdict: Box jump: quadriceps, gluteus maximus, and gastrocnemius primary; hamstrings secondary; no visible support muscles added.
evidence.clinicalShort: EMG and force-plate data estimate acute jump demand, not hypertrophy or a guarantee of safe landing mechanics.
evidence.limitsShort: Box height, approach stance, arm swing, depth of countermovement, intent, landing depth, fatigue, and step-down method all change the training signal.
evidence.summary: The box jump is classified as an unloaded bilateral plyometric jump. Exact box-jump EMG and performance studies support a lower-body power profile, and jump-family biomechanics support the visible quadriceps, gluteus maximus, gastrocnemius, and hamstring map. Progression is scored low because box height does not cleanly equal increased propulsive output.
evidence.clinicalInterpretation: Box-jump value comes primarily from explosive intent, takeoff coordination, and landing quality rather than from high external load. Ratings should be interpreted as a power and motor-control tool, not a hypertrophy or maximal-strength anchor.
evidence.limitations: The evidence base combines exact box-jump studies with countermovement-jump and broader plyometric-jump evidence. The entry assumes a two-leg standing box jump with a controlled landing on the box and step-down return, not depth jumps, drop jumps, repeated hurdle hops, single-leg jumps, or weighted jumps.

studies.type: Plyometric exercise EMG study
studies.finding: Plyometric intensity was evaluated using EMG of the quadriceps, hamstrings, and gastrocnemius across multiple jump exercises including box jumps.
studies.citation: Ebben WP, Simenz C, Jensen RL. Evaluation of Plyometric Intensity Using Electromyography. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2008;22(3):861-868. doi:10.1519/JSC.0b013e31816a834b.
studies.relevance: Direct plyometric EMG source that includes box jumps and measures the quadriceps, hamstrings, and gastrocnemius groups available in the local anatomy map.

studies.type: Box-height performance study
studies.finding: Men and women performed maximal-effort box jumps at different relative box heights; box height generally did not change propulsive performance measures, supporting caution when using height as progression.
studies.citation: Dos Santos ML, Shields J, Berton R, Dinyer-McNeely T, Trevino M, Anderson O, Dawes JJ. Does Box Height Matter? A Comparative Analysis of Box Height on Box Jump Performance in Men and Women. International Journal of Exercise Science. 2024;17(1):720-729. doi:10.70252/MTLS9089.
studies.relevance: Exact box-jump source for box-height progression limits and power-performance interpretation.

studies.type: Box-height performance study
studies.finding: Elite female handball players showed similar key performance measures across low and high box jump heights, reinforcing that box height is not a pure overload measure.
studies.citation: Koefoed N, Dam S, Kersting UG. Effect of Box Height on Box Jump Performance in Elite Female Handball Players. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2022;36(2):508-512. doi:10.1519/JSC.0000000000003481.
studies.relevance: Exact box-jump performance source for progression and setup scoring in trained team-sport athletes.

studies.type: Countermovement and drop-jump biomechanics study
studies.shortCitation: Bobbert et al., Eur J Appl Physiol, 1986
studies.finding: Biomechanical analysis of countermovement and drop jumps supports coordinated lower-extremity extension and landing mechanics as the main jumping demand.
studies.citation: Bobbert MF, Mackay MT, Schinkelshoek D, Huijing PA, van Ingen Schenau GJ. Biomechanical analysis of drop and countermovement jumps. European Journal of Applied Physiology and Occupational Physiology. 1986;54(6):566-573. doi:10.1007/BF00943342.
studies.relevance: Jump-biomechanics support for lower-extremity extension and calf contribution when exact box-jump EMG is limited.

studies.type: Vertical-jump EMG and landing-force study
studies.finding: Double-leg vertical jump tasks measured lower-extremity muscle recruitment including gluteus maximus, quadriceps, and hamstrings across takeoff, contact, and landing phases.
studies.citation: Jankaew A, Jan YK, Hwang IS, Kuo LC, Lin CF. Hamstring Muscle Stiffness Affects Lower Extremity Muscle Recruitment and Landing Forces during Double-Legs Vertical Jump. Sports Biomechanics. 2025;24(4):1096-1114. doi:10.1080/14763141.2023.2219670.
studies.relevance: Close jump-family EMG source supporting gluteus maximus, quadriceps, and hamstring roles during takeoff and landing.

studies.type: Plyometric jump training EMG systematic review
studies.finding: The systematic review found plyometric jump training can improve muscle activation in strength and jumping tasks, while results vary across methods and outcomes.
studies.citation: Ramirez-Campillo R, Moran J, Chaabene H, Granacher U, Behm DG, Garcia-Hermoso A, Izquierdo M. Effects of Plyometric Jump Training on Electromyographic Activity and Its Relationship to Strength and Jump Performance in Healthy Trained and Untrained Populations: A Systematic Review of Randomized Controlled Trials. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2021;35(7):2053-2065. doi:10.1519/JSC.0000000000004056.
studies.relevance: Synthesis context for plyometric training adaptation and interpretation limits.

movements.name: Bulgarian Split Squat
movements.variant: Rear-foot-elevated split squat with the front leg doing most of the work; external load may be held at the sides but the movement is not machine-guided.
movements.description: Stand in a split stance with the rear foot elevated on a bench, keep most pressure through the front foot, lower under control until the front knee and hip are deeply flexed, then drive through the front foot to stand while keeping the knee tracking over the toes and the pelvis steady.

hypertrophy.rationale: Strong quad and glute stimulus through long range, but balance and discomfort can limit loading before target muscles are fully exhausted.

strength.rationale: Builds unilateral leg force well, but absolute loading and force expression are less clean than bilateral barbell or machine patterns.

joint_resilience.rationale: Useful knee, hip, ankle, and tendon tolerance stimulus through deep single-leg ranges when progressed gradually.

athletic_transfer.rationale: High carryover potential from unilateral support, hip-knee-ankle coordination, pelvic control, and force production from one leg.

control.rationale: High motor-control demand from front-foot balance, pelvis control, knee tracking, trunk position, and rear-foot constraint.

fatigue_efficiency.rationale: Good local stimulus, but balance, breathing, discomfort, and unilateral set volume create meaningful systemic and coordination fatigue.

setup.rationale: Requires a bench or platform, reproducible stance distance, and sometimes dumbbell setup; friction is moderate.

ease.rationale: Technically demanding because stance length, rear-foot height, depth, balance, pelvis position, and knee path are easy to vary.

progression.rationale: Progression is possible with reps and load, but measurement is noisy because stance length, depth, balance, and rear-foot placement change difficulty.

support.rationale: Very little external support; the bench constrains the rear foot but the working leg and trunk self-stabilize the movement.

primary.name: Quadriceps
primary.evidenceShort: RFESS EMG shows high vastus lateralis activity.
primary.evidence: Rear-foot-elevated split squat evidence reports substantial vastus lateralis activation, especially in the bottom portion of the repetition, supporting quadriceps as a primary target.

primary.name: Gluteus maximus
primary.evidenceShort: RFESS and Bulgarian squat studies measure meaningful gluteal activation.
primary.evidence: Rear-foot-elevated split squat and Bulgarian squat studies measure gluteus maximus activation and support a primary hip-extension role, with emphasis changing by depth and trunk position.

secondary.name: Hamstrings
secondary.evidenceShort: Measured posterior-chain assistant in RFESS.
secondary.evidence: RFESS evidence measured medial and lateral hamstring activation; the role is meaningful but secondary to the stronger knee-extension and hip-extension targets.

support.name: Gluteus medius
support.evidenceShort: Hip-abductor control demand in lunge/single-leg patterns.
support.evidence: Bulgarian squat and related single-leg/lunge EMG evidence supports gluteus medius involvement for frontal-plane hip and pelvic control.

support.name: Trunk stabilizers
support.evidenceShort: Trunk position changes lunge-family muscle activation.
support.evidence: Lunge-family evidence shows trunk position changes muscular activation; trunk stabilizers are listed as support because the unsupported split stance requires bracing and postural control.

evidence.verdict: Rear-foot-elevated split squat: quadriceps and gluteus maximus primary; hamstrings secondary; gluteus medius and trunk stabilizers support.
evidence.clinicalShort: EMG estimates acute excitation, not hypertrophy, mechanical tension, adaptation, or injury risk.
evidence.limitsShort: Rear-foot height, stance length, trunk angle, load position, depth, balance, and suspension or instability devices materially change emphasis.
evidence.summary: The Bulgarian split squat is classified as an unsupported unilateral lower-body compound movement. Current evidence supports quadriceps and gluteus maximus as the main visible targets, with hamstrings contributing as assistants and gluteus medius/trunk stabilizers supporting single-leg control.
evidence.clinicalInterpretation: Surface electromyography is condition-specific and should be interpreted alongside joint action, range of motion, load, and technique.
evidence.limitations: The entry assumes a stable rear-foot-elevated split squat. Suspended, vibration, unstable-surface, Smith-machine, barbell, and heavy dumbbell variants should be split later if the app needs variant-specific scoring.

studies.type: Rear-foot-elevated split squat EMG
studies.finding: RFESS produced high vastus lateralis activation and measured gluteus maximus plus medial and lateral hamstrings.
studies.citation: McCurdy K, Walker J, Kelly C, Polinski M. Hip and Knee Extensor Activation During the Hip Thrust and Rear-Foot-Elevated Split Squat in Trained Females. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2021;35(5):1201-1207. doi:10.1519/JSC.0000000000004035.
studies.relevance: Direct RFESS EMG source for quadriceps, gluteus maximus, and hamstrings.

studies.type: Bulgarian squat EMG variation study
studies.finding: Bulgarian squat variants changed lower-limb muscle activity under vibration, suspension, and unstable-surface conditions.
studies.citation: Aguilera-Castells J, Buscà B, Arboix-Alió J, et al. Muscle activity of Bulgarian squat. Effects of additional vibration, suspension and unstable surface. PLOS ONE. 2019;14(8):e0221710. doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0221710.
studies.relevance: Direct Bulgarian squat evidence for muscle activation and instability-sensitive control demand.

studies.type: Hip muscle activation in lunge and single-leg tasks
studies.shortCitation: Boudreau et al., J Sport Rehabil, 2009
studies.finding: Lunge, single-leg squat, and step-up tasks produced meaningful hip-muscle activation.
studies.citation: Boudreau SN, Dwyer MK, Mattacola CG, Lattermann C, Uhl TL, McKeon JM. Hip-muscle activation during the lunge, single-leg squat, and step-up-and-over exercises. Journal of Sport Rehabilitation. 2009;18(1):91-103. doi:10.1123/jsr.18.1.91.
studies.relevance: Close single-leg/lunge-family source supporting gluteus medius support classification.

studies.type: Lunge trunk-position EMG
studies.finding: Trunk position during lunge exercises changed muscular activation in trained women.
studies.citation: Bezerra ES, et al. Influence of Trunk Position during Three Lunge Exercises on Muscular Activation in Trained Women. International Journal of Exercise Science. 2021;14(1):202-214. doi:10.70252/IGJM9937.
studies.relevance: Close lunge-family evidence for trunk-position sensitivity and support-role limitations.

movements.name: Cable Chest Fly
movements.variant: Bilateral standing cable chest fly or cable crossover using dual cable handles, treated separately from pec-deck, dumbbell fly, and cable chest press variations.
movements.description: Stand between two cable pulleys with the handles slightly behind or beside the shoulders, feet staggered or shoulder width, and a small fixed bend in the elbows. Brace the torso, keep the shoulders controlled, sweep the handles forward and together through shoulder horizontal adduction, then return slowly until the chest is stretched without letting the elbows drift behind a comfortable shoulder range.

hypertrophy.rationale: Strong chest hypertrophy option because cable crossover evidence shows high pectoralis activation and the cable path keeps useful tension through much of the fly arc.

strength.rationale: Builds shoulder-adduction force in a narrow pattern, but low absolute loading and limited pressing specificity keep it from being a major strength anchor.

joint_resilience.rationale: Can expose the shoulder to controlled horizontal-abduction range, but the stretched long-arm position makes it a narrow and technique-sensitive resilience tool.

athletic_transfer.rationale: Standing posture and free cable path add a little whole-body organization, but the movement remains a bilateral chest isolation pattern.

control.rationale: Moderate-low control demand from free handles, cable line, torso position, and scapular control, but balance and coordination demands remain limited.

fatigue_efficiency.rationale: High local chest stimulus with little systemic fatigue and minimal triceps fatigue leakage compared with pressing.

setup.rationale: Requires a dual cable station, two handles, matched pulley heights, and a repeatable stance, so setup is more involved than a machine fly.

ease.rationale: The task is easy to understand, but repeatable shoulder range, torso angle, cable path, and elbow position need attention.

progression.rationale: Cable stack loads and reps are easy to record, with deductions for stack increments, cable friction, pulley height, and stance changes.

support.rationale: The cable stack supplies consistent resistance, but the user must stabilize the torso, shoulder path, and handle position without a guided arm path.

primary.name: Pectoralis major
primary.evidenceShort: Direct cable-crossover EMG supports the pec as the main target.
primary.evidence: A university EMG thesis directly tested bent-forward cable crossovers and found pectoralis major activation not significantly different from the barbell bench press. A pectoralis-exercise systematic review and close fly-pattern studies support pectoralis major as the intended prime mover for horizontal adduction.

secondary.name: Anterior deltoid
secondary.evidenceShort: Fly-pattern EMG supports meaningful shoulder-flexion/adduction assistance.
secondary.evidence: Direct dumbbell-fly and upper-body lift EMG measured anterior deltoid activity during fly-pattern work. It is classified as secondary because the cable chest fly is programmed as a chest isolation movement and pectoralis major remains the best-supported target.

evidence.verdict: Standing cable chest fly: pectoralis major primary; anterior deltoid secondary; no visible support muscles added.
evidence.clinicalShort: EMG estimates acute excitation, not hypertrophy, mechanical tension, adaptation, pain, or injury risk.
evidence.limitsShort: Pulley height, torso lean, arm path, shoulder rotation, elbow bend, range of motion, and cable friction can shift emphasis.
evidence.summary: The cable chest fly is classified as a standing cable horizontal-adduction isolation movement. Direct bent-forward cable-crossover evidence supports pectoralis major as the primary visible target. Anterior deltoid is included as a secondary contributor from close fly-pattern EMG, while biceps brachii, serratus anterior, rotator cuff, and trunk stabilizers are not shown because the reviewed evidence did not support a concise visible role for this exact app entry.
evidence.clinicalInterpretation: Surface electromyography is useful for estimating acute muscle excitation under a specific load, setup, and technique. It should not be interpreted as a direct measure of hypertrophy, mechanical tension, long-term adaptation, pain risk, or injury risk.
evidence.limitations: The most direct cable evidence is a master's thesis rather than a peer-reviewed journal article, and it measured pectoralis major rather than a full set of shoulder and arm muscles. The remaining direct peer-reviewed fly evidence uses dumbbells rather than cables. Cable fly variants differ meaningfully by pulley height, whether the hands meet or cross, stance, torso lean, stretch depth, elbow angle, and whether the movement is performed seated, standing, high-to-low, or low-to-high.

studies.type: Direct bent-forward cable crossover pectoralis EMG thesis
studies.shortCitation: Schanke, University of Wisconsin-La Crosse thesis, 2012
studies.finding: Bent-forward cable crossovers produced pectoralis major activation not significantly different from barbell bench press in the tested protocol.
studies.citation: Schanke W. Electromyographical analysis of the pectoralis major muscle during various chest exercises. Master's thesis. University of Wisconsin-La Crosse; 2012.
studies.relevance: Directly included bent-forward cable crossovers in 14 males using 80% 1RM for loaded exercises and compared pectoralis major EMG with other chest movements.

studies.type: Pectoralis exercise EMG systematic review and meta-analysis
studies.finding: Reviewed pectoralis major EMG across traditional bench press and other pectoral exercise variants, supporting conservative interpretation of chest-exercise EMG.
studies.citation: Lopez-Vivancos A, Gonzalez-Galvez N, Orquin-Castrillon FJ, Vale RGDS, Marcos-Pardo PJ. Electromyographic Activity of the Pectoralis Major Muscle during Traditional Bench Press and Other Variants of Pectoral Exercises: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Applied Sciences. 2023;13(8):5203. doi:10.3390/app13085203.
studies.relevance: Provides movement-family context for pectoralis major activation and EMG limitations across chest exercise variants.

studies.type: Direct dumbbell-fly and press EMG
