studies.finding: Compared pectoralis major and anterior deltoid activity during barbell bench press, dumbbell bench press, and dumbbell fly.
studies.citation: Welsch EA, Bird M, Mayhew JL. Electromyographic activity of the pectoralis major and anterior deltoid muscles during three upper-body lifts. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2005;19(2):449-452. doi:10.1519/14513.1.
studies.relevance: Close fly-pattern evidence for pectoralis major and anterior deltoid contribution; less direct because it used dumbbells rather than cables.

studies.type: Direct dumbbell fly EMG comparison
studies.shortCitation: Solstad et al., J Sports Sci Med, 2020
studies.finding: Dumbbell flyes involved pectoralis major and anterior deltoid but showed lower agonist activation than barbell bench press overall; biceps brachii was higher in flyes, likely from elbow and arm stabilization.
studies.citation: Solstad TE, Andersen V, Shaw M, Hoel EM, Vonheim A, Saeterbakken AH. A Comparison of Muscle Activation between Barbell Bench Press and Dumbbell Flyes in Resistance-Trained Males. Journal of Sports Science and Medicine. 2020;19(4):645-651.
studies.relevance: Close fly-pattern evidence in resistance-trained males; used for secondary anterior deltoid role, biceps exclusion boundary, and rating limits.

movements.name: Cable Triceps Pushdown
movements.variant: Standing high-pulley cable elbow extension with the upper arms held near the torso, using a bar, rope, V-handle, or similar attachment.
movements.description: Stand facing a high cable with the elbows close to the sides and the forearms bent near 90 degrees. Brace lightly, keep the upper arms mostly still, press the handle down by extending the elbows until the arms are straight, then let the handle rise under control without letting the shoulders roll forward or the elbows drift up.

hypertrophy.rationale: Strong triceps hypertrophy accessory because direct pushdown EMG and cable training studies support targeted elbow-extension loading with low unrelated fatigue.

strength.rationale: Useful for elbow-extension strength, but the single-joint cable setup is less representative of heavy compound pressing or maximal force expression.

joint_resilience.rationale: Can load the elbow extensors through controlled range, but it is not a broad shoulder or elbow resilience exercise.

athletic_transfer.rationale: Minimal athletic-transfer signal because the movement is isolated, bilateral, and stationary.

control.rationale: Low control demand because the cable constrains resistance direction and the main task is keeping the upper arms still.

fatigue_efficiency.rationale: Very efficient local triceps work with little systemic fatigue, low setup leakage, and minimal chest or shoulder fatigue compared with presses.

setup.rationale: Requires a cable station, high pulley, attachment, and stack adjustment, but no bench or complex body setup.

ease.rationale: One of the easiest triceps movements to learn and repeat because posture and elbow extension are simple to control.

progression.rationale: Stack load and reps are easy to record, with deductions for cable friction, attachment changes, and stack increment size.

support.rationale: Moderately supported by the cable path and stable stance, though the torso and upper arms still need to resist movement.

primary.name: Triceps brachii
primary.evidenceShort: Direct pushdown EMG measures triceps heads during loaded elbow extension.
primary.evidence: Direct standing cable pushdown studies measured triceps brachii heads during dynamic elbow extension and fatigue conditions. Training studies using neutral-arm cable pushdowns also support the pushdown as a targeted triceps hypertrophy and strength exercise.

evidence.verdict: Cable triceps pushdown: triceps brachii primary; no visible secondary or support muscles added.
evidence.clinicalShort: EMG estimates acute excitation, not hypertrophy, mechanical tension, adaptation, pain, or injury risk.
evidence.limitsShort: Attachment, grip, elbow path, shoulder position, torso lean, cable height, load, speed, and fatigue can shift head-level emphasis and technique.
evidence.summary: The cable triceps pushdown is classified as a standing neutral-arm elbow-extension isolation movement. Direct EMG evidence supports the triceps brachii as the visible primary target. Forearm muscles were measured in handle-comparison work but are not available as local anatomy entries and are not central to the app classification. Shoulder and trunk muscles are not shown because the reviewed sources did not justify a concise visible role beyond posture control.
evidence.clinicalInterpretation: Surface electromyography is useful for estimating acute triceps excitation under a specific attachment, load, tempo, and fatigue state. It should not be interpreted as a direct measure of hypertrophy, mechanical tension, long-term adaptation, pain risk, or injury risk.
evidence.limitations: The local anatomy dataset exposes triceps brachii as a whole muscle, not separate long, lateral, and medial heads. Direct pushdown studies measured head-level behavior, but the app entry collapses that evidence into the aggregate Triceps brachii role. Rope, straight-bar, V-bar, unilateral, reverse-grip, and bent-over pushdowns can alter forearm and shoulder mechanics and should be separate variants if the app needs that detail.

studies.type: Direct cable triceps pushdown handle EMG
studies.finding: Standing triceps pushdowns from 90 to 0 degrees elbow flexion measured lateral and long triceps heads; handle type did not significantly change triceps RMS EMG.
studies.citation: Rendos NK, Heredia Vargas HM, Alipio TC, Regis RC, Romero MA, Signorile JF. Differences in Muscle Activity During Cable Resistance Training Are Influenced by Variations in Handle Types. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2016;30(7):2001-2009. doi:10.1519/JSC.0000000000001293.
studies.relevance: Directly studied standing triceps pushdown with cable attachments and measured triceps brachii lateral and long heads plus forearm muscles.

studies.type: Direct triceps pushdown fatigue EMG
studies.finding: Measured all three triceps heads during straight-bar triceps pushdowns across intensity, speed, and fatigue conditions.
studies.citation: Hussain J, Sundaraj K, Subramaniam ID, Lam CK. Muscle Fatigue in the Three Heads of Triceps Brachii During Intensity and Speed Variations of Triceps Push-Down Exercise. Frontiers in Physiology. 2020;11:112. doi:10.3389/fphys.2020.00112.
studies.relevance: Directly matches the standing straight-bar triceps pushdown setup and supports triceps as the target muscle across load, speed, and fatigue contexts.

studies.type: Cable pushdown versus overhead extension training study
studies.shortCitation: Stasinaki et al., J Funct Morphol Kinesiol, 2018
studies.finding: Novice women trained unilateral cable push-downs at short fascicle length or overhead extensions at long fascicle length for six weeks; both conditions improved elbow-extension strength and triceps architecture.
studies.citation: Stasinaki AN, Zaras N, Methenitis S, Tsitkanou S, Krase A, Kavvoura A, Terzis G. Triceps Brachii Muscle Strength and Architectural Adaptations with Resistance Training Exercises at Short or Long Fascicle Length. Journal of Functional Morphology and Kinesiology. 2018;3(2):28. doi:10.3390/jfmk3020028.
studies.relevance: Directly used cable push-downs as a neutral-arm triceps training condition and informs hypertrophy, strength, and limitations.

studies.type: Cable overhead versus neutral-arm elbow-extension hypertrophy study
studies.shortCitation: Maeo et al., Eur J Sport Sci, 2023
studies.finding: Using a cable machine, overhead-arm elbow extension produced greater triceps hypertrophy than neutral-arm elbow extension, but both conditions increased triceps size and strength.
studies.citation: Maeo S, Wu Y, Huang M, Sakurai H, Kusagawa Y, Sugiyama T, Kanehisa H, Isaka T. Triceps brachii hypertrophy is substantially greater after elbow extension training performed in the overhead versus neutral arm position. European Journal of Sport Science. 2023;23(7):1240-1250. doi:10.1080/17461391.2022.2100279.
studies.relevance: Direct cable training comparison including a neutral-arm condition corresponding to pushdown-style elbow extension.

studies.type: Triceps head function by shoulder elevation
studies.shortCitation: Kholinne et al., Acta Orthop Traumatol Turc, 2018
studies.finding: Each triceps head showed different force and activity patterns across shoulder elevation angles during elbow-extension tasks.
studies.citation: Kholinne E, Zulkarnain RF, Sun YC, Lim S, Chun JM, Jeon IH. The different role of each head of the triceps brachii muscle in elbow extension. Acta Orthopaedica et Traumatologica Turcica. 2018;52(3):201-205. doi:10.1016/j.aott.2018.02.005.
studies.relevance: Biomechanics and EMG context for head-level triceps contribution in elbow extension at neutral and elevated shoulder angles.

movements.name: Cable Woodchop
movements.variant: Standing diagonal cable woodchop using a cable handle, with the trunk and hips rotating as the handle moves across the body.
movements.description: Stand side-on to a cable station, hold the handle with both hands, brace, rotate through the trunk and hips to move the cable diagonally across the body, then return under control without letting the cable pull you out of position.

hypertrophy.rationale: Can load the obliques, but rotation, momentum, and whole-body contribution make local hypertrophy less precise than a stable flexion or anti-rotation drill.

strength.rationale: Useful for resisted trunk rotation, but technical execution and stance often limit maximal force expression.

joint_resilience.rationale: Controlled rotation can build trunk, hip, and shoulder tolerance, but careless loading can add unwanted lumbar rotation or shoulder strain.

athletic_transfer.rationale: Strong transfer signal for rotational force transfer because it is standing, multiplanar, and can be trained for power or controlled strength.

control.rationale: Requires coordinated bracing, trunk rotation, hip pivoting, stance control, and cable deceleration.

fatigue_efficiency.rationale: Moderate fatigue efficiency: it gives useful core and coordination stimulus but can leak effort into arms, hips, and balance.

setup.rationale: Requires a cable station, handle, pulley-height choice, and enough space to rotate.

ease.rationale: More technical than most core accessories because stance, pivot, arm path, and trunk timing have to match the cable line.

progression.rationale: Cable stacks make loading trackable, though speed, range, and stance can still change the stimulus.

support.rationale: The cable provides a consistent line of resistance, but the user stands freely and self-stabilizes through rotation.

primary.name: External oblique
primary.evidenceShort: Rotational throwing EMG and oblique-task EMG support the role.
primary.evidence: A side medicine-ball throw EMG study found external oblique activity distinguished longer from shorter rotational throws, and oblique-task EMG supports high external-oblique activity under rotational trunk demand.

primary.name: Internal oblique
primary.evidenceShort: Oblique-task EMG supports internal-oblique loading under rotational demand.
primary.evidence: Self-oblique exercise EMG showed internal oblique activation when the upper limb created a rotational demand through the trunk; the cable woodchop uses a loadable standing cable version of a similar trunk-rotation demand.

secondary.name: Rectus abdominis
secondary.evidenceShort: Rotational and oblique-task studies measured rectus activity.
secondary.evidence: The rectus abdominis is included as a secondary trunk bracer because rotational throw and oblique-task EMG studies measured abdominal activity while the exact cable woodchop source frames the exercise as a core power and endurance test.

evidence.verdict: Cable woodchop: external and internal oblique primary; rectus abdominis secondary; no separate support muscles listed.
evidence.clinicalShort: EMG and power tests describe acute performance demands, not hypertrophy, adaptation, or injury risk.
evidence.limitsShort: High-to-low versus low-to-high path, pulley height, stance width, hip pivot, arm dominance, speed, and load can change emphasis.
evidence.summary: The cable woodchop is classified as a standing rotational core exercise. The exact cable study supports the movement as a reliable core power/endurance test, while close rotational and oblique EMG studies support external and internal oblique emphasis.
evidence.clinicalInterpretation: The best use case is controlled rotational force transfer or power, not isolated abdominal hypertrophy.
evidence.limitations: The exact standing cable woodchop study did not report individual-muscle EMG, so muscle roles use close rotational and oblique EMG evidence. Transversus abdominis, quadratus lumborum, and deep hip rotators were not added as visible roles because they are not locally mapped as display muscles.

studies.type: Standing cable woodchop power assessment
studies.finding: Standing cable woodchop power and endurance measures were reliable and sensitive across different weight-stack loads in fit men.
studies.citation: Zemkova E, Cepkova A, Uvacek M, Soos L. A novel method for assessing muscle power during the standing cable wood chop exercise. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2017;31(8):2246-2254. doi:10.1519/JSC.0000000000001692.
studies.relevance: Exact standing cable woodchop source for loadability, power, endurance, progression, and movement-family specificity.

studies.type: Rotational medicine-ball throw EMG
studies.finding: During fast side medicine-ball throws, external oblique EMG was the major difference between longer and shorter throwers.
studies.citation: Ikeda Y, Miyatsuji K, Kawabata K, Fuchimoto T, Ito A. Analysis of trunk muscle activity in the side medicine-ball throw. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2009;23(8):2231-2240. doi:10.1519/JSC.0b013e3181b8676f.
studies.relevance: Close dynamic rotational-power EMG source for external oblique and rectus abdominis involvement.

studies.type: Oblique and hip muscle EMG
studies.finding: Self-oblique exercise produced coordinated external oblique, internal oblique, gluteus medius, and adductor activity and allowed load modulation.
studies.citation: Nakai Y, Kawada M, Miyazaki T, Araki S, Takeshita Y, Kiyama R. A self-oblique exercise that activates the coordinated activity of abdominal and hip muscles: a pilot study. PLoS One. 2021;16(8):e0255035. doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0255035.
studies.relevance: Close oblique-task EMG source for internal and external oblique activation under rotational trunk demand.

movements.name: Chest-Supported Dumbbell Row
movements.variant: Bilateral dumbbell row performed prone or chest-supported on an incline bench, with both dumbbells pulled toward the lower ribs or torso.
movements.description: Lie chest-down on an incline bench with the feet planted, let the dumbbells hang under the shoulders, and keep the chest in contact with the pad. Pull both elbows back toward the lower ribs, pause with the shoulder blades drawn back without lifting the torso, then lower the dumbbells until the arms are long and the shoulder blades can reach forward under control.

hypertrophy.rationale: Strong back hypertrophy option because chest support reduces trunk fatigue and lets the row focus on lats, mid-back, posterior deltoid, and elbow flexors.

strength.rationale: Builds upper-body pulling force, but dumbbell setup and chest support make it less useful as a maximal strength expression than heavy barbell rows.

joint_resilience.rationale: Useful controlled shoulder and scapular loading, but it is not a broad joint-resilience movement.

athletic_transfer.rationale: Limited transfer because the torso is externally supported and the movement is bilateral and constrained by the bench.

control.rationale: Requires scapular and elbow-path control with independent dumbbells, but the bench removes most trunk and balance demands.

fatigue_efficiency.rationale: Efficient upper-back stimulus with lower axial and trunk fatigue than unsupported rows, though grip and biceps can still limit sets.

setup.rationale: Requires an adjustable bench, enough floor space, and matched dumbbells, with some friction from bench angle and heavy dumbbell handling.

ease.rationale: The chest pad makes the row repeatable and easy to learn, though elbow flare and shoulder range still affect execution.

progression.rationale: Load and reps are straightforward to track, but dumbbell increments are often coarse and bench angle changes can alter performance.

support.rationale: The bench strongly supports the torso, while the shoulders, elbows, and wrists still control two free dumbbells.

primary.name: Latissimus dorsi
primary.evidenceShort: Supported row EMG includes latissimus as a prime mover.
primary.evidence: Prone row EMG directly measured latissimus dorsi as a prime mover, and seated cable row data show greater latissimus activation with lower-abduction, tucked-elbow rowing. The chest-supported dumbbell row uses that same shoulder-extension and adduction bias when pulled toward the lower ribs.

secondary.name: Teres major
secondary.evidenceShort: Measured shoulder-extension assistant in row-family EMG.
secondary.evidence: Fujita et al. measured teres major during the seated row and treated it with latissimus dorsi as a back-muscle target; for the chest-supported dumbbell row it is classified as a secondary shoulder-extension assistant.

secondary.name: Middle trapezius
secondary.evidenceShort: Measured scapular retractor in supported and seated rows.
secondary.evidence: Prone barbell row EMG measured transverse trapezius, and seated row studies measured middle trapezius activity that rises with more abducted row paths. Chest support preserves the scapular-retraction demand while reducing trunk contribution.

secondary.name: Rhomboids
secondary.evidenceShort: Inferred from grouped row EMG and scapular retraction.
secondary.evidence: This role is marked as inference: row EMG has grouped middle trapezius/rhomboid signals, and the chest-supported row requires scapular retraction as the dumbbells are pulled toward the torso.

secondary.name: Posterior deltoid
secondary.evidenceShort: Measured row contributor in prone and seated rows.
secondary.evidence: Rear or posterior deltoid activity is directly measured in prone row and seated row EMG studies. It assists shoulder extension and horizontal abduction, especially if the elbows travel wider.

secondary.name: Biceps brachii
secondary.evidenceShort: Measured elbow-flexion assistant in rows.
secondary.evidence: Prone and seated row EMG studies measured biceps brachii activity; it assists elbow flexion during the row but is not the primary back target.

support.name: Rotator cuff
support.evidenceShort: Shoulder stabilization role during row tasks.
support.evidence: Row tasks recruit the rotator cuff in a direction-specific way consistent with stabilizing the glenohumeral joint during loaded shoulder extension and retraction.

evidence.verdict: Chest-supported dumbbell row: latissimus dorsi primary; teres major, middle trapezius, rhomboids, posterior deltoid, and biceps brachii secondary; rotator cuff support.
evidence.clinicalShort: EMG estimates acute excitation, not hypertrophy, mechanical tension, adaptation, or injury risk.
evidence.limitsShort: Bench angle, elbow flare, grip, pull target, dumbbell size, and whether the chest stays fully supported can shift emphasis between lats, middle trapezius, rhomboids, posterior deltoid, and elbow flexors.
evidence.summary: The chest-supported dumbbell row is classified as a supported horizontal pull. Chest support reduces trunk and lumbar demand, so no visible trunk support muscles are added. Supported and seated row-family EMG support latissimus dorsi as the main back target for tucked-elbow rows, with teres major, middle trapezius, rhomboids, posterior deltoid, and biceps brachii assisting. Rotator cuff involvement is included as support because it stabilizes the shoulder during loaded rowing.
evidence.clinicalInterpretation: The evidence mixes exact bench-supported bent-over row work, prone barbell row EMG, seated cable row EMG, and shoulder-stability evidence. These data support a conservative role classification but do not prove identical activation for every incline bench angle or dumbbell handle path.
evidence.limitations: A chest-supported dumbbell row can become an upper-back row if the elbows flare high, or a lat-biased row if the elbows track close toward the hips. The local anatomy map has biceps brachii but not brachialis or brachioradialis, so those elbow flexors are not shown.

studies.type: Prone row range-of-motion EMG study
studies.shortCitation: Fischer et al., J Electromyogr Kinesiol, 2025
studies.finding: Prone barbell row EMG measured latissimus dorsi, transverse trapezius, rear deltoid, and biceps brachii across full and partial ranges of motion.
studies.citation: Fischer J, Burger C, Seguel JM, Rodoplu C, Paternoster FK, Tilp M, Konrad A. Impact of different ranges of motion in the prone barbell row on muscle excitation. Journal of Electromyography and Kinesiology. 2025;83:103025. doi:10.1016/j.jelekin.2025.103025.
studies.relevance: Very close supported-row evidence because the prone row fixes the torso while measuring the main visible row muscles.

studies.type: Standing vs bench-supported bent-over row EMG
studies.finding: Compared lumbar, dorsal, and shoulder muscle responses during standing and bench-supported bent-over row postures.
studies.citation: Garcia-Jaen M, Sanchis-Soler G, Carrion-Adan A, Cortell-Tormo JM. Electromyographical responses of the lumbar, dorsal and shoulder musculature during the bent-over row exercise: A comparison between standing and bench postures (a preliminary study). Journal of Physical Education and Sport. 2021;21(4):1871-1877. doi:10.7752/jpes.2021.04236.
studies.relevance: Directly addresses the effect of bench support during bent-over rowing and supports the reduced-trunk-demand interpretation.

studies.type: Seated cable row EMG and force study
studies.shortCitation: Vasconcelos et al., Int J Strength Cond, 2023
studies.finding: Lower-abduction row paths emphasized latissimus dorsi, while higher-abduction paths emphasized trapezius and posterior deltoid.
studies.citation: Vasconcelos CMWA, Lopes CR, Almeida VM, Neto WK, Soares EG. Effect Of Different Grip Position And Shoulder-Abduction Angle On Muscle Strength And Activation During The Seated Cable Row. International Journal of Strength and Conditioning. 2023;3(1):1-13. doi:10.47206/ijsc.v3i1.190.
studies.relevance: Direct row-family EMG for latissimus dorsi, middle trapezius, posterior deltoid, and biceps brachii by elbow path.

studies.type: Latissimus dorsi exercise EMG study
studies.finding: Seated row produced high latissimus and grouped middle trapezius/rhomboid activity among traditional back exercises.
studies.citation: Lehman GJ, Buchan DD, Lundy A, Myers N, Nalborczyk A. Variations in muscle activation levels during traditional latissimus dorsi weight training exercises: An experimental study. Dynamic Medicine. 2004;3:4. doi:10.1186/1476-5918-3-4.
studies.relevance: Row-family EMG evidence for lats and grouped middle trapezius/rhomboids.

studies.type: Seated row EMG and verbal-instruction study
studies.finding: At 70% 1RM, seated row produced substantial latissimus dorsi, teres major, posterior deltoid, and biceps brachii activity.
studies.citation: Fujita RA, De Marchi PU, Silva NRS, Gomes MM. Verbal instruction does not change myoelectric activity during seated row exercise in trained and untrained men. Motriz: Revista de Educacao Fisica. 2019;25(4):e10190100. doi:10.1590/s1980-6574201900040100.
studies.relevance: Close row-family EMG for teres major, posterior deltoid, and biceps brachii roles.

studies.type: Rotator cuff recruitment study
studies.shortCitation: Wattanaprakornkul et al., J Electromyogr Kinesiol, 2011
studies.finding: Rotator cuff recruitment during bench press and row was direction-specific, consistent with dynamic shoulder stabilization.
studies.citation: Wattanaprakornkul D, Halaki M, Cathers I, Ginn KA. Direction-specific recruitment of rotator cuff muscles during bench press and row. Journal of Electromyography and Kinesiology. 2011;21(6):1041-1049. doi:10.1016/j.jelekin.2011.09.002.
studies.relevance: Supports rotator cuff stabilization during rowing.

movements.name: Conventional Barbell Deadlift
movements.variant: Free-weight conventional barbell deadlift from the floor with hands outside the legs and a hip-width stance.
movements.description: Stand with the bar over the midfoot, hinge down with the hands outside the legs, set the back and lats, brace, and push the floor away while keeping the bar close. Stand tall by extending the knees and hips together, then lower the bar under control back to the floor without letting it drift forward.

hypertrophy.rationale: Loads many large muscles, but the high systemic cost, floor-start constraints, grip demand, and limited eccentric focus make it less targeted than dedicated hypertrophy lifts.

strength.rationale: Elite whole-body strength signal because the barbell floor pull allows heavy progressive loading through coordinated hip, knee, and trunk extension.

joint_resilience.rationale: Can build tolerance to heavy hip-hinge and spinal-position demands, but the high load and technical sensitivity keep it from being a broadly easy resilience drill.

athletic_transfer.rationale: Useful transfer to forceful lifting from the floor and posterior-chain strength, though bilateral stance and slow heavy loading limit sport-specific coordination.

control.rationale: Requires bracing, lat tension, bar path control, coordinated knee and hip extension, and consistent floor-start position under load.

fatigue_efficiency.rationale: The strength signal is high, but systemic fatigue, warm-up cost, grip demand, and spinal erector loading make the stimulus expensive.

setup.rationale: Needs barbell, plates, floor space, plate changes, warm-up jumps, and usually platform or floor clearance management.

ease.rationale: Technique is demanding because start position, slack pull, bracing, hip height, bar path, and lockout timing all matter.

progression.rationale: Very trackable with load and reps, but fatigue, technique drift, and dead-start consistency can limit clean progression.

support.rationale: Almost no external support: the user controls the bar path, torso, hips, knees, grip, and balance from the floor.

primary.name: Erector spinae
primary.evidenceShort: Deadlift EMG reviews and direct studies show high trunk-extensor demand.
primary.evidence: Deadlift systematic-review evidence reports high erector spinae activation across deadlift variants, and direct conventional deadlift studies measure paraspinal and erector activity under heavy floor-pull conditions.

primary.name: Quadriceps
primary.evidenceShort: Conventional deadlift requires substantial knee-extension contribution from the floor.
primary.evidence: Deadlift review evidence reports greater quadriceps activation than gluteus maximus and hamstrings in deadlift tasks, and direct conventional deadlift research measures knee-extensor activity during floor pulls.

primary.name: Gluteus maximus
primary.evidenceShort: Measured hip-extensor contributor in direct conventional deadlift studies.
primary.evidence: Conventional deadlift studies measure gluteus maximus activity and biomechanics support a major hip-extension role from the floor to lockout. It is classified as primary because the movement heavily trains hip extension alongside the knee and trunk extensors.

secondary.name: Hamstrings
secondary.evidenceShort: Measured posterior-thigh contribution, but not the dominant conventional-deadlift signal.
secondary.evidence: Direct conventional deadlift EMG studies and the deadlift systematic review measure hamstrings during floor pulls. They are classified as secondary because the conventional deadlift combines hip extension with substantial knee-extension and trunk-extension demand.

support.name: Gastrocnemius
support.evidenceShort: Direct conventional deadlift EMG reported calf co-contraction.
support.evidence: Conventional and sumo deadlift EMG research measured gastrocnemius activity and reported lower-limb co-contraction during heavy 12RM pulls. It is included as support because ankle and knee stabilization are meaningful but not the main training target.

support.name: Trapezius
support.evidenceShort: Measured shoulder-girdle support during conventional deadlifts.
support.evidence: Deadlift EMG research measured upper and middle trapezius during conventional deadlift conditions. The role is classified as support because the trapezius helps maintain shoulder girdle position and bar control rather than producing the main lift.

support.name: Trunk stabilizers
support.evidenceShort: Direct deadlift EMG measured abdominal and oblique bracing demand.
support.evidence: Conventional deadlift EMG research included trunk muscles such as rectus abdominis and external oblique under belt and no-belt conditions. The app uses the local trunk stabilizers group to represent bracing support.

evidence.verdict: Conventional barbell deadlift: erector spinae, quadriceps, and gluteus maximus primary; hamstrings secondary; gastrocnemius, trapezius, and trunk stabilizers support.
evidence.clinicalShort: EMG and biomechanics estimate acute demand under tested conditions, not hypertrophy, pain risk, or long-term adaptation for a specific lifter.
evidence.limitsShort: Stance, hip height, bar path, grip, belt use, footwear, load, fatigue, and anthropometry can substantially shift the deadlift profile.
evidence.summary: The conventional barbell deadlift is classified as a free-weight floor pull with major trunk, knee, and hip extension demands. The visible map emphasizes erector spinae, quadriceps, and gluteus maximus as primary contributors, with hamstrings as a meaningful secondary posterior-chain contributor and selected support roles only where direct EMG evidence exists.
evidence.clinicalInterpretation: Surface EMG is condition-specific and should be read alongside biomechanics, range of motion, load, and technique. Ratings reflect the conventional deadlift as a high-force barbell skill with a large systemic fatigue cost.
evidence.limitations: The entry assumes a conventional straight-bar pull from the floor, not sumo, trap-bar, rack pull, deficit pull, Romanian deadlift, stiff-leg deadlift, or chain/band variation. Hamstring contribution varies because the knee and hip extend together, and direct studies differ in loads, normalization methods, lifter training status, belt use, and phase analysis.

studies.type: Conventional and sumo deadlift EMG study
studies.finding: Collegiate football players performed sumo and conventional deadlifts at 12RM with and without a belt while quadriceps, hamstrings, gastrocnemius, gluteus maximus, paraspinals, trapezius, and trunk muscles were measured.
studies.citation: Escamilla RF, Francisco AC, Kayes AV, Speer KP, Moorman CT 3rd. An electromyographic analysis of sumo and conventional style deadlifts. Medicine and Science in Sports and Exercise. 2002;34(4):682-688. doi:10.1097/00005768-200204000-00019.
studies.relevance: Direct conventional deadlift EMG source for prime movers and selected support muscles.

studies.type: Conventional and sumo deadlift biomechanics study
studies.finding: Three-dimensional analysis compared sumo and conventional deadlift mechanics, supporting the conventional deadlift's combined hip, knee, and trunk-extension loading profile.
studies.citation: Escamilla RF, Francisco AC, Fleisig GS, Barrentine SW, Welch CM, Kayes AV, Speer KP, Andrews JR. A three-dimensional biomechanical analysis of sumo and conventional style deadlifts. Medicine and Science in Sports and Exercise. 2000;32(7):1265-1275. doi:10.1097/00005768-200007000-00013.
studies.relevance: Biomechanical support for knee, hip, trunk, and load-path interpretation in conventional deadlifts.

studies.type: Deadlift EMG systematic review
studies.finding: Across deadlift studies, erector spinae and quadriceps showed greater activation than gluteus maximus and hamstrings, and deadlift variants showed different hamstring and trunk profiles.
studies.citation: Martin-Fuentes I, Oliva-Lozano JM, Muyor JM. Electromyographic activity in deadlift exercise and its variants. A systematic review. PLOS ONE. 2020;15(2):e0229507. doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0229507.
studies.relevance: Systematic-review context for conventional deadlift muscle hierarchy and EMG interpretation limits.

studies.type: Conventional versus Romanian deadlift EMG and kinetics study
studies.shortCitation: Lee et al., J Exerc Sci Fit, 2018
studies.finding: Compared conventional and Romanian deadlifts with electromyographic and kinetic measures, supporting different glute, hamstring, quadriceps, and trunk demands between the variants.
studies.citation: Lee S, Schultz J, Timgren J, Staelgraeve K, Miller M, Liu Y. An electromyographic and kinetic comparison of conventional and Romanian deadlifts. Journal of Exercise Science & Fitness. 2018;16(3):87-93. doi:10.1016/j.jesf.2018.08.001.
studies.relevance: Directly compares conventional and Romanian deadlift variants and informs the different visible maps.

studies.type: Conventional deadlift variable-resistance EMG study
studies.finding: Resistance-trained men performed heavy conventional barbell deadlifts with constant and reverse-band resistance while gluteus maximus, biceps femoris, semitendinosus, vastus lateralis, and erector spinae were measured.
studies.citation: Andersen V, Fimland MS, Mo DA, Iversen VM, Larsen TM, Solheim F, Saeterbakken AH. Electromyographic comparison of the barbell deadlift using constant versus variable resistance in healthy, trained men. PLOS ONE. 2019;14(1):e0211021. doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0211021.
studies.relevance: Direct conventional barbell deadlift EMG source under heavy loading for erector spinae, hamstrings, quadriceps, and gluteus maximus.

studies.type: Straight-bar versus hex-bar deadlift EMG and power study
studies.finding: Compared muscle activation and power characteristics during straight-bar and hex-bar deadlifts, supporting conventional straight-bar classification against a distinct trap-bar variant.
studies.citation: Camara KD, Coburn JW, Dunnick DD, Brown LE, Galpin AJ, Costa PB. An Examination of Muscle Activation and Power Characteristics While Performing the Deadlift Exercise With Straight and Hexagonal Barbells. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2016;30(5):1183-1188. doi:10.1519/JSC.0000000000001352.
studies.relevance: Close direct evidence for straight-bar deadlift muscle activation and power characteristics.

studies.type: Conventional deadlift chain-loading EMG and force-plate study
studies.finding: Compared conventional deadlifts with and without chains using EMG and force-plate measures, informing trunk, hip, and knee extensor demand under heavy deadlift loading.
studies.citation: Nijem RM, Coburn JW, Brown LE, Lynn SK, Ciccone AB. Electromyographic and Force Plate Analysis of the Deadlift Performed With and Without Chains. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2016;30(5):1177-1182. doi:10.1519/JSC.0000000000001351.
studies.relevance: Direct conventional deadlift movement-family source for heavy loading, EMG, and force production context.

movements.name: Dumbbell Bench Press
movements.variant: Flat dumbbell bench press, treated as an independent free-weight horizontal pressing pattern.
movements.description: Sit at the end of a flat bench with matching dumbbells on the thighs, lie back while guiding the weights to shoulder level, set the feet and shoulder blades, lower with wrists stacked over elbows until the chest is loaded without losing shoulder position, then press the dumbbells up and slightly together under control.

hypertrophy.rationale: High chest stimulus with independent arm paths and useful range of motion, making hypertrophy a main positive dimension.

strength.rationale: Builds pressing strength well, but absolute loading and measurement precision are lower than barbell bench because each dumbbell must be positioned and stabilized independently.

joint_resilience.rationale: Can train shoulder tolerance through a freer path, but it is not primarily a resilience drill and can become demanding at the bottom range.

athletic_transfer.rationale: Some transfer from independent limb control, but the supine supported position keeps sport-like coordination demand low.

control.rationale: Meaningful control demand from independent dumbbells, but the bench removes balance, locomotion, and most whole-body coordination.

fatigue_efficiency.rationale: Strong local stimulus, but setup, stabilizer demand, and heavy dumbbell handling reduce efficiency compared with guided chest work.

setup.rationale: Needs a bench and matched dumbbells, with extra friction as weights get heavy or crowded.

ease.rationale: Simple conceptually, but safe heavy reps require independent arm control, shoulder positioning, and getting dumbbells into and out of position.

progression.rationale: Load and reps are trackable, but dumbbell jumps are often coarse and heavy setup can limit progression before the target muscles do.

support.rationale: The torso is bench-supported, but each arm stabilizes a separate free load, so external support is modest.

primary.name: Pectoralis major
primary.evidenceShort: Direct DBP and bench-press EMG support major chest involvement.
primary.evidence: Dumbbell bench press studies measure pectoralis major activity during the horizontal press, and bench-press EMG review evidence supports pectoralis major as a dominant mover in the movement family.

secondary.name: Anterior deltoid
secondary.evidenceShort: Measured DBP contributor; path and depth sensitive.
secondary.evidence: Anterior deltoid is directly measured during dumbbell bench press and close bench-press variants; its contribution is meaningful but generally secondary to the intended chest target.

secondary.name: Triceps brachii
secondary.evidenceShort: Elbow-extension contributor in DBP and bench press.
secondary.evidence: Dumbbell bench press EMG studies record triceps brachii activity, and the bench-press EMG literature identifies triceps brachii as a major contributor to the elbow-extension component of pressing.

support.name: Biceps brachii
support.evidenceShort: Independent dumbbells increase antagonist/stabilizer demand.
support.evidence: Direct dumbbell bench press comparisons report biceps brachii activity consistent with antagonist and stabilizing demand when controlling two independent dumbbells.

support.name: Serratus anterior
support.evidenceShort: Scapulothoracic support during horizontal pressing.
support.evidence: Bench and chest-press comparison evidence includes serratus anterior activity with scapular kinematics; for dumbbell pressing this is classified as scapulothoracic support rather than a primary hypertrophy target.

support.name: Rotator cuff
support.evidenceShort: Glenohumeral stabilization during free pressing.
support.evidence: Bench press research demonstrates direction-specific rotator cuff recruitment consistent with glenohumeral stabilization; independent dumbbell paths make this a support classification.

evidence.verdict: Flat dumbbell horizontal press: pectoralis major primary; anterior deltoid and triceps secondary; biceps brachii, serratus anterior, and rotator cuff support.
evidence.clinicalShort: EMG estimates acute excitation, not hypertrophy, mechanical tension, adaptation, or injury risk.
evidence.limitsShort: Dumbbell path, depth, grip angle, load, bench angle, shoulder range, and start/finish handling can shift emphasis; incline, neutral-grip, and machine versions should be separate movements.
evidence.summary: The flat dumbbell bench press is classified as an independent free-weight horizontal pressing exercise. Direct dumbbell press evidence supports pectoralis major, anterior deltoid, triceps brachii, and biceps brachii involvement. Pectoralis major is the primary target, anterior deltoid and triceps brachii are secondary movers, and biceps brachii is included as support because independent dumbbells increase antagonist/stabilizer demand.
evidence.clinicalInterpretation: Surface electromyography is useful for estimating acute muscle excitation during a specific exercise condition. It should not be interpreted as a direct measure of hypertrophy, mechanical tension, long-term adaptation, or injury risk.
evidence.limitations: Dumbbell bench press studies differ in load prescription, normalization method, range of motion, grip, participant training status, and whether the comparison condition is barbell, Smith machine, cable, or fly variation. Scapular and rotator cuff support roles are inferred from close pressing-family evidence rather than direct dumbbell-only measurements.

studies.type: Dumbbell bench press vs cable bench press EMG
studies.shortCitation: Rosa et al., Int J Strength Cond, 2024
studies.finding: DBP and cable bench press showed similar pectoralis major and anterior deltoid activity; DBP showed higher triceps activity.
studies.citation: Rosa M, Martins R, Loureiro N. The Effects of Different Types of External Load Equipment on Muscle Activation Comparing Two Bench Press Exercises Variations. International Journal of Strength and Conditioning. 2024;4(1). doi:10.47206/ijsc.v4i1.254.
studies.relevance: Directly measured pectoralis major, anterior deltoid, biceps brachii, and triceps brachii during dumbbell bench press in resistance-trained participants.

studies.type: Dumbbell, barbell, and Smith machine bench press EMG
studies.finding: Compared DBP, barbell, and Smith machine bench press over multiple sets and measured pec, anterior deltoid, biceps, and triceps.
studies.citation: Farias D de A, Willardson JM, Paz GA, Bezerra E de S, Miranda H. Maximal Strength Performance and Muscle Activation for the Bench Press and Triceps Extension Exercises Adopting Dumbbell, Barbell, and Machine Modalities Over Multiple Sets. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2017;31(7):1879-1887. doi:10.1519/JSC.0000000000001651.
studies.relevance: Directly supports DBP muscle-role classification and the stabilizer demand distinction between dumbbell and bar/machine modalities.

studies.type: Chest-press stability comparison
studies.shortCitation: Saeterbakken et al., J Sports Sci, 2011
studies.finding: Compared Smith machine, barbell, and dumbbell chest press 1RM and EMG under different stability requirements.
studies.citation: Saeterbakken AH, van den Tillaar R, Fimland MS. A comparison of muscle activity and 1-RM strength of three chest-press exercises with different stability requirements. Journal of Sports Sciences. 2011;29(5):533-538. doi:10.1080/02640414.2010.543916.
studies.relevance: Directly compares dumbbell pressing with more stable press modes and supports the support/stability scoring and biceps support classification.

studies.type: Upper-body lift EMG comparison
studies.finding: Measured pectoralis major and anterior deltoid activity during barbell bench press, dumbbell bench press, and dumbbell fly.
studies.citation: Welsch EA, Bird M, Mayhew JL. Electromyographic Activity of the Pectoralis Major and Anterior Deltoid Muscles During Three Upper-Body Lifts. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2005;19(2):449-452. doi:10.1519/14513.1.
studies.relevance: Directly includes dumbbell bench press and supports pectoralis major and anterior deltoid classification.

studies.type: Systematic review of bench press EMG
studies.finding: Bench press EMG literature supports pec/triceps dominance and highlights stability, intensity, phase, and technique limits.
studies.citation: Stastny P, Golas A, Blazek D, Maszczyk A, Wilk M, Pietraszewski P, Petr M, Uhlir P, Zajac A. A systematic review of surface electromyography analyses of the bench press movement task. PLOS ONE. 2017;12(2):e0171632. doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0171632.
studies.relevance: Provides movement-family context for pectoralis major, triceps brachii, anterior deltoid, and stability-condition interpretation.

studies.type: Rotator cuff recruitment study
studies.shortCitation: Wattanaprakornkul et al., J Electromyogr Kinesiol, 2011
studies.finding: Rotator cuff recruitment is direction-specific during bench press and row tasks.
studies.citation: Wattanaprakornkul D, Halaki M, Cathers I, Ginn KA. Direction-specific recruitment of rotator cuff muscles during bench press and row. Journal of Electromyography and Kinesiology. 2011;21(6):1041-1049. doi:10.1016/j.jelekin.2011.09.002.
studies.relevance: Supports rotator cuff involvement as shoulder stabilization during pressing tasks.

studies.type: Chest press lever machine EMG and scapular kinematics
studies.finding: Chest press lever machine data includes pec, anterior deltoid, serratus, and scapular kinematics.
studies.citation: Borges E, Dalla H, Mastandrea L, Nunes S, Santarem J. Comparative evaluation of muscular activation and scapular kinematics in a chest press lever machine and a barbell bench press. Journal of Physical Education and Sport. 2019;19:912-916. doi:10.7752/jpes.2019.s3131.
studies.relevance: Supports serratus anterior as scapulothoracic support in the close horizontal pressing family.

movements.name: Dumbbell Shrug
movements.variant: Standing bilateral dumbbell shrug with arms at the sides and scapular elevation performed without rolling the shoulders.
movements.description: Stand tall holding dumbbells at the sides, keep the elbows long and ribs stacked, then lift the shoulders straight up toward the ears without bending the arms or rolling the shoulders. Pause briefly at the top, then lower the shoulder blades under control until the traps are lengthened.

hypertrophy.rationale: Good local trap hypertrophy accessory, but the visible anatomy entry is broad and the movement is narrow.

strength.rationale: Can be loaded heavily for scapular-elevation strength, though range is short and force expression is not broadly transferable.

joint_resilience.rationale: Can build neck and shoulder-girdle loading tolerance, but it is not a broad joint-resilience anchor.

athletic_transfer.rationale: Limited transfer outside loaded carrying and shoulder-girdle bracing contexts.

control.rationale: Low-to-moderate control demand: the main requirements are posture, straight-up scapular elevation, and avoiding shoulder rolling.

fatigue_efficiency.rationale: Focused local stimulus with modest systemic cost, although heavy dumbbells add grip and postural fatigue.

setup.rationale: Requires only dumbbells and standing space, with no bench or machine adjustment.

ease.rationale: Very easy to learn, with the main errors being arm pull, shoulder rolling, and excessive load.

progression.rationale: Dumbbell loading and reps are easy to track, but dumbbell jumps and grip can limit smooth progression.

support.rationale: The movement path is simple, but standing free weights provide little external support.

primary.name: Trapezius
primary.evidenceShort: Shrug EMG shows very high trapezius activation.
primary.evidence: Direct shrug EMG evidence reports the highest trapezius activation during shrug variations, with loaded shrugs reaching very high upper-trapezius activity compared with other neck and shoulder strengthening exercises.

evidence.verdict: Standing dumbbell shrug: trapezius primary; no separate secondary or support muscles listed.
evidence.clinicalShort: EMG estimates acute excitation, not hypertrophy, mechanical tension, adaptation, or injury risk.
evidence.limitsShort: The visible anatomy entry is whole trapezius even though most shrug evidence emphasizes upper trapezius.
evidence.summary: The dumbbell shrug is classified as a simple loaded scapular-elevation exercise. Direct EMG evidence supports trapezius as the main target, especially upper-trapezius fibers. No separate support roles are listed because available local anatomy does not expose levator scapulae, and other stabilization claims would not add a clear visible app role.
evidence.clinicalInterpretation: Shrugs can provide a focused local trap stimulus when performed without shoulder rolling or elbow flexion. EMG evidence supports acute trapezius excitation but does not by itself define hypertrophy, pain outcomes, or injury risk.
evidence.limitations: The strongest evidence reports upper trapezius, but local anatomy maps Trapezius as a whole and does not provide standalone upper trapezius or levator scapulae meshes. Barbell shrugs, trap-bar shrugs, behind-the-back shrugs, seated dumbbell shrugs, and incline shrugs should be separate entries if added later.

studies.type: Neck and shoulder strength-exercise EMG
studies.finding: Shrugs produced the highest trapezius activation among the tested neck and shoulder strengthening exercises in women with trapezius myalgia.
studies.citation: Andersen LL, Kjaer M, Andersen CH, Hansen PB, Zebis MK, Hansen K, Sjoegaard G. Muscle activation during selected strength exercises in women with chronic neck muscle pain. Physical Therapy. 2008;88(6):703-711. doi:10.2522/ptj.20070304.
studies.relevance: Direct loaded shrug EMG evidence supporting trapezius as the primary visible target.

studies.type: Trapezius and serratus anterior exercise EMG
studies.finding: The unilateral shoulder shrug produced the greatest upper-trapezius EMG activity among tested trapezius exercises.
studies.citation: Ekstrom RA, Donatelli RA, Soderberg GL. Surface electromyographic analysis of exercises for the trapezius and serratus anterior muscles. Journal of Orthopaedic and Sports Physical Therapy. 2003;33(5):247-258. doi:10.2519/jospt.2003.33.5.247.
studies.relevance: Direct shrug-family EMG evidence for upper-trapezius dominance.

movements.name: Dumbbell Walking Lunge
movements.variant: Alternating dumbbell walking lunge with two free weights held at the sides.
movements.description: Stand tall holding matching dumbbells at the sides, step forward into a long enough stride to lower under control without the front heel lifting, descend until the rear knee approaches the floor, then drive through the lead foot and bring the trailing leg forward into the next step. Alternate legs while keeping the torso controlled, the front knee tracking over the foot, and each step length consistent.

hypertrophy.rationale: Meaningful lower-body hypertrophy stimulus, especially for quads and glutes, but balance, breathing, and locomotion can limit target-muscle loading.

strength.rationale: Builds unilateral force capacity, but load expression is less clean than bilateral barbell or machine patterns.

joint_resilience.rationale: Excellent knee, hip, ankle, and connective-tissue capacity builder when progressed well because it loads long ranges, single-leg support, and repeated deceleration.

athletic_transfer.rationale: Elite transfer dimension because it combines loaded gait, unilateral support, hip-knee-ankle coordination, trunk control, and forward force transfer.

control.rationale: Very high control demand from dynamic balance, step length, pelvis control, trunk position, grip, and repeated single-leg transitions.

fatigue_efficiency.rationale: Low efficiency for isolated stimulus because breathing, grip, balance, locomotion, and large-muscle systemic fatigue accumulate quickly.

setup.rationale: Requires only dumbbells and floor space, but usable lane length, turning, matched loads, and heavy dumbbell pickup add friction.

ease.rationale: Technically and physically demanding: stride length, knee tracking, balance, depth, torso angle, and continuous stepping are all easy to vary unintentionally.

progression.rationale: Progression is possible through load, steps, and reps, but measurement is noisy because stride length, lane length, balance, and fatigue alter difficulty.

support.rationale: Almost no external support: the user stabilizes each step through the foot, ankle, knee, hip, pelvis, trunk, and grip.

primary.name: Quadriceps
primary.evidenceShort: High VM/VL/RF activity in loaded forward and walking lunges.
primary.evidence: Direct dumbbell forward-lunge-with-stride and walking-lunge studies report high vastus medialis and vastus lateralis activation, with rectus femoris also measured; lunge studies consistently place quadriceps among the main knee-extension contributors.

primary.name: Gluteus maximus
primary.evidenceShort: High hip-extension demand in loaded lunge evidence.
primary.evidence: The closest two-dumbbell forward-lunge-with-stride study reported high gluteus maximus activity during ascent, and loaded anterior-lunge biomechanics identify the lunge as hip-extensor dominant. This supports gluteus maximus as a primary hip-extension target, while recognizing that step length and trunk angle shift emphasis.

secondary.name: Hamstrings
secondary.evidenceShort: Measured moderate posterior-chain contribution.
secondary.evidence: Walking-lunge and dumbbell forward-lunge studies measure biceps femoris and semitendinosus activity; activation is meaningful but generally below the strongest quadriceps and gluteal signals, so hamstrings are classified as secondary rather than primary.

support.name: Gluteus medius
support.evidenceShort: High frontal-plane and pelvic-control demand in walking lunges.
support.evidence: Walking-lunge evidence reports substantial gluteus medius activity, and the dynamic walking or with-stride component increases demand compared with more static lunge patterns. It is listed as support because its main role is pelvic, hip, and frontal-plane control rather than sagittal-plane propulsion.

support.name: Adductor longus
support.evidenceShort: Moderate activation in dumbbell forward-lunge variants.
support.evidence: The closest bilateral-dumbbell forward-lunge study measured moderate adductor longus activity, especially with longer step conditions, supporting a visible support role for hip and stance control.

support.name: Gastrocnemius
support.evidenceShort: Measured ankle/stance contribution during loaded lunges.
support.evidence: Dumbbell forward-lunge evidence measured moderate gastrocnemius activation, and external-load biomechanics show ankle work rising with load. This supports a calf support role for ankle control and forward stepping rather than a primary hypertrophy target.

support.name: Trunk stabilizers
support.evidenceShort: Dumbbell lunge loading changes trunk muscle activation.
support.evidence: A lunge load-distribution EMG study measured erector spinae, external oblique, rectus abdominis, and latissimus dorsi responses to dumbbell loading positions; this supports a trunk stabilization role, especially when dumbbells challenge posture and anti-rotation.

evidence.verdict: Alternating dumbbell walking lunge: quadriceps and gluteus maximus primary; hamstrings secondary; gluteus medius, adductor longus, gastrocnemius, and trunk stabilizers support.
evidence.clinicalShort: EMG estimates acute excitation, not hypertrophy, mechanical tension, long-term adaptation, or injury risk.
evidence.limitsShort: Continuous walking, push-back forward lunges, step length, trunk angle, dumbbell load, and dumbbell carrying position all change emphasis.
evidence.summary: The dumbbell walking lunge is classified as a dynamic unilateral lower-body compound exercise. The best evidence includes a direct dumbbell forward-lunge-with-stride EMG study using two dumbbells, walking-lunge EMG studies using load-carrying variants, forward-lunge EMG studies, and loaded lunge biomechanics. These sources support quadriceps and gluteus maximus as the main prime movers, hamstrings as meaningful assistants, and gluteus medius, adductor longus, gastrocnemius, and trunk stabilizers as control or support contributors.
evidence.clinicalInterpretation: Surface electromyography is useful for estimating acute muscle excitation in a given technique and load condition. It should not be interpreted as a direct measure of hypertrophy, mechanical tension, training adaptation, soreness, joint safety, or injury risk.
evidence.limitations: Exact evidence for a continuous alternating two-dumbbell walking lunge is limited. The strongest exact walking-lunge studies used walking lunges with dumbbell carrying-position variations or examined associations with strength ratios, while the strongest bilateral-dumbbell source used forward lunges with a stride and a push back to the start. Step length, trunk lean, stride continuity, load, fatigue, footwear, and participant training status can materially alter muscle activity and joint loading.

studies.type: Dumbbell forward-lunge stride and step-length EMG
studies.finding: With two dumbbells and 12RM loads, forward lunges with stride showed high to very high quadriceps, gluteus maximus, and gluteus medius activity, with moderate hamstrings, gastrocnemius, and adductor longus activity.
studies.citation: Escamilla RF, Thompson IS, Asuncion R, Bravo J, Chang T, Fournier T, Garcia H, Hockenbery E, Nagasawa K, Ozor J, Snoeberger H, Wilk KE, Bizzini M. Effects of Step Length and Stride Variation During Forward Lunges on Lower-Extremity Muscle Activity. Journal of Functional Morphology and Kinesiology. 2025;10(1):42. doi:10.3390/jfmk10010042.
studies.relevance: Closest bilateral-dumbbell source: participants held one dumbbell in each hand and performed forward lunge variations with and without a stride while lower-extremity EMG was recorded.

studies.type: Walking-lunge dumbbell carrying-position EMG
studies.finding: Compared dumbbell carrying positions during split squats and walking lunges, measuring gluteus medius, vastus medialis, vastus lateralis, and biceps femoris.
studies.citation: Stastny P, Lehnert M, Zaatar AMZ, Svoboda Z, Xaverova Z. Does the Dumbbell-Carrying Position Change the Muscle Activity in Split Squats and Walking Lunges? Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2015;29(11):3177-3187. doi:10.1519/JSC.0000000000000976.
studies.relevance: Directly includes walking lunges and dumbbell loading, but the loading arrangement studied carrying position rather than the exact bilateral-at-sides assumption.

studies.type: Walking-lunge and split-squat EMG
studies.finding: Resistance-trained men performed walking lunges and split squats at 5RM; walking lunges produced higher gluteus medius activity than split squats and were recommended when gluteus medius or vastus medialis strengthening is the aim.
studies.citation: Stastny P, Tufano JJ, Lehnert M, Golas A, Zaatar A, Xaverova Z, Maszczyk A. Hip abductors and thigh muscles strength ratios and their relation to electromyography amplitude during split squat and walking lunge exercises. Acta Gymnica. 2015;45(2):51-59. doi:10.5507/ag.2015.011.
studies.relevance: Direct walking-lunge EMG evidence for vastus medialis, vastus lateralis, biceps femoris, and gluteus medius in trained men.

studies.type: Forward-lunge EMG comparison
studies.finding: In forward lunges, vastus lateralis and vastus medialis showed the highest activation, followed by gluteus medius and gluteus maximus, then rectus femoris and biceps femoris.
studies.citation: Muyor JM, Martin-Fuentes I, Rodriguez-Ridao D, Antequera-Vique JA. Electromyographic activity in the gluteus medius, gluteus maximus, biceps femoris, vastus lateralis, vastus medialis and rectus femoris during the Monopodal Squat, Forward Lunge and Lateral Step-Up exercises. PLOS ONE. 2020;15(4):e0230841. doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0230841.
studies.relevance: Close lunge-family EMG evidence measuring key quadriceps, gluteal, and hamstring muscles during forward lunges at 60% of 5RM.

studies.type: Loaded anterior-lunge biomechanics
studies.shortCitation: Riemann et al., J Athl Train, 2012
studies.finding: Anterior lunges with added external load were hip-extensor dominant kinetically; adding load increased mechanical work mainly at the hip and ankle.
studies.citation: Riemann BL, Lapinski S, Smith L, Davies G. Biomechanical Analysis of the Anterior Lunge During 4 External-Load Conditions. Journal of Athletic Training. 2012;47(4):372-378. doi:10.4085/1062-6050-47.4.16.
studies.relevance: Biomechanical evidence for hip and ankle joint demand under external loading in a close anterior-lunge pattern.

studies.type: Squat and lunge loading-device EMG
studies.shortCitation: Wu et al., J Sport Rehabil, 2020
studies.finding: Loaded lunges showed higher activation than unloaded lunges; quadriceps and hamstring activities were higher in lunge than squat, and lunge muscle activation did not differ meaningfully among the tested loading devices.
studies.citation: Wu HW, Tsai CF, Liang KH, Chang YW. Effect of Loading Devices on Muscle Activation in Squat and Lunge. Journal of Sport Rehabilitation. 2020;29(2):200-205. doi:10.1123/jsr.2018-0182.
studies.relevance: Supports the interpretation that loading increases lunge muscle activity and that dumbbell loading is a reasonable free-weight lunge condition.

studies.type: Dumbbell forward-lunge EMG load and contraction comparison
studies.shortCitation: Jakobsen et al., Hum Mov Sci, 2013
studies.finding: Standardized forward lunges performed with dumbbells and elastic resistance showed load-dependent EMG increases; quadriceps and gluteus EMG increased at flexed knee positions.
studies.citation: Jakobsen MD, Sundstrup E, Andersen CH, Aagaard P, Andersen LL. Muscle activity during leg strengthening exercise using free weights and elastic resistance: Effects of ballistic vs controlled contractions. Human Movement Science. 2013;32(1):65-78. doi:10.1016/j.humov.2012.07.002.
studies.relevance: Directly includes dumbbell forward lunges and supports load-dependent quadriceps and gluteal activation in a close free-weight lunge pattern.

studies.type: Lunge load-distribution trunk EMG
studies.finding: Dumbbell lunge load placement changed erector spinae, external oblique, rectus abdominis, and latissimus dorsi activation, supporting trunk stabilization demands.
studies.citation: Lopez-de-Celis C, Labata-Lezaun N, Romani-Sanchez S, Gasso-Villarejo S, Garcia-Ribell E, Rodriguez-Sanz J, Perez-Bellmunt A. Effect of Load Distribution on Trunk Muscle Activity with Lunge Exercises in Amateur Athletes: Cross-Sectional Study. Healthcare. 2023;11(6):916. doi:10.3390/healthcare11060916.
studies.relevance: Direct lunge evidence for trunk muscle support under dumbbell loading arrangements.

studies.type: Dumbbell lunge-squat biomechanics
studies.finding: In novice men, dumbbell-loaded lunge squats showed smaller center-of-pressure displacement and high hip-joint moment changes compared with other loading conditions.
studies.citation: Gao L, Lu Z, Liang M, Baker JS, Gu Y. Influence of Different Load Conditions on Lower Extremity Biomechanics during the Lunge Squat in Novice Men. Bioengineering. 2022;9(7):272. doi:10.3390/bioengineering9070272.
studies.relevance: Supports dumbbell-loading rating interpretation for stability, hip demand, and load-condition limitations in a close lunge-squat task.

movements.name: EZ-Bar Skull Crusher
movements.variant: Supine EZ-bar lying triceps extension on a flat bench, lowering the bar toward the forehead or slightly behind the head and extending the elbows without turning it into a press.
movements.description: Lie on a flat bench holding an EZ bar with the arms angled slightly back from vertical and the elbows about shoulder width. Keep the upper arms mostly fixed, lower the bar under control toward the forehead or just behind the head by bending the elbows, then extend the elbows to return the bar without flaring the elbows or letting the shoulders take over the rep.

hypertrophy.rationale: Strong triceps hypertrophy accessory because lying barbell triceps press and lying elbow-extension studies support targeted triceps growth and loading.

strength.rationale: Useful for elbow-extension strength and pressing assistance, but the single-joint setup is less suited to maximal force expression than compound presses.

joint_resilience.rationale: Can provide controlled elbow-extension loading, but loaded deep elbow flexion and the free bar make it only a narrow resilience tool.

athletic_transfer.rationale: Very little athletic-transfer signal because the lift is supine, isolated, and not coordinated with whole-body force transfer.

control.rationale: Requires moderate elbow path, wrist, shoulder angle, and free-bar control, but the bench removes most balance and trunk demand.

fatigue_efficiency.rationale: Good local triceps stimulus with low systemic fatigue, though elbow irritation and shoulder drift can limit efficient hard sets.

setup.rationale: Requires a bench, EZ bar, plates or fixed bar selection, and a safe start position, so setup is moderate.

ease.rationale: The movement is straightforward, but consistent elbow position, bar path, depth, and avoiding a press-out pattern take practice.

progression.rationale: Load and reps are trackable, with deductions for plate jumps, elbow tolerance, and technique changes as load increases.

support.rationale: The bench supports the body, but the bar path and elbow position remain free and require user control.

primary.name: Triceps brachii
primary.evidenceShort: Lying barbell triceps-extension studies support triceps as the target.
primary.evidence: Longitudinal training studies using lying barbell triceps press or lying elbow extension measured triceps brachii size and strength adaptations. Exercise-order EMG work also used lying triceps extension as the single-joint triceps task, while elbow-extension biomechanics supports triceps brachii as the prime elbow extensor.

evidence.verdict: EZ-bar skull crusher: triceps brachii primary; no visible secondary or support muscles added.
evidence.clinicalShort: EMG and imaging studies estimate excitation and adaptation under specific protocols, not pain or injury risk.
evidence.limitsShort: Bar type, grip angle, upper-arm angle, lowering target, bench angle, elbow range, load, tempo, and shoulder movement can shift emphasis and tolerance.
evidence.summary: The EZ-bar skull crusher is classified as a supine free-bar elbow-extension isolation movement. Direct evidence is closest for lying barbell triceps press or lying elbow extension rather than the EZ-bar grip specifically, but those studies support triceps brachii as the primary visible target. No secondary or support muscles are shown because the movement is intended to isolate elbow extension and the reviewed studies did not justify additional mapped visible roles.
evidence.clinicalInterpretation: Surface electromyography and longitudinal muscle-size measures help interpret triceps involvement under specific setups. They should not be treated as direct measures of mechanical tension, individual hypertrophy response, pain risk, or injury risk.
evidence.limitations: Direct evidence usually uses straight barbell or dumbbell lying triceps extension labels rather than an EZ bar specifically. The EZ bar mainly changes wrist and grip comfort, so the muscle classification is inferred from lying barbell triceps extension and elbow-extension evidence. Lowering to the forehead, lowering behind the head, incline/decline benches, dumbbells, cables, and close-grip press hybrids should be separate variants if detailed distinctions are needed.

studies.type: Lying barbell triceps press hypertrophy and strength study
studies.finding: A 10-week program including lying barbell triceps press measured triceps brachii cross-sectional area and lying triceps press 1RM adaptations.
studies.citation: Brandao L, de Salles Painelli V, Lasevicius T, Silva-Batista C, Brendon H, Schoenfeld BJ, Aihara AY, Cardoso FN, de Almeida Peres B, Teixeira EL. Varying the Order of Combinations of Single- and Multi-Joint Exercises Differentially Affects Resistance Training Adaptations. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2020;34(5):1254-1263. doi:10.1519/JSC.0000000000003550.
studies.relevance: Directly used the lying barbell triceps press, the closest loaded barbell skull-crusher variant, and measured triceps size and strength outcomes.

studies.type: Lying elbow extension partial versus full ROM training study
studies.finding: Young trained men performing lying elbow extension increased triceps brachii cross-sectional area and strength after both partial and full range-of-motion protocols.
studies.citation: Goto M, Maeda C, Hirayama T, Terada S, Nirengi S, Kurosawa Y, Nagano A, Hamaoka T. Partial Range of Motion Exercise Is Effective for Facilitating Muscle Hypertrophy and Function Through Sustained Intramuscular Hypoxia in Young Trained Men. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2019;33(5):1286-1294. doi:10.1519/JSC.0000000000002051.
studies.relevance: Direct lying elbow-extension training evidence for triceps hypertrophy and strength, though not specific to an EZ-bar grip.

studies.type: Upper-body exercise-order EMG including lying triceps extension
studies.finding: Upper-body exercise-order study included lying triceps extension as the single-joint triceps exercise while monitoring muscle activation and performance.
studies.citation: Gentil P, Oliveira E, de Araujo Rocha Junior V, do Carmo J, Bottaro M. Effects of exercise order on upper-body muscle activation and exercise performance. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2007;21(4):1082-1086. doi:10.1519/R-21216.1.
studies.relevance: Directly includes lying triceps extension in an EMG exercise-order protocol; used as supporting evidence that the lift functions as a triceps-focused single-joint movement.

studies.type: Triceps head function by shoulder elevation
studies.shortCitation: Kholinne et al., Acta Orthop Traumatol Turc, 2018
studies.finding: Each triceps head showed different force and activity patterns across shoulder elevation angles during elbow-extension tasks.
studies.citation: Kholinne E, Zulkarnain RF, Sun YC, Lim S, Chun JM, Jeon IH. The different role of each head of the triceps brachii muscle in elbow extension. Acta Orthopaedica et Traumatologica Turcica. 2018;52(3):201-205. doi:10.1016/j.aott.2018.02.005.
studies.relevance: Biomechanics and EMG context for triceps contribution to elbow extension when the shoulder is flexed in a lying extension setup.

movements.name: Face Pull
movements.variant: Standing cable rope face pull to eye or forehead height, finished with shoulder horizontal abduction, scapular retraction, and mild external rotation.
movements.description: Set a cable near face height with a rope handle, stand tall with the arms long, and pull the rope toward the eyes or forehead by driving the elbows out and back. Let the hands separate beside the face, pause with the shoulder blades pulled together without shrugging hard, then return under control until the arms are long again.

hypertrophy.rationale: Useful rear-shoulder and upper-back hypertrophy accessory, but loading is usually limited by shoulder position and external-rotation control.

strength.rationale: Builds local pulling strength, but it is not a high-force strength anchor and heavy loading often turns it into a row.

joint_resilience.rationale: Good shoulder-girdle tolerance signal from controlled scapular retraction and external rotation, although it is still an accessory exercise.

athletic_transfer.rationale: Some carryover to shoulder positioning and throwing/postural control, but little whole-body force transfer.

control.rationale: Requires elbow path, scapular timing, external-rotation finish, and load selection discipline.

fatigue_efficiency.rationale: Low systemic fatigue and focused local stimulus when performed with moderate load and strict control.

setup.rationale: Requires a cable station and rope attachment, but height and load changes are quick once the station is available.

ease.rationale: Simple to start, but easy to compensate with lumbar extension, elbow drop, biceps pulling, or excessive shrugging.

progression.rationale: Cable stacks progress measurably, but useful overload is constrained by technique quality and small target muscles.

support.rationale: The cable provides a consistent line of pull, but the user must stabilize the trunk, shoulder blades, and free arm path.

primary.name: Posterior deltoid
primary.evidenceShort: High-abduction row and rear-delt EMG support the main role.
primary.evidence: A face pull combines a high horizontal pulling path with shoulder horizontal abduction; seated cable row evidence shows posterior deltoid activity rises as shoulder abduction approaches 60-90 degrees, and rear-delt EMG studies identify rear-lateral-raise and incline-row patterns as strong posterior-deltoid tasks.

secondary.name: Middle trapezius
secondary.evidenceShort: Measured high-abduction row and horizontal-abduction contributor.
secondary.evidence: Cable row evidence shows middle trapezius activity increases at larger shoulder-abduction angles, and trapezius exercise EMG identifies shoulder horizontal extension with external rotation as a high middle-trapezius task.

secondary.name: Rhomboids
secondary.evidenceShort: Included by scapular-retraction inference from row-family evidence.
secondary.evidence: This is an explicit anatomy and movement-pattern inference: the face pull requires scapular retraction, and row-family EMG plus technique evidence supports rhomboid involvement alongside middle trapezius during retraction-dominant pulling.

secondary.name: Rotator cuff
secondary.evidenceShort: External-rotation evidence supports cuff contribution.
secondary.evidence: The face-pull finish adds shoulder external rotation; pulley external-rotation EMG shows increasing rotator-cuff recruitment with rotation resistance, supporting a meaningful cuff role when the exercise is not performed as a plain row.

evidence.verdict: Standing cable face pull: posterior deltoid primary; middle trapezius, rhomboids, and rotator cuff secondary; no separate support muscles listed.
evidence.clinicalShort: EMG estimates acute excitation, not hypertrophy, mechanical tension, adaptation, or injury risk.
evidence.limitsShort: No peer-reviewed exact face-pull EMG study was found; this entry uses high-abduction row, posterior-deltoid, scapular, and external-rotation evidence.
evidence.summary: The face pull is classified as a light-to-moderate cable upper-back and rear-shoulder accessory. The best available evidence supports posterior deltoid as the main visible target because high-abduction cable rows and rear-delt exercise studies load similar shoulder horizontal-abduction demands. Middle trapezius and rhomboids are included for scapular retraction, and rotator cuff is included because the chosen variant finishes with shoulder external rotation.
evidence.clinicalInterpretation: The exercise is most useful when the load is light enough to preserve the face-height pull and external-rotation finish. Heavy loading shifts the pattern toward a high row and reduces the specificity of the cuff and posterior-shoulder stimulus.
evidence.limitations: Direct exact-variant face-pull EMG evidence was not found in the reviewed peer-reviewed sources. Infraspinatus, teres minor, and upper trapezius are important in the literature, but this project exposes only a rotator cuff aggregate and a full trapezius or middle/lower trapezius mapping, so the visible roles stay within the available anatomy. Band face pulls, chest-supported face pulls, no-external-rotation high rows, and rear-delt cable flyes should be separate variants if added later.

studies.type: Seated cable row EMG and force study
studies.shortCitation: Vasconcelos et al., Int J Strength Cond, 2023
studies.finding: Upper-back activation, including middle trapezius and posterior deltoid, increased as seated cable row shoulder abduction moved toward 60-90 degrees.
studies.citation: Vasconcelos CMWA, Lopes CR, Almeida VM, Neto WK, Soares EG. Effect Of Different Grip Position And Shoulder-Abduction Angle On Muscle Strength And Activation During The Seated Cable Row. International Journal of Strength and Conditioning. 2023;3(1):1-13. doi:10.47206/ijsc.v3i1.190.
studies.relevance: Closest cable-pull evidence for the high-abduction pulling component of a face pull.

studies.type: Deltoid exercise EMG thesis
studies.shortCitation: Sweeney, University of Wisconsin-La Crosse thesis, 2014
studies.finding: Seated rear lateral raise and 45-degree incline row produced the greatest posterior-deltoid activation among the tested shoulder exercises.
studies.citation: Sweeney SP. Electromyographic analysis of the deltoid muscle during various shoulder exercises. Master's thesis, University of Wisconsin-La Crosse. 2014.
studies.relevance: Primary EMG source for posterior-deltoid loading in close rear-shoulder and high-row patterns.

studies.type: Trapezius and serratus anterior exercise EMG
studies.finding: Shoulder horizontal extension with external rotation generated high middle-trapezius activity, and prone overhead arm raise strongly activated lower trapezius.
studies.citation: Ekstrom RA, Donatelli RA, Soderberg GL. Surface electromyographic analysis of exercises for the trapezius and serratus anterior muscles. Journal of Orthopaedic and Sports Physical Therapy. 2003;33(5):247-258. doi:10.2519/jospt.2003.33.5.247.
studies.relevance: Close shoulder horizontal-abduction and scapular-control EMG evidence for middle trapezius and retraction mechanics.

studies.type: Rotator cuff pulley external-rotation EMG
studies.finding: Pulley shoulder external-rotation tasks increased recruitment of rotator-cuff and other shoulder rotation torque-generating muscles as resistance increased.
studies.citation: Dark A, Ginn KA, Halaki M. Shoulder muscle recruitment patterns during commonly used rotator cuff exercises: an electromyographic study. Physical Therapy. 2007;87(8):1039-1046. doi:10.2522/ptj.20060068.
studies.relevance: Supports the external-rotation component of a face pull as a rotator-cuff contribution.

movements.name: Forearm Plank
movements.variant: Standard forearm plank hold from elbows and toes with a straight body line and neutral spine.
movements.description: Set the elbows under the shoulders, step both feet back, brace the ribs toward the pelvis, and hold a straight line from shoulders through heels without sagging the low back or hiking the hips.

hypertrophy.rationale: Useful abdominal tension for beginners, but the load is mostly bodyweight isometric endurance and has a low local hypertrophy ceiling.

strength.rationale: Builds basic trunk anti-extension strength, but progression is indirect and peak force is much lower than loaded core or compound lifts.

joint_resilience.rationale: Can build shoulder, trunk, and lumbopelvic tolerance when alignment is held, but it is not a broad joint-loading stimulus.

athletic_transfer.rationale: Static bracing carries over to general trunk control, but the movement lacks standing force transfer, gait, rotation, or limb coordination.

control.rationale: High positional-control demand from maintaining rib, pelvis, shoulder, and spinal alignment without external support.

fatigue_efficiency.rationale: Low systemic fatigue and easy recovery cost, though long holds can drift toward endurance fatigue rather than targeted loading.

setup.rationale: Requires only floor space and no equipment adjustment.

ease.rationale: Simple to understand, but many users lose pelvic or lumbar position as fatigue accumulates.
