progression.rationale: Progression is usually by time, lever length, or variation rather than clean load increments.

support.rationale: The floor supports the forearms and toes, but trunk and shoulder stability are mostly self-generated.

primary.name: Rectus abdominis
primary.evidenceShort: Traditional and modified plank EMG supports rectus activation.
primary.evidence: Direct prone-plank EMG studies measured rectus abdominis activity during standard planks, with higher activation when lever length, posterior pelvic tilt, hip adduction, or instability increased the demand.

primary.name: External oblique
primary.evidenceShort: Plank EMG studies consistently measure external-oblique demand.
primary.evidence: Traditional plank and modified plank EMG studies measured external oblique activity, and posterior pelvic tilt or additional hip adduction increased external-oblique activation relative to the standard plank.

secondary.name: Internal oblique
secondary.evidenceShort: Standard plank EMG measured internal-oblique activation.
secondary.evidence: A plank EMG study measuring rectus abdominis, internal oblique, and external oblique supports internal oblique as a meaningful trunk-stability contributor, though not the main visible target.

support.name: Erector spinae
support.evidenceShort: Prone-bridge studies measure spinal-extensor stabilization demand.
support.evidence: Plank and prone-bridge EMG studies measured erector spinae or related spinal extensor activity, supporting a stabilizing role rather than a primary target in the stable forearm plank.

evidence.verdict: Forearm plank: rectus abdominis and external oblique primary; internal oblique secondary; erector spinae support.
evidence.clinicalShort: EMG estimates acute excitation; it does not prove hypertrophy, adaptation, or injury risk.
evidence.limitsShort: Lever length, pelvic tilt, hip adduction, surface stability, fatigue, and hold duration can materially change activation.
evidence.summary: The standard forearm plank is classified as a low-setup trunk anti-extension hold. Direct plank EMG supports rectus abdominis, external oblique, and internal oblique involvement, while erector spinae is included as a stabilizer.
evidence.clinicalInterpretation: The movement is most useful as a bracing and endurance-control drill, not as a high-load abdominal hypertrophy anchor.
evidence.limitations: Several high-activation results come from modified or unstable plank variations rather than the standard stable forearm plank. Transversus abdominis and quadratus lumborum were not added as visible roles because local anatomy mapping does not provide those muscles as separate display targets.

studies.type: Plank variation EMG
studies.finding: Compared traditional stable planks with instability-device planks and measured rectus abdominis, external oblique, and erector spinae EMG.
studies.citation: Snarr RL, Esco MR. Electromyographical comparison of plank variations performed with and without instability devices. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2014;28(11):3298-3305. doi:10.1519/JSC.0000000000000521.
studies.relevance: Direct plank-family EMG source for rectus abdominis, external oblique, and erector spinae roles.

studies.type: Traditional and modified prone plank EMG
studies.finding: Long-lever posterior-tilt plank increased upper rectus abdominis, lower abdominal stabilizer, and external oblique activation compared with the traditional prone plank.
studies.citation: Schoenfeld BJ, Contreras B, Tiryaki-Sonmez G, Willardson JM, Fontana F. An electromyographic comparison of a modified version of the plank with a long lever and posterior tilt versus the traditional plank exercise. Sports Biomechanics. 2014;13(3):296-306. doi:10.1080/14763141.2014.942355.
studies.relevance: Direct comparison against traditional prone plank; used to classify abdominal emphasis and note modification effects.

studies.type: Plank abdominal EMG
studies.shortCitation: Kim et al., J Electromyogr Kinesiol, 2016
studies.finding: Measured rectus abdominis, internal oblique, and external oblique during standard plank and plank with additional hip adduction; added hip adduction increased abdominal activity.
studies.citation: Kim SY, Kang MH, Kim ER, Jung IG, Seo EY, Oh JS. Comparison of EMG activity on abdominal muscles during plank exercise with unilateral and bilateral additional isometric hip adduction. Journal of Electromyography and Kinesiology. 2016;30:9-14. doi:10.1016/j.jelekin.2016.05.003.
studies.relevance: Direct plank source measuring rectus abdominis plus both oblique muscles.

studies.type: Core rehabilitation exercise EMG
studies.finding: Measured core, hip, and thigh EMG during prone bridge on elbows and toes and other rehabilitation exercises.
studies.citation: Ekstrom RA, Donatelli RA, Carp KC. Electromyographic analysis of core trunk, hip, and thigh muscles during 9 rehabilitation exercises. Journal of Orthopaedic and Sports Physical Therapy. 2007;37(12):754-762. doi:10.2519/jospt.2007.2471.
studies.relevance: Direct prone-bridge source for stabilizer interpretation and rating boundaries.

movements.name: 45-Degree Back Extension
movements.variant: 45-degree Roman chair back extension performed through hip extension with the pelvis supported by the pad.
movements.description: Set the hip pad just below the pelvis, brace the feet, cross the arms or hold the load securely, and start with the body in a straight line. Hinge down from the hips without collapsing the lower back, then extend the hips and trunk until the body returns to a straight line without hyperextending at the top.

hypertrophy.rationale: Strong hamstring, glute, and erector stimulus for a hinge accessory, with load limited by station setup and torso-held resistance.

strength.rationale: Builds hip and trunk extension strength well as an accessory, but absolute loading and force expression are lower than barbell hinges.

joint_resilience.rationale: Useful controlled exposure for the posterior chain and trunk extensors through repeatable range when pad setup and spinal position are appropriate.

athletic_transfer.rationale: Can support posterior-chain capacity, but the fixed station and bilateral path are less transferable than loaded free-standing or sport-like patterns.

control.rationale: Requires hip-hinge, pelvic, and trunk-position control, but the foot brace and pad reduce balance and whole-body coordination demands.

fatigue_efficiency.rationale: Provides useful posterior-chain stimulus with less systemic cost than heavy barbell deadlifts, though local back and hamstring fatigue can still be high.

setup.rationale: Quick once a 45-degree Roman chair is available, with only pad height, stance, and optional load to set.

ease.rationale: The station is approachable, but users still need to separate hip motion from lumbar rounding or excessive lockout extension.

progression.rationale: Load can be added with plates, dumbbells, or vests, but increments and secure loading become awkward compared with barbells or machines.

support.rationale: The pad and foot brace provide meaningful external support, while the torso still moves freely and requires active trunk control.

primary.name: Hamstrings
primary.evidenceShort: Direct 45-degree back-extension studies show high biceps femoris and hamstring activation.
primary.evidence: Direct Roman chair and 45-degree hip-extension studies report high biceps femoris or hamstring activation, with Roman chair back extension outperforming Romanian deadlift for biceps femoris in one trained-women comparison.

primary.name: Gluteus maximus
primary.evidenceShort: Measured gluteus maximus activity supports a primary hip-extension role.
primary.evidence: The 45-degree Roman chair back extension directly activated gluteus maximus more than seated machine back extension and similarly to Romanian deadlift across the whole movement in trained women. Hip-extension angle and setup can shift glute versus hamstring emphasis.

primary.name: Erector spinae
primary.evidenceShort: Direct studies support lower-back extensor activation during the movement.
primary.evidence: Direct 45-degree hip-extension and Roman chair studies measure erector spinae activity, and comparison data conclude the exercise is an appropriate selection for lower-back muscle activation.

evidence.verdict: 45-degree back extension: hamstrings, gluteus maximus, and erector spinae primary; no visible secondary or support roles added.
evidence.clinicalShort: EMG estimates acute excitation in the tested setup, not hypertrophy, tissue tolerance, or pain risk.
evidence.limitsShort: Pad height, knee angle, spinal strategy, load position, top-range lockout, and whether the user biases hip or lumbar motion can change the target profile.
evidence.summary: The 45-degree back extension is classified as a supported hip-extension and trunk-extension exercise. Direct EMG supports hamstrings, gluteus maximus, and erector spinae as visible primary contributors. No additional support muscles are shown because the reviewed evidence did not justify a concise visible role beyond those three local anatomy mappings.
evidence.clinicalInterpretation: Surface EMG is useful for classifying acute muscle excitation under a specific Roman chair setup. Ratings treat the movement as a posterior-chain accessory with moderate support and less systemic cost than heavy free-bar hinges.
evidence.limitations: This entry assumes a 45-degree Roman chair with the hips supported and body moving through roughly hip-extension range. Horizontal back extensions, glute-biased rounded-back styles, heavy barbell good mornings, reverse hypers, and seated back-extension machines should remain separate movement entries.

studies.type: Hip-extension exercise EMG comparison
studies.finding: In resistance-trained women, the 45-degree Roman chair back extension activated biceps femoris more than Romanian deadlift and seated machine back extension, activated gluteus maximus more than seated machine back extension, and showed no erector spinae difference versus the other exercises.
studies.citation: Andersen V, Pedersen H, Fimland MS, Shaw M, Solstad TEJ, Stien N, Cumming KT, Saeterbakken AH. Comparison of Muscle Activity in Three Single-Joint, Hip Extension Exercises in Resistance-Trained Women. Journal of Sports Science and Medicine. 2021;20(2):181-187. doi:10.52082/jssm.2021.181.
studies.relevance: Direct 45-degree Roman chair back-extension EMG source for biceps femoris, gluteus maximus, and erector spinae.

studies.type: Hamstring exercise selection EMG and fMRI study
studies.finding: Exercise selection altered hamstring activation, and the 45-degree hip extension emphasized biceps femoris long head relative to other hamstring exercises.
studies.citation: Bourne MN, Williams MD, Opar DA, Al Najjar A, Kerr GK, Shield AJ. Impact of exercise selection on hamstring muscle activation. British Journal of Sports Medicine. 2017;51(13):1021-1028. doi:10.1136/bjsports-2015-095739.
studies.relevance: Directly includes 45-degree hip extension and supports the hamstrings primary classification and hamstring-region limitations.

studies.type: 45-degree hip-extension knee-angle EMG study
studies.finding: Altered knee angle and contraction type changed hamstring EMG during 45-degree hip extension, with measured biceps femoris long head, semitendinosus, semimembranosus, gluteus maximus, and erector spinae activity.
studies.citation: Keerasomboon T, Mineta S, Hirose N. Influence of Altered Knee Angle and Muscular Contraction Type on Electromyographic Activity of Hamstring Muscles during 45-degree Hip Extension Exercise. Journal of Sports Science and Medicine. 2020;19(4):630-636.
studies.relevance: Direct 45-degree hip-extension evidence for hamstring heads, gluteus maximus, and erector spinae, and for setup-dependent emphasis.

movements.name: 45 Degree Leg Press
movements.variant: Inclined 45 degree sled leg press with both feet on the platform; treated separately from horizontal, vertical, unilateral, and calf-raise leg press variants.
movements.description: Sit into the sled with the back and hips braced against the pads, place both feet on the platform at a repeatable width and height, unlock the safety handles, and lower the sled until the hips and knees reach a controlled depth without the pelvis lifting. Press the platform away through the whole foot, stop short of slamming into lockout, and reset the safeties before exiting.

hypertrophy.rationale: Excellent supported lower-body loading, especially for quadriceps, with meaningful glute contribution that depends strongly on foot height, depth, and hip motion.

strength.rationale: Allows heavy lower-body force production and clean progressive loading, but the fixed seated path is less transferable as a global strength anchor than free squatting.

joint_resilience.rationale: Provides controlled knee and hip loading with less balance demand, but fixed machine geometry, deep hip flexion, and heavy sled loads can concentrate stress if setup is poor.

athletic_transfer.rationale: Closed-chain leg force has some carryover, but training evidence shows weaker jump transfer than back squat and the seated guided path removes most sport-like coordination.

control.rationale: Low Motor Control demand because the seat and sled guide the path, leaving mostly foot placement, depth, tempo, and knee tracking to control.

fatigue_efficiency.rationale: High local lower-body stimulus with less trunk fatigue than squats, though very heavy bilateral loading still creates substantial peripheral and systemic fatigue.

setup.rationale: Requires a large specific machine, plate loading, safeties, and seat setup, but execution is repeatable once loaded.

ease.rationale: Generally easy to learn because balance and bar control are removed, though depth, pelvic position, foot placement, and safety handles still matter.

progression.rationale: Load, reps, range, and foot placement are trackable, with deductions for large plate jumps, sled friction, and machine-to-machine variability.

support.rationale: Very high external support from the back pad, hip support, sled rails, platform, and safety stops.

primary.name: Quadriceps
primary.evidenceShort: Inclined leg press EMG supports high quadriceps activation.
primary.evidence: Direct leg press studies measuring rectus femoris, vastus lateralis, and vastus medialis show substantial quadriceps activation, with foot placement and load changing regional emphasis.

secondary.name: Gluteus maximus
secondary.evidenceShort: Meaningful hip-extension contributor, especially with higher feet and deeper range.
secondary.evidence: Leg press EMG studies measure gluteus maximus activity and show that foot placement can increase its contribution, but generic 45 degree leg press evidence is more consistently quadriceps-dominant.

secondary.name: Hamstrings
secondary.evidenceShort: Measured assistant during leg press, generally below main extensor targets.
secondary.evidence: Leg press and squat comparison studies measure hamstring activation, but hamstring activity is generally secondary because the machine task is dominated by knee and hip extension rather than isolated knee flexion.

support.name: Gastrocnemius
support.evidenceShort: Measured ankle/knee support contribution in leg press variants.
support.evidence: Direct leg press studies measured gastrocnemius activity and found technique-sensitive involvement, supporting a support role during loaded sled pressing rather than a primary calf-training role.

evidence.verdict: 45 degree leg press: quadriceps primary; gluteus maximus and hamstrings secondary; gastrocnemius support.
evidence.clinicalShort: Leg press EMG is sensitive to machine geometry, foot placement, load, range, and normalization method; it does not directly measure hypertrophy or injury risk.
evidence.limitsShort: Foot height, stance width, toe angle, sled angle, seat/back angle, pelvic control, depth, lockout, and machine friction materially change emphasis.
evidence.summary: The 45 degree leg press is classified as a supported inclined sled lower-body press. Direct leg press evidence supports quadriceps as the most consistent primary target, with gluteus maximus and hamstrings as secondary contributors and gastrocnemius as a support muscle for ankle/knee control during the press.
evidence.clinicalInterpretation: Surface EMG studies show acute excitation under specific foot positions and loads, while biomechanics and training studies clarify load transfer and joint demands. These findings should not be interpreted as exact hypertrophy predictions for every commercial machine.
evidence.limitations: This entry assumes a bilateral 45 degree sled with a moderate foot position. High-foot, low-foot, wide-stance, narrow-stance, single-leg, horizontal, vertical, and calf-press variations can change the visible emphasis enough to deserve separate entries if needed.

studies.type: 45 degree leg press EMG variation study
studies.finding: 45 degree, high-foot, and low-foot leg press variations changed rectus femoris, vastus lateralis, biceps femoris, gastrocnemius, and gluteus maximus activity.
studies.citation: Da Silva EM, Brentano MA, Cadore EL, De Almeida AP, Kruel LF. Analysis of muscle activation during different leg press exercises at submaximum effort levels. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2008;22(4):1059-1065. doi:10.1519/JSC.0b013e3181739445.
studies.relevance: Direct 45 degree leg press EMG source measuring major thigh, hip, and calf muscles under different foot-placement and load conditions.

studies.type: Inclined leg press foot-position and velocity EMG
studies.finding: Feet position and execution velocity influenced muscle activation and kinematic outputs during inclined leg press exercise.
studies.citation: Martin-Fuentes I, Oliva-Lozano JM, Muyor JM. Influence of Feet Position and Execution Velocity on Muscle Activation and Kinematic Parameters During the Inclined Leg Press Exercise. Sports Health. 2022;14(3):317-327. doi:10.1177/19417381211016357.
studies.relevance: Direct inclined leg press source for foot-position and execution-velocity effects on lower-limb muscle activation and movement mechanics.

studies.type: Leg press quadriceps technique EMG
studies.finding: Quadriceps myoelectric activity varied across leg press techniques.
studies.citation: Machado W, Paz G, Mendes L, Maia M, Winchester JB, Lima V, Willardson JM, Miranda H. Myoeletric Activity of the Quadriceps During Leg Press Exercise Performed With Differing Techniques. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2017;31(2):422-429. doi:10.1519/JSC.0000000000001494.
studies.relevance: Direct leg press source for quadriceps activation under technique variations.

studies.type: Leg press versus single-joint lower-limb EMG
studies.finding: Leg press produced high vastus lateralis activity and meaningful gluteus maximus activation compared with single-joint exercises in trained men.
studies.citation: Stien N, Saeterbakken AH, Andersen V. Electromyographic Comparison of Five Lower-Limb Muscles between Single- and Multi-Joint Exercises among Trained Men. Journal of Sports Science and Medicine. 2021;20(1):56-61. doi:10.52082/jssm.2021.56.
studies.relevance: Direct leg press comparison measuring vastus lateralis, vastus medialis, rectus femoris, gluteus maximus, and biceps femoris in trained men.

studies.type: Squat and leg press biomechanics and EMG
studies.finding: Squat and high/low foot-placement leg press variations differed in quadriceps, hamstrings, gastrocnemius activity, and knee joint forces.
studies.citation: Escamilla RF, Fleisig GS, Zheng N, Lander JE, Barrentine SW, Andrews JR, Bergemann BW, Moorman CT 3rd. Effects of technique variations on knee biomechanics during the squat and leg press. Medicine and Science in Sports and Exercise. 2001;33(9):1552-1566. doi:10.1097/00005768-200109000-00020.
studies.relevance: Direct leg press and squat source for lower-body muscle activity, knee forces, foot placement, stance width, and technique limitations.

studies.type: Back squat versus 45 degree leg press training transfer
studies.finding: Parallel squat training improved jump outcomes more than 45 degree leg press training after eight weeks.
studies.citation: Wirth K, Hartmann H, Sander A, Mickel C, Szilvas E, Keiner M. The Impact of Back Squat and Leg-Press Exercises on Maximal Strength and Speed-Strength Parameters. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2016;30(5):1205-1212. doi:10.1519/JSC.0000000000001228.
studies.relevance: Direct 45 degree leg press training comparison for transfer and strength-score interpretation.

movements.name: Ground Oblique Crunch
movements.variant: Bodyweight floor crunch biased toward trunk rotation or lateral flexion for the obliques.
movements.description: Lie on the floor with the knees bent, brace lightly, curl the ribs toward the opposite hip or side-crunch toward one hip without yanking the neck, pause with the trunk shortened, then lower under control before repeating on the same side or alternating.

hypertrophy.rationale: Can train the obliques locally, but load is light and progression is limited.

strength.rationale: Low strength signal because it is mostly bodyweight trunk flexion with poor external loading.

joint_resilience.rationale: Low joint-resilience value; repeated spinal flexion/rotation is not broadly useful as a resilience anchor.

athletic_transfer.rationale: Low transfer because it lacks standing force transfer, anti-rotation demand, or integrated limb coordination.

control.rationale: Some trunk-position control is required, but the floor and short range make coordination demands low.

fatigue_efficiency.rationale: Low systemic fatigue and quick local abdominal stimulus, though the stimulus ceiling is low.

setup.rationale: Almost no setup: floor space only.

ease.rationale: Easy to understand, though users can compensate with neck pulling or hip flexion.

progression.rationale: Difficult to progressively overload precisely without changing to a cable, machine, or loaded variation.

support.rationale: The floor supports the body and removes balance demand.

primary.name: External oblique
primary.evidenceShort: Crunch/side-bridge EMG supports oblique activation.
primary.evidence: Crunch and side-bridge EMG evidence measures external oblique activity; the oblique-biased crunch is classified as targeting this role directly.

primary.name: Internal oblique
primary.evidenceShort: Crunch/side-bridge EMG supports internal-oblique activation.
primary.evidence: Abdominal crunch, side bridge, and related abdominal EMG evidence measure internal oblique activity, supporting a primary oblique role for this variant.

secondary.name: Rectus abdominis
secondary.evidenceShort: Crunch evidence shows rectus activity, but this variant is oblique-biased.
secondary.evidence: Crunch EMG evidence reports substantial rectus abdominis activity; it is secondary here because the movement is intentionally oblique-biased.

evidence.verdict: Ground oblique crunch: external and internal oblique primary; rectus abdominis secondary; no separate support muscles listed.
evidence.clinicalShort: EMG estimates acute excitation, not hypertrophy, mechanical tension, adaptation, or injury risk.
evidence.limitsShort: Side-lying versus supine rotation, hand position, range, tempo, neck compensation, and hip flexion change emphasis.
evidence.summary: The ground oblique crunch is classified as a low-setup trunk flexion or rotation movement. Evidence is from the abdominal crunch and side-bridge family rather than a single standardized oblique-crunch protocol, so classification is conservative.
evidence.clinicalInterpretation: This is a low-friction accessory movement, not a high-load core progression anchor.
evidence.limitations: The exact phrase 'oblique crunch' covers several setups. Cable wood chops, cable crunches, side planks, and weighted oblique crunches should be separate entries.

studies.type: Commercial and common abdominal exercise EMG
studies.finding: Crunch and abdominal-device exercises activated rectus abdominis plus external and internal obliques.
studies.citation: Escamilla RF, McTaggart MSC, Fricklas EJ, et al. An electromyographic analysis of commercial and common abdominal exercises: implications for rehabilitation and training. Journal of Orthopaedic and Sports Physical Therapy. 2006;36(2):45-57. doi:10.2519/jospt.2006.36.2.45.
studies.relevance: Common abdominal exercise EMG source for rectus abdominis and oblique activation.

studies.type: Crunch and side-bridge abdominal EMG
studies.finding: Compared Ab-Slide, abdominal crunch, supine double leg thrust, and side bridge using rectus abdominis and oblique EMG.
studies.citation: Youdas JW, Guck BR, Hebrink RC, Rugotzke JD, Madson TJ, Hollman JH. An electromyographic analysis of the Ab-Slide exercise, abdominal crunch, supine double leg thrust, and side bridge in healthy young adults. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2008;22(6):1939-1946. doi:10.1519/JSC.0b013e31818745bf.
studies.relevance: Close evidence for external oblique, internal oblique, and rectus abdominis activation during accessible floor core exercises.

movements.name: Hanging Leg Raise
movements.variant: Hanging leg or knee raise from a pull-up bar or straps, emphasizing controlled hip flexion and posterior pelvic tilt.
movements.description: Hang from a bar or straps with the shoulders controlled, brace the ribs down, raise the knees or legs by flexing the hips and curling the pelvis upward, pause without swinging, then lower under control until the trunk is stable again.

hypertrophy.rationale: Useful abdominal and hip-flexor loading, but grip, swing control, and hip flexion often limit local hypertrophy progression.

strength.rationale: Good trunk and hip-flexion strength signal, especially when done with posterior pelvic tilt and long lever control.

joint_resilience.rationale: Can build shoulder hanging tolerance and anterior-core control, but it is not a broad joint-resilience anchor.

athletic_transfer.rationale: Moderate transfer to hanging, climbing, and trunk-control tasks, but low direct transfer to loaded lower-body or gait patterns.

control.rationale: High motor-control demand from grip/hang stability, swing suppression, hip flexion, pelvic curl, and eccentric lowering.

fatigue_efficiency.rationale: Can be effective, but grip, shoulder, and hip-flexor fatigue often leak into the stimulus.

setup.rationale: Requires a bar or straps and enough clearance, but little loading setup.

ease.rationale: Difficult to repeat cleanly because swinging and hip-flexor dominance can hide poor trunk control.

progression.rationale: Progression can use reps, knee-to-leg leverage, tempo, or load, but the main difficulty variable is hard to quantify.

support.rationale: Almost no external support; the body hangs freely and self-stabilizes.

primary.name: Rectus abdominis
primary.evidenceShort: Hanging knee-up evidence shows high rectus activation.
primary.evidence: Hanging knee-up EMG evidence reports high upper and lower rectus abdominis activation, supporting a primary abdominal role.

primary.name: Iliopsoas
primary.evidenceShort: Hip-flexor EMG supports primary hip-flexion role.
primary.evidence: Hanging leg raises require resisted hip flexion, and hip-flexor EMG evidence supports iliopsoas involvement in leg-raise and hip-flexion tasks.

secondary.name: External oblique
secondary.evidenceShort: Hanging knee-up evidence shows high external-oblique activity.
secondary.evidence: Hanging knee-up EMG evidence reports high external oblique activity, supporting a secondary trunk-control role.

secondary.name: Internal oblique
secondary.evidenceShort: Abdominal EMG supports oblique contribution.
secondary.evidence: Traditional and nontraditional abdominal exercise EMG supports internal oblique contribution during high-demand leg-raise and knee-up patterns.

support.name: Latissimus dorsi
support.evidenceShort: Hanging setup requires shoulder-girdle support.
support.evidence: Latissimus dorsi is included as support because hanging from a bar requires shoulder-girdle control while the trunk and hips move; abdominal-device evidence also measured latissimus involvement in related high-demand abdominal tasks.

evidence.verdict: Hanging leg raise: rectus abdominis and iliopsoas primary; external and internal oblique secondary; latissimus dorsi support.
evidence.clinicalShort: EMG estimates acute excitation, not hypertrophy, mechanical tension, adaptation, or injury risk.
evidence.limitsShort: Knee bend, straight-leg lever length, pelvic curl, straps versus bar, swing, grip fatigue, and load change emphasis.
evidence.summary: The hanging leg raise is classified as a hanging trunk and hip-flexion exercise. Evidence supports high abdominal activation in hanging knee-up variants, with iliopsoas included from hip-flexor EMG and the movement's primary hip-flexion mechanics.
evidence.clinicalInterpretation: A clean posterior pelvic tilt makes this more abdominal; a pure hip-flexion swing makes it more hip-flexor dominant.
evidence.limitations: Most direct evidence uses hanging knee-ups with straps rather than every straight-leg bar-hanging variant. Straight-leg raises, captain's-chair raises, toes-to-bar, and weighted raises should be split later if precision matters.

studies.type: Traditional and nontraditional abdominal exercise EMG
studies.finding: Hanging knee-up with straps was among the highest abdominal activation exercises for rectus abdominis and obliques.
studies.citation: Escamilla RF, Babb E, DeWitt R, et al. Electromyographic analysis of traditional and nontraditional abdominal exercises: implications for rehabilitation and training. Physical Therapy. 2006;86(5):656-671.
studies.relevance: Direct hanging knee-up abdominal EMG source for rectus abdominis and obliques.

studies.type: Sit-up and leg-raise abdominal/lower-limb EMG
studies.shortCitation: Lee et al., J Phys Ther Sci, 2016
studies.finding: Compared abdominal and lower-limb muscle activity during sit-up and leg-raise tasks.
studies.citation: Lee DK, Kang MH, Lee TS, Oh JS. Comparison of muscular activities in the abdomen and lower limbs while performing sit-up and leg-raise. Journal of Physical Therapy Science. 2016;28(2):491-494. doi:10.1589/jpts.28.491.
studies.relevance: Close leg-raise source supporting abdominal and hip-flexion interpretation.

studies.type: Hip flexor EMG
studies.shortCitation: Czuppon et al., J Clin Med, 2024
studies.finding: Measured hip-flexor muscle activation during common rehabilitation and strength exercises.
studies.citation: Czuppon S, et al. Hip Flexor Muscle Activation During Common Rehabilitation and Strength Exercises. Journal of Clinical Medicine. 2024;13(21):6617. doi:10.3390/jcm13216617.
studies.relevance: Supports iliopsoas inclusion for the hip-flexion component.

movements.name: Incline Bar Bench Press
movements.variant: Incline barbell bench press using a fixed incline bench and a free barbell, treated as an upward-angled free-weight chest press.
movements.description: Lie back on a fixed incline bench with the eyes slightly behind the racked bar, feet planted, shoulder blades set against the pad, and hands slightly wider than shoulder width; unrack to a stacked wrist-over-elbow position, lower the bar under control toward the upper chest without letting the elbows flare excessively, then press up and slightly back toward the rack line while keeping the torso and shoulder position stable.

hypertrophy.rationale: Strong upper-chest and anterior-shoulder hypertrophy stimulus, with useful overload but less flat-pec emphasis than the flat press.

strength.rationale: Strong barbell strength movement with clear loading, though absolute force is usually lower and setup is more angle-specific than flat bench.

joint_resilience.rationale: Provides controlled shoulder exposure but is not a resilience-focused drill and can be shoulder-demanding for some users.

athletic_transfer.rationale: Low athletic-transfer score because the task is bilateral, supine, braced, and not coordination-rich.

control.rationale: Requires bar path and upper-body position control, but balance and whole-body coordination demands remain low.

fatigue_efficiency.rationale: Useful pressing stimulus but heavy setup, shoulder/triceps overlap, and warm-up demands keep efficiency moderate-low.

setup.rationale: Needs rack, bench-angle setup, bar, plates, safeties or spotter judgment, and consistent bench placement.

ease.rationale: Less automatic than flat bench because angle, touch point, shoulder position, and unrack path are harder to standardize.

progression.rationale: Excellent overload tracking because barbell load and reps are precise, with small deductions for bench-angle and rack-position variability.

support.rationale: The bench supports the torso, but the bar is still a free path and shoulder stabilization remains meaningful.

primary.name: Pectoralis major
primary.evidenceShort: Incline barbell EMG supports major chest involvement, especially upper pec at moderate inclines.
primary.evidence: Free-weight bench-angle EMG studies show substantial pectoralis major activity during incline bench pressing; the upper/clavicular region is emphasized around moderate incline angles, while very high inclines shift more activity toward the anterior deltoid.

secondary.name: Anterior deltoid
secondary.evidenceShort: Incline angle increases anterior deltoid contribution.
secondary.evidence: Bench-angle EMG studies repeatedly show anterior deltoid activity during incline pressing, with greater contribution as the bench angle rises; it is classified as secondary for a chest-focused incline press because it assists shoulder flexion and can become dominant at steeper inclines.

secondary.name: Triceps brachii
secondary.evidenceShort: Measured elbow-extension contributor during incline pressing.
secondary.evidence: Incline and bench-press EMG studies measure triceps brachii activity during the press; its role is meaningful for elbow extension, though incline-angle studies report it as similar across angles or lower than chest and anterior deltoid activation.

support.name: Serratus anterior
support.evidenceShort: Inference from close bench/chest-press scapular evidence.
support.evidence: This support role is inferred from chest-press and bench-press evidence showing serratus anterior activity with scapular kinematics; it is included as scapulothoracic support, not as a direct incline-specific hypertrophy target.

support.name: Rotator cuff
support.evidenceShort: Inference from bench-press shoulder-stabilization evidence.
support.evidence: This support role is inferred from bench-press research showing direction-specific rotator cuff recruitment consistent with glenohumeral stabilization under pressing loads; direct incline-only rotator cuff EMG was not found.

evidence.verdict: Incline free-bar chest press: pectoralis major primary; anterior deltoid and triceps brachii secondary; serratus anterior and rotator cuff support by marked inference from close bench-press evidence.
evidence.clinicalShort: EMG estimates acute excitation, not hypertrophy, mechanical tension, adaptation, pain risk, or long-term training outcome.
evidence.limitsShort: Bench angle is the main modifier: moderate inclines emphasize upper pectoralis, while steeper inclines increase anterior deltoid demand and may reduce pectoralis performance.
evidence.summary: The incline bar bench press is classified as a free-weight upward-angled chest press performed on a fixed incline bench. Direct bench-angle studies support pectoralis major as the primary target, especially the upper/clavicular region at moderate inclines. Anterior deltoid and triceps brachii are visible secondary movers because shoulder flexion and elbow extension are both required, and their activity is directly measured in incline bench research.
evidence.clinicalInterpretation: Surface electromyography should be interpreted as exercise-condition-specific muscle excitation. It does not directly measure hypertrophy, mechanical tension, joint loading, tissue tolerance, or injury probability. Ratings combine direct bench-angle evidence with explicit product judgment about setup, progression, support, and fatigue.
evidence.limitations: The exact fixed bench angle is not specified in the movement ID. Most direct evidence uses 25-45 degree incline conditions, but studies also test 60 degrees, where anterior deltoid activity becomes much more prominent. Grip width, bar touch point, load prescription, arch, rack height, spotter/safeties, tempo, and participant training status can all change the observed stimulus.

studies.type: Free-weight bench inclination EMG study
studies.finding: At 30 degrees, upper pectoralis major and anterior deltoid were among the highest measured activations; above 45 degrees, anterior deltoid increased and pectoralis performance decreased, while triceps activity was similar across inclines.
studies.citation: Rodriguez-Ridao D, Antequera-Vique JA, Martin-Fuentes I, Muyor JM. Effect of Five Bench Inclinations on the Electromyographic Activity of the Pectoralis Major, Anterior Deltoid, and Triceps Brachii during the Bench Press Exercise. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. 2020;17(19):7339. doi:10.3390/ijerph17197339.
studies.relevance: Directly tested free-weight bench press at 0, 15, 30, 45, and 60 degrees and measured upper, middle, and lower pectoralis major, anterior deltoid, and triceps brachii.

studies.type: Free-weight bench angle EMG study
studies.shortCitation: Lauver et al., Eur J Sport Sci, 2016
studies.finding: Free-weight barbell bench pressing at different angles changed upper-extremity activation patterns, supporting the angle-sensitive classification of pectoralis major, anterior deltoid, and triceps brachii.
studies.citation: Lauver JD, Cayot TE, Scheuermann BW. Influence of bench angle on upper extremity muscular activation during bench press exercise. European Journal of Sport Science. 2016;16(3):309-316. doi:10.1080/17461391.2015.1022605.
studies.relevance: Direct incline/flat/decline free-weight barbell bench-angle evidence measuring pectoralis major regions, anterior deltoid, and triceps brachii.

studies.type: High-density pectoralis EMG during flat and incline bench press
studies.shortCitation: Cabral et al., Scand J Med Sci Sports, 2022
studies.finding: High-density EMG showed pectoralis major excitation shifted toward the clavicular region during a 45-degree incline bench press compared with the flat press.
studies.citation: Cabral HV, de Souza LML, de Oliveira LF, Vieira TM. Non-uniform excitation of the pectoralis major muscle during flat and inclined bench press exercises. Scandinavian Journal of Medicine & Science in Sports. 2022;32(2):381-390. doi:10.1111/sms.14082.
studies.relevance: Directly supports pectoralis major as the main target and clarifies regional pectoralis excitation in a 45-degree incline bench press.

studies.type: Competitive-athlete bench press variation EMG
studies.shortCitation: Saeterbakken et al., J Hum Kinet, 2017
studies.finding: In competitive bench press athletes, incline and decline wide-grip variations changed some arm-muscle activation and performance outcomes compared with competition-style flat pressing.
studies.citation: Saeterbakken AH, Mo DA, Scott S, Andersen V. The Effects of Bench Press Variations in Competitive Athletes on Muscle Activity and Performance. Journal of Human Kinetics. 2017;57(1):61-71. doi:10.1515/hukin-2017-0047.
studies.relevance: Close direct evidence in trained bench press athletes comparing incline, decline, and grip-width variations while measuring pectoralis major, deltoids, biceps, triceps, and latissimus dorsi.

studies.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of pectoralis EMG in bench press variants
studies.finding: The review found pectoralis major activation differs across bench-press variants and that incline benching tends to increase clavicular emphasis while reducing sternal emphasis compared with the horizontal bench press.
studies.citation: Lopez-Vivancos A, Gonzalez-Galvez N, Orquin-Castrillon FJ, de Souza Vale RG, Marcos-Pardo PJ. Electromyographic Activity of the Pectoralis Major Muscle during Traditional Bench Press and Other Variants of Pectoral Exercises: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Applied Sciences. 2023;13(8):5203. doi:10.3390/app13085203.
studies.relevance: Provides synthesis-level context for pectoralis major activation across bench-press variants, including bench inclination.

studies.type: Systematic review of bench press EMG
studies.finding: Bench press EMG literature supports pectoralis major and triceps brachii as major contributors and highlights technique, intensity, and phase-specific interpretation limits.
studies.citation: Stastny P, Golas A, Blazek D, Maszczyk A, Wilk M, Pietraszewski P, Petr M, Uhlir P, Zajac A. A systematic review of surface electromyography analyses of the bench press movement task. PLOS ONE. 2017;12(2):e0171632. doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0171632.
studies.relevance: Movement-family synthesis used to support triceps classification and general EMG interpretation limits for barbell bench pressing.

studies.type: Rotator cuff recruitment study
studies.shortCitation: Wattanaprakornkul et al., J Electromyogr Kinesiol, 2011
studies.finding: Rotator cuff recruitment during bench press and row tasks was direction-specific, supporting a stabilizing shoulder role during pressing.
studies.citation: Wattanaprakornkul D, Halaki M, Cathers I, Ginn KA. Direction-specific recruitment of rotator cuff muscles during bench press and row. Journal of Electromyography and Kinesiology. 2011;21(6):1041-1049. doi:10.1016/j.jelekin.2011.09.002.
studies.relevance: Close bench-press evidence used as an explicit inference for glenohumeral stabilization in the free-weight incline press.

studies.type: Chest press and barbell bench press EMG with scapular kinematics
studies.finding: Chest press lever machine and barbell bench press comparisons included serratus anterior activity and scapular kinematics.
studies.citation: Borges E, Dalla H, Mastandrea L, Nunes S, Santarem J. Comparative evaluation of muscular activation and scapular kinematics in a chest press lever machine and a barbell bench press. Journal of Physical Education and Sport. 2019;19:912-916. doi:10.7752/jpes.2019.s3131.
studies.relevance: Close horizontal pressing evidence used as an explicit inference for serratus anterior scapulothoracic support during incline pressing.

movements.name: Incline Dumbbell Bench Press
movements.variant: Incline dumbbell bench press on an angled bench, treated as an independent free-weight upward-angled chest press.
movements.description: Set an incline bench, bring matching dumbbells to the shoulders, plant the feet, and set the shoulder blades against the pad. Lower the dumbbells with wrists stacked over elbows until the upper chest and shoulders are loaded, then press up and slightly together without losing control of either weight.

hypertrophy.rationale: Strong upper-chest hypertrophy signal with independent arm paths and useful pressing range, though deltoid contribution rises as incline steepens.

strength.rationale: Builds incline pressing strength, but dumbbell setup and stabilization limit absolute loading and measurement precision compared with a barbell.

joint_resilience.rationale: Can train shoulder control through a freer path, but the inclined position and bottom range can be demanding and are not resilience-specific.

athletic_transfer.rationale: Independent-arm control adds some transfer value, but the movement is still supine, supported, bilateral, and not sport-like.

control.rationale: Requires independent dumbbell control, shoulder positioning, scapular control, and symmetrical pressing without a fixed path.

fatigue_efficiency.rationale: Good local chest and shoulder stimulus, with efficiency reduced by heavy dumbbell handling and stabilizer fatigue.

setup.rationale: Needs an adjustable or fixed incline bench and matched dumbbells, but no rack or plate loading.

ease.rationale: The concept is simple, but users need to manage bench angle, kick-up, dumbbell path, wrist position, and safe set termination.

progression.rationale: Load and reps are trackable, but dumbbell jumps are often coarse and heavy starting/ending positions can limit progression.

support.rationale: The bench supports the torso, but each shoulder controls a separate free load through an angled path.

primary.name: Pectoralis major
primary.evidenceShort: Incline dumbbell and bench-angle EMG support major chest involvement.
primary.evidence: Direct dumbbell press research measured pectoralis major during incline dumbbell pressing, and bench-angle studies support pectoralis major involvement with clavicular emphasis at moderate inclines.

secondary.name: Anterior deltoid
secondary.evidenceShort: Incline pressing increases shoulder-flexion demand.
secondary.evidence: Incline dumbbell pressing directly measures anterior deltoid activity, and free-weight bench-angle evidence shows anterior deltoid contribution rises as the bench angle increases. It is secondary because the card remains chest-focused.

secondary.name: Triceps brachii
secondary.evidenceShort: Elbow-extension contributor in incline and dumbbell pressing evidence.
secondary.evidence: Bench-angle and dumbbell bench-press evidence measure triceps brachii during pressing tasks. It is classified as secondary because it supplies elbow extension but is not the main incline chest target.

support.name: Biceps brachii
support.evidenceShort: Independent dumbbells add antagonist and stabilizer demand.
support.evidence: Dumbbell bench-press studies show biceps brachii activity consistent with antagonist and shoulder-stabilizing demand under independent free weights. This support role is inferred for the incline dumbbell variant from direct dumbbell pressing evidence.

support.name: Serratus anterior
support.evidenceShort: Scapulothoracic support inferred from close chest-press evidence.
support.evidence: Chest-press and bench-press comparison evidence includes serratus anterior activity with scapular kinematics. It is included as scapulothoracic support rather than as a direct incline dumbbell target.

support.name: Rotator cuff
support.evidenceShort: Shoulder stabilization inferred from bench-press rotator cuff research.
support.evidence: Bench press research demonstrates direction-specific rotator cuff recruitment consistent with glenohumeral stabilization. Independent dumbbells plausibly increase this control requirement, so the role is listed as support.

evidence.verdict: Incline dumbbell bench press: pectoralis major primary; anterior deltoid and triceps brachii secondary; biceps brachii, serratus anterior, and rotator cuff support.
evidence.clinicalShort: EMG estimates acute excitation, not hypertrophy, mechanical tension, adaptation, pain risk, or injury probability.
evidence.limitsShort: Bench angle, grip angle, depth, dumbbell path, load, tempo, shoulder range, and heavy dumbbell handling can shift emphasis.
evidence.summary: The incline dumbbell bench press is classified as an independent free-weight upward-angled chest press. Direct incline dumbbell evidence and bench-angle EMG support pectoralis major as the visible primary target, with anterior deltoid and triceps brachii as secondary movers. Dumbbell stability and close pressing evidence support the listed shoulder and scapular support roles.
evidence.clinicalInterpretation: Surface EMG should be interpreted as a task-specific estimate of acute muscle excitation. Ratings combine direct dumbbell and incline pressing evidence with explicit product judgment about setup, loadability, progression, support, and fatigue.
evidence.limitations: The movement ID does not specify bench angle. Evidence is strongest for moderate incline ranges; steeper inclines can shift emphasis toward anterior deltoid. Serratus anterior and rotator cuff support are inferred from close pressing-family evidence rather than exact incline dumbbell-only measurements.

studies.type: Dumbbell bench, incline, and shoulder press EMG study
studies.shortCitation: Luczak et al., J Sports Med, 2013
studies.finding: Novice and resistance-trained women performed dumbbell bench, incline, and shoulder presses while anterior deltoid, pectoralis major regions, and upper trapezius were measured; incline pressing showed meaningful pectoralis and anterior deltoid activity.
studies.citation: Luczak J, Bosak A, Riemann BL. Shoulder Muscle Activation of Novice and Resistance Trained Women during Variations of Dumbbell Press Exercises. Journal of Sports Medicine. 2013;2013:612650. doi:10.1155/2013/612650.
studies.relevance: Directly includes the incline dumbbell press and supports pectoralis major and anterior deltoid classification.

studies.type: Free-weight bench inclination EMG study
studies.finding: At 30 degrees, upper pectoralis major and anterior deltoid were among the highest measured activations; above 45 degrees, anterior deltoid increased and pectoralis performance decreased, while triceps activity was similar across inclines.
studies.citation: Rodriguez-Ridao D, Antequera-Vique JA, Martin-Fuentes I, Muyor JM. Effect of Five Bench Inclinations on the Electromyographic Activity of the Pectoralis Major, Anterior Deltoid, and Triceps Brachii during the Bench Press Exercise. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. 2020;17(19):7339. doi:10.3390/ijerph17197339.
studies.relevance: Direct free-weight incline bench-angle evidence for pectoralis major, anterior deltoid, and triceps brachii; applied to dumbbell incline pressing with modality limitations.

studies.type: Free-weight bench angle EMG study
studies.shortCitation: Lauver et al., Eur J Sport Sci, 2016
studies.finding: Bench angle changed upper-extremity activation during free-weight bench pressing, supporting angle-sensitive anterior deltoid and triceps interpretation.
studies.citation: Lauver JD, Cayot TE, Scheuermann BW. Influence of bench angle on upper extremity muscular activation during bench press exercise. European Journal of Sport Science. 2016;16(3):309-316. doi:10.1080/17461391.2015.1022605.
studies.relevance: Close bench-angle evidence supporting secondary pressing roles and incline-angle limits.

studies.type: High-density pectoralis EMG during flat and incline bench press
studies.shortCitation: Cabral et al., Scand J Med Sci Sports, 2022
studies.finding: High-density EMG showed pectoralis major excitation shifted toward the clavicular region during a 45-degree incline bench press compared with the flat press.
studies.citation: Cabral HV, de Souza LML, de Oliveira LF, Vieira TM. Non-uniform excitation of the pectoralis major muscle during flat and inclined bench press exercises. Scandinavian Journal of Medicine & Science in Sports. 2022;32(2):381-390. doi:10.1111/sms.14082.
studies.relevance: Close incline pressing evidence for pectoralis major regional emphasis.

studies.type: Systematic review and meta-analysis of pectoralis EMG in bench press variants
studies.finding: The review found pectoralis major activation differs across bench-press variants and that incline benching tends to increase clavicular emphasis while reducing sternal emphasis compared with horizontal bench press.
studies.citation: Lopez-Vivancos A, Gonzalez-Galvez N, Orquin-Castrillon FJ, de Souza Vale RG, Marcos-Pardo PJ. Electromyographic Activity of the Pectoralis Major Muscle during Traditional Bench Press and Other Variants of Pectoral Exercises: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Applied Sciences. 2023;13(8):5203. doi:10.3390/app13085203.
studies.relevance: Synthesis evidence for pectoralis major classification and incline pressing limits.

studies.type: Dumbbell, barbell, and Smith machine bench press EMG
studies.finding: Compared dumbbell, barbell, and Smith machine bench press over multiple sets while measuring pectoralis major, anterior deltoid, biceps brachii, and triceps brachii.
studies.citation: Farias D de A, Willardson JM, Paz GA, Bezerra E de S, Miranda H. Maximal Strength Performance and Muscle Activation for the Bench Press and Triceps Extension Exercises Adopting Dumbbell, Barbell, and Machine Modalities Over Multiple Sets. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2017;31(7):1879-1887. doi:10.1519/JSC.0000000000001651.
studies.relevance: Close dumbbell pressing evidence for triceps and biceps support roles plus modality-specific setup and stability scoring.

studies.type: Chest-press stability comparison
studies.shortCitation: Saeterbakken et al., J Sports Sci, 2011
studies.finding: Compared Smith machine, barbell, and dumbbell chest press strength and muscle activity under different stability requirements.
studies.citation: Saeterbakken AH, van den Tillaar R, Fimland MS. A comparison of muscle activity and 1-RM strength of three chest-press exercises with different stability requirements. Journal of Sports Sciences. 2011;29(5):533-538. doi:10.1080/02640414.2010.543916.
studies.relevance: Close dumbbell pressing source for independent free-weight stabilization and support scoring.

studies.type: Rotator cuff recruitment study
studies.shortCitation: Wattanaprakornkul et al., J Electromyogr Kinesiol, 2011
studies.finding: Rotator cuff recruitment during bench press and row tasks was direction-specific, supporting a stabilizing shoulder role during pressing.
studies.citation: Wattanaprakornkul D, Halaki M, Cathers I, Ginn KA. Direction-specific recruitment of rotator cuff muscles during bench press and row. Journal of Electromyography and Kinesiology. 2011;21(6):1041-1049. doi:10.1016/j.jelekin.2011.09.002.
studies.relevance: Close bench-press evidence used as explicit inference for glenohumeral stabilization in free-weight incline dumbbell pressing.

studies.type: Chest press EMG and scapular kinematics study
studies.finding: Chest press comparison data included serratus anterior activity and scapular kinematics during pressing tasks.
studies.citation: Borges E, Dalla H, Mastandrea L, Nunes S, Santarem J. Comparative evaluation of muscular activation and scapular kinematics in a chest press lever machine and a barbell bench press. Journal of Physical Education and Sport. 2019;19:912-916. doi:10.7752/jpes.2019.s3131.
studies.relevance: Close pressing-family evidence for serratus anterior as scapulothoracic support.

movements.name: Incline Dumbbell Y Raise
movements.variant: Chest-supported incline-bench dumbbell Y raise with the arms lifted in the scapular plane using light dumbbells and a thumbs-up or neutral hand position.
movements.description: Set an incline bench around 30 to 45 degrees and lie chest-down with light dumbbells hanging under the shoulders. Brace against the bench, raise the arms up and out into a Y while keeping the elbows soft and the shoulders away from the ears, pause briefly near the top, then lower under control without bouncing off the bottom.

hypertrophy.rationale: Focused scapular muscle stimulus, but loads are intentionally light and the hypertrophy ceiling is modest.

strength.rationale: Low global strength signal because the lever arm is long and load progression is deliberately conservative.

joint_resilience.rationale: Strong shoulder-girdle resilience accessory when range and load are controlled, especially for scapular upward-rotation tolerance.

athletic_transfer.rationale: Useful shoulder-positioning carryover, but little direct transfer to whole-body athletic force expression.

control.rationale: Requires precise scapular motion, arm angle, tempo, and avoidance of shrugging or lumbar compensation.

fatigue_efficiency.rationale: Very low systemic fatigue with a focused local scapular stimulus when performed strictly.

setup.rationale: Needs an adjustable bench and light dumbbells, with bench angle and body position affecting repeatability.

ease.rationale: The motion is simple, but many users over-shrug, use too much load, or lose the intended Y path.

progression.rationale: Progression is limited by small muscle targets, long lever arms, and dumbbell jump size.

support.rationale: The bench supports the torso, though the shoulder blades and arms still move freely.

primary.name: Trapezius (middle and lower fibers)
primary.evidenceShort: Prone Y-family EMG supports middle/lower trap emphasis.
primary.evidence: Trapezius EMG evidence identifies the prone overhead arm raise in line with the lower trapezius as a maximal lower-trapezius exercise, while scapular-balance studies support exercises that emphasize lower and middle trapezius with controlled upper-trapezius contribution.

secondary.name: Serratus anterior
secondary.evidenceShort: Scapular upward-rotation evidence supports assistance.
secondary.evidence: The Y raise requires scapular upward rotation and posterior tilt as the arms elevate; shoulder rehabilitation evidence identifies serratus anterior as a key scapular-control muscle during shoulder elevation tasks.

secondary.name: Posterior deltoid
secondary.evidenceShort: Rear-shoulder EMG supports an assisting role.
secondary.evidence: Rear-deltoid EMG from close prone and incline shoulder exercises supports posterior deltoid involvement during chest-supported arm elevation and horizontal-abduction-biased shoulder work, but the intended Y-raise target remains scapular upward-rotation control.

support.name: Rotator cuff
support.evidenceShort: Shoulder-elevation control requires cuff stabilization.
support.evidence: This support role is a biomechanics inference from shoulder rehabilitation review evidence: the rotator cuff stabilizes the humeral head during arm elevation while the scapular muscles control upward rotation.

evidence.verdict: Incline dumbbell Y raise: middle/lower trapezius primary; serratus anterior and posterior deltoid secondary; rotator cuff support.
evidence.clinicalShort: EMG estimates acute excitation, not hypertrophy, mechanical tension, adaptation, or injury risk.
evidence.limitsShort: Exact incline-bench dumbbell Y-raise evidence is limited; most evidence uses prone floor or rehabilitation Y/full-can variants.
evidence.summary: The incline dumbbell Y raise is classified as a chest-supported scapular-control accessory. The primary visible target is the project's mapped middle/lower trapezius aggregate because the evidence most strongly supports lower-trapezius activation during prone Y-family arm raises. Serratus anterior is included as an assisting scapular upward-rotation muscle, posterior deltoid as a rear-shoulder assistant, and rotator cuff as support for glenohumeral control.
evidence.clinicalInterpretation: This movement should usually be loaded lightly enough to keep the arm path, scapular upward rotation, and neck position clean. EMG evidence supports the intended muscle emphasis, but it does not prove injury prevention or long-term adaptation by itself.
evidence.limitations: The available anatomy map does not expose a standalone lower trapezius mesh, so the visible role uses the existing Trapezius (middle and lower fibers) entry. Upper trapezius is intentionally not listed as a separate visible role because the exercise is typically programmed to minimize shrugging, and no standalone upper-trapezius anatomy entry exists. Standing Y raises, cable Y raises, prone floor Y raises, and heavy rear-delt raises should be separate variants if added later.

studies.type: Trapezius and serratus anterior exercise EMG
studies.finding: Prone overhead arm raise in line with the lower trapezius produced the maximum lower-trapezius EMG activity among tested trapezius exercises.
studies.citation: Ekstrom RA, Donatelli RA, Soderberg GL. Surface electromyographic analysis of exercises for the trapezius and serratus anterior muscles. Journal of Orthopaedic and Sports Physical Therapy. 2003;33(5):247-258. doi:10.2519/jospt.2003.33.5.247.
studies.relevance: Most direct Y-family evidence for the lower-trapezius emphasis of the movement.

studies.type: Scapular muscle-balance EMG
studies.shortCitation: Cools et al., Am J Sports Med, 2007
studies.finding: Several scapular exercises produced favorable upper-to-lower and upper-to-middle trapezius ratios, supporting selective scapular muscle balance training.
studies.citation: Cools AM, Dewitte V, Lanszweert F, Notebaert D, Roets A, Soetens B, Cagnie B, Witvrouw EE. Rehabilitation of scapular muscle balance: which exercises to prescribe? American Journal of Sports Medicine. 2007;35(10):1744-1751. doi:10.1177/0363546507303560.
studies.relevance: Supports the scapular-balance rationale and secondary serratus contribution for light Y-raise programming.

studies.type: Scapular-control exercise EMG
studies.shortCitation: Kibler et al., Am J Sports Med, 2008
studies.finding: Low row, inferior glide, lawnmower, and robbery exercises activated serratus anterior and lower trapezius in clinically meaningful scapular-control patterns.
studies.citation: Kibler WB, Sciascia AD, Uhl TL, Tambay N, Cunningham T. Electromyographic analysis of specific exercises for scapular control in early phases of shoulder rehabilitation. American Journal of Sports Medicine. 2008;36(9):1789-1798. doi:10.1177/0363546508316281.
studies.relevance: Close scapular-control evidence for serratus anterior and lower-trapezius coordination.

studies.type: Shoulder rehabilitation exercise review
studies.finding: Review describes trapezius, serratus anterior, and rotator cuff roles in shoulder elevation and rehabilitation exercises.
studies.citation: Escamilla RF, Yamashiro K, Paulos L, Andrews JR. Shoulder muscle activity and function in common shoulder rehabilitation exercises. Sports Medicine. 2009;39(8):663-685. doi:10.2165/00007256-200939080-00004.
studies.relevance: Review-level support for scapular upward-rotation and rotator-cuff stabilization interpretation.

studies.type: Deltoid exercise EMG thesis
studies.shortCitation: Sweeney, University of Wisconsin-La Crosse thesis, 2014
studies.finding: Seated rear lateral raise and 45-degree incline row were the strongest tested exercises for posterior-deltoid activation.
studies.citation: Sweeney SP. Electromyographic analysis of the deltoid muscle during various shoulder exercises. Master's thesis, University of Wisconsin-La Crosse. 2014.
studies.relevance: Close evidence for posterior-deltoid assistance in chest-supported rear-shoulder lifting patterns.

studies.type: Rotator cuff pulley external-rotation EMG
studies.finding: Shoulder rotation resistance increased recruitment of rotator-cuff and other shoulder rotation torque-generating muscles.
studies.citation: Dark A, Ginn KA, Halaki M. Shoulder muscle recruitment patterns during commonly used rotator cuff exercises: an electromyographic study. Physical Therapy. 2007;87(8):1039-1046. doi:10.2522/ptj.20060068.
studies.relevance: Supports the rotator-cuff stabilization interpretation during resisted shoulder elevation and rotation control.

movements.name: Kneeling Cable Crunch
movements.variant: Kneeling cable crunch with a high pulley and rope or handle attachment, emphasizing loaded trunk flexion.
movements.description: Kneel facing the cable with the attachment held near the head or shoulders, keep the hips mostly fixed, curl the ribs toward the pelvis against the cable, then return under control without turning it into a hip hinge.

hypertrophy.rationale: One of the more loadable abdominal isolation options, though technique can shift effort away from the abdominal wall.

strength.rationale: Good loaded trunk-flexion strength signal, but it is not a global strength anchor and the force path is narrow.

joint_resilience.rationale: Can build tolerance to controlled spinal flexion, but repeated loaded flexion is not broadly useful for every back or program context.

athletic_transfer.rationale: Low direct transfer because it is kneeling, externally stabilized, and mainly sagittal-plane trunk flexion.

control.rationale: Requires enough control to keep the hips fixed and flex through the trunk, but balance and coordination demands are moderate.

fatigue_efficiency.rationale: Provides a focused abdominal stimulus with low systemic fatigue when the load and range are appropriate.

setup.rationale: Requires a cable station, high pulley, attachment, and often a pad, but no plate loading.

ease.rationale: Easy to set up conceptually, but many users compensate with hip flexion, arm pulling, or excessive lumbar motion.

progression.rationale: Cable-stack increments make load progression much cleaner than most bodyweight abdominal drills.

support.rationale: The kneeling position and cable path provide moderate stability, though the trunk still has to control the flexion arc.

primary.name: Rectus abdominis
primary.evidenceShort: Loaded and common crunch EMG support rectus as the main target.
primary.evidence: Loaded crunch and common abdominal-crunch EMG studies show rectus abdominis is strongly activated during trunk-flexion crunch tasks, supporting the cable crunch as a loadable rectus-focused variant.

secondary.name: External oblique
secondary.evidenceShort: Crunch EMG measured external-oblique activation.
secondary.evidence: Loaded crunch and common crunch EMG studies measured external oblique activity, supporting a meaningful assistive trunk-flexion and bracing role.

secondary.name: Internal oblique
secondary.evidenceShort: Common crunch EMG supports internal-oblique assistance.
secondary.evidence: Common abdominal exercise studies that included the crunch measured internal oblique activity, supporting a secondary abdominal-wall role in the kneeling cable crunch.

evidence.verdict: Kneeling cable crunch: rectus abdominis primary; external and internal oblique secondary; no separate support muscles listed.
evidence.clinicalShort: EMG estimates acute excitation, not hypertrophy, adaptation, pain response, or long-term safety.
evidence.limitsShort: Pulley height, rope position, hip motion, spinal range, load, and whether the user rotates or side-bends can change emphasis.
evidence.summary: The kneeling cable crunch is classified as a loadable trunk-flexion abdominal exercise. Direct evidence for the exact cable variant is limited, so visible roles are based on loaded crunch and common crunch EMG plus the cable variant's same trunk-flexion mechanics.
evidence.clinicalInterpretation: It is most useful when the cable provides progressive resistance while the hips stay relatively fixed and the trunk curls rather than hinges.
evidence.limitations: The strongest direct load study used externally loaded floor crunches rather than a kneeling high-pulley cable. Standing cable crunches, oblique cable crunches, and machine crunches should remain separate variants.

studies.type: Loaded abdominal crunch EMG
studies.shortCitation: Moraes et al., Phys Ther Sport, 2009
studies.finding: Loaded crunches measured rectus abdominis, external oblique, and rectus femoris EMG; abdominal activation was greatest at the highest tested load condition.
studies.citation: Moraes AC, Pinto RS, Valamatos MJ, Valamatos MJ, Pezarat-Correia PL, Okano AH, Santos PM, Cabri JM. EMG activation of abdominal muscles in the crunch exercise performed with different external loads. Physical Therapy in Sport. 2009;10(2):57-62. doi:10.1016/j.ptsp.2009.01.001.
studies.relevance: Closest load-progression crunch EMG source for the cable crunch's main advantage.

studies.type: Commercial and common abdominal exercise EMG
studies.finding: Crunch and several abdominal-machine exercises produced high rectus abdominis and oblique activity.
studies.citation: Escamilla RF, McTaggart MSC, Fricklas EJ, DeWitt R, Kelleher P, Taylor MK, Hreljac A, Moorman CT. An electromyographic analysis of commercial and common abdominal exercises: implications for rehabilitation and training. Journal of Orthopaedic and Sports Physical Therapy. 2006;36(2):45-57. doi:10.2519/jospt.2006.36.2.45.
studies.relevance: Common crunch and abdominal-device EMG source for rectus abdominis and oblique classification.

studies.type: Crunch and abdominal exercise EMG
studies.finding: Compared abdominal crunch, Ab-Slide, supine double leg thrust, and side bridge using rectus abdominis, external oblique, internal oblique, and rectus femoris EMG.
studies.citation: Youdas JW, Guck BR, Hebrink RC, Rugotzke JD, Madson TJ, Hollman JH. An electromyographic analysis of the Ab-Slide exercise, abdominal crunch, supine double leg thrust, and side bridge in healthy young adults: implications for rehabilitation professionals. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2008;22(6):1939-1946. doi:10.1519/JSC.0b013e31818745bf.
studies.relevance: Common crunch EMG source including internal oblique and rectus femoris boundary information.

movements.name: Lying Floor Leg Raise
movements.variant: Supine floor straight-leg raise performed with the low back controlled against the floor.
movements.description: Lie on your back with the legs straight, brace the ribs down, raise the legs without letting the low back arch, pause under control, then lower slowly until the pelvis can still stay stable.

hypertrophy.rationale: Provides local abdominal and hip-flexor loading, but bodyweight leverage and pelvic control limit progressive hypertrophy potential.

strength.rationale: Builds hip-flexion and anterior-core strength through a long lever, but peak force and progression are modest.

joint_resilience.rationale: Can build controlled lumbopelvic tolerance, but excessive hip-flexor dominance or lumbar extension can make it a poor resilience choice for some users.

athletic_transfer.rationale: Useful for basic pelvic control and hip-flexion capacity, but it is supine and has limited carryover to standing or sport-like force transfer.

control.rationale: Meaningful motor-control demand from keeping the pelvis and lumbar spine stable while the long leg lever moves.

fatigue_efficiency.rationale: Low systemic fatigue, though hip flexor and low-back compensation can dilute the abdominal stimulus.

setup.rationale: Requires only floor space and no equipment.

ease.rationale: The task is simple, but maintaining lumbar position with straight legs is harder than it looks.

progression.rationale: Progression relies mostly on range, tempo, reps, or ankle loading rather than precise load increments.

support.rationale: The floor supports the trunk and removes balance demand, though the pelvis must still be actively controlled.

primary.name: Iliopsoas
primary.evidenceShort: Supine leg-raise studies support a primary hip-flexor role.
primary.evidence: Supine leg-raise and active straight-leg-raise EMG studies show high hip-flexor demand, with fine-wire psoas major activity increasing toward end-range hip flexion.

primary.name: Rectus abdominis
primary.evidenceShort: Leg-raise studies measure rectus activity for pelvic control.
primary.evidence: Supine leg-raise studies measured upper and lower rectus abdominis activity; the rectus is classified as primary because the movement is only useful when it controls posterior pelvic tilt and lumbar position against the leg lever.

secondary.name: External oblique
secondary.evidenceShort: Leg-raise EMG measured external-oblique involvement.
secondary.evidence: Supine leg-raise EMG measured external oblique activity, supporting a secondary trunk-stability role during the long-lever raise and lower.

secondary.name: Internal oblique
secondary.evidenceShort: Active straight-leg raise evidence supports internal-oblique control.
secondary.evidence: Fine-wire and surface EMG during active straight-leg raise found obliquus internus/transversus activity increased during later raising, holding, and early lowering phases, supporting a secondary pelvic-control role.

support.name: Quadriceps
support.evidenceShort: Rectus femoris EMG supports visible quadriceps assistance.
support.evidence: Supine leg-raise and active straight-leg-raise studies measured rectus femoris activity; it is shown as quadriceps support because the rectus femoris component helps hold the knee extended and assists hip flexion.

evidence.verdict: Lying floor leg raise: iliopsoas and rectus abdominis primary; external and internal oblique secondary; quadriceps support.
evidence.clinicalShort: EMG estimates acute excitation and timing, not hypertrophy, adaptation, or injury risk.
evidence.limitsShort: Knee bend, range, posterior pelvic tilt, hand support, ankle load, tempo, and lumbar control strongly change emphasis.
evidence.summary: The lying floor leg raise is classified as a hip-flexion plus anterior-core control exercise. Direct supine leg-raise evidence supports hip-flexor demand and abdominal stabilization, with the rectus femoris component of the quadriceps assisting the straight-leg lever.
evidence.clinicalInterpretation: The movement becomes more abdominal when the pelvis stays posteriorly controlled; it becomes more hip-flexor dominant when the low back arches or the pelvis anteriorly tilts.
evidence.limitations: Evidence covers supine straight-leg raise and active straight-leg raise, not every gym variation with hands under hips, bent knees, ankle weights, reverse-curl finish, or decline benches.

studies.type: Supine sit-up and leg-raise EMG
studies.shortCitation: Kim and Lee, J Phys Ther Sci, 2016
studies.finding: Compared supine sit-up and leg-raise activity in upper/lower rectus abdominis, external oblique, rectus femoris, and iliopsoas; leg raises increased hip-flexor activation.
studies.citation: Kim K, Lee T. Comparison of muscular activities in the abdomen and lower limbs while performing sit-up and leg-raise. Journal of Physical Therapy Science. 2016;28(2):491-494. doi:10.1589/jpts.28.491.
studies.relevance: Direct supine leg-raise source for rectus abdominis, external oblique, iliopsoas, and rectus femoris involvement.

studies.type: Active straight-leg raise hip-flexor and abdominal EMG
studies.shortCitation: Okubo et al., J Electromyogr Kinesiol, 2021
studies.finding: Fine-wire psoas major EMG increased toward end-range hip flexion during active straight-leg raise; obliquus internus/transversus activity increased during trunk and pelvic control phases.
studies.citation: Okubo Y, Kaneoka K, Hasebe K, Matsunaga N, Imai A, Hodges PW. Differential activation of psoas major and rectus femoris during active straight leg raise to end range. Journal of Electromyography and Kinesiology. 2021;60:102588. doi:10.1016/j.jelekin.2021.102588.
studies.relevance: Direct straight-leg-raise source for iliopsoas, rectus femoris, rectus abdominis, external oblique, and internal-oblique/transversus activity.

movements.name: Lying Machine Hamstring Curl
movements.variant: Prone or lying hamstring curl machine with the thighs supported and a lower-leg roller or pad applying knee-flexion resistance.
movements.description: Lie prone on the leg-curl machine with the knees aligned near the machine pivot and the roller set just above the heels. Brace lightly into the pads without letting the hips lift, flex the knees to curl the roller toward the back of the thighs, pause under control, then lower until the knees are nearly straight without losing hamstring tension.

hypertrophy.rationale: Excellent direct knee-flexion hypertrophy movement for hamstrings, though hip position is less lengthened than seated curls.

strength.rationale: Builds isolated knee-flexion force, but it does not express integrated lower-body strength.

joint_resilience.rationale: Meaningful posterior-knee and hamstring tolerance builder under controlled loading, but less broad than integrated lower-body resilience work.

athletic_transfer.rationale: Very low athletic-transfer contribution because the task is supported and isolates knee flexion without gait, balance, or hip-knee coordination.

control.rationale: The machine constrains almost everything; the user mainly controls tempo, pelvis position, and ankle position.

fatigue_efficiency.rationale: High local hamstring stimulus with low systemic fatigue and little unrelated recovery cost.

setup.rationale: Low setup once the machine is available, but pad fit, machine availability, and reproducible body position still matter.

ease.rationale: Easy guided pattern with minimal balance demand, limited mainly by knee-axis alignment, pad position, and controlled range.

progression.rationale: Load and reps are easy to track, with deductions for machine-specific geometry, stack increments, and pad setup.

support.rationale: Very high external support from the machine pad, torso position, and guided lever path.

primary.name: Biceps femoris
primary.evidenceShort: Direct lying/prone leg-curl EMG and MRI support biceps femoris involvement.
primary.evidence: Direct lying and prone leg-curl studies measured lateral hamstrings or biceps femoris long-head activity, and MRI training evidence showed biceps femoris long- and short-head adaptation after prone leg-curl training. It is classified as a primary knee-flexion target.

primary.name: Semitendinosus
primary.evidenceShort: Direct prone leg-curl EMG supports high semitendinosus activity.
primary.evidence: High-density and conventional EMG studies directly measured semitendinosus activity during prone or lying leg-curl conditions, with leg-curl variants producing high hamstring activity and meaningful medial-hamstring involvement.

primary.name: Semimembranosus
primary.evidenceShort: Prone leg-curl MRI supports biarticular medial-hamstring adaptation.
primary.evidence: Semimembranosus is included conservatively from MRI evidence showing prone leg-curl training increased biarticular hamstring muscle volume, including semimembranosus. It is not isolated by the surface EMG studies, so the role relies primarily on MRI and knee-flexion biomechanics.

secondary.name: Gastrocnemius
secondary.evidenceShort: Measured prone leg-curl knee-flexion assistant.
secondary.evidence: A prone leg-curl study measured gastrocnemius lateralis activity during knee-flexion contractions and evaluated how ankle and knee position affected force and activation. It is classified as a secondary assistant, not the intended hamstring target.

evidence.verdict: Prone machine knee-flexion leg curl: biceps femoris, semitendinosus, and semimembranosus primary; gastrocnemius secondary; no separate support muscles listed.
evidence.clinicalShort: EMG estimates acute excitation, while MRI training studies estimate adaptation; neither alone proves hypertrophy, mechanical tension, injury risk, or best programming.
evidence.limitsShort: Machine geometry, hip angle, knee angle, ankle position, range of motion, load, tempo, unilateral versus bilateral setup, and seated versus prone position can shift emphasis.
evidence.summary: The lying machine leg curl is classified as a supported knee-flexion isolation exercise for the hamstrings. Direct lying and prone leg-curl EMG supports high biceps femoris and semitendinosus involvement, with lying leg curl showing high hamstring-to-quadriceps activation relative to other lower-body exercises. MRI training evidence supports semimembranosus inclusion because prone leg-curl training increased biarticular hamstring muscle volume. Gastrocnemius is visible as a secondary role because it was directly measured during prone leg-curl contractions and can assist knee flexion, especially as ankle position changes its mechanical contribution.
evidence.clinicalInterpretation: Surface EMG, high-density EMG, and MRI answer different questions.
