EMG is condition-specific excitation data affected by electrode placement, normalization, contraction mode, and load; MRI volume and T2 data provide adaptation or muscle-damage context but do not identify every acute force contributor.
evidence.limitations: Several useful studies used prone leg curls, lying leg curls, or band/manual prone knee flexion rather than one standardized commercial lying machine. Surface EMG evidence is strongest for biceps femoris long head and semitendinosus; semimembranosus is included mainly from MRI training data, not isolated surface EMG. Prone leg curls train the biarticular hamstrings at shorter lengths than seated leg curls, and Maeo et al. found greater hypertrophy after seated versus prone training for the biarticular hamstrings. Local BodyParts3D mappings are now available for biceps femoris, semitendinosus, semimembranosus, and gastrocnemius.

studies.type: Lying leg curl regional EMG
studies.finding: Lying leg curl produced greater normalized mean activation of lower lateral and lower medial hamstrings than stiff-legged deadlift in trained men.
studies.citation: Schoenfeld BJ, Contreras B, Tiryaki-Sonmez G, Wilson JM, Kolber MJ, Peterson MD. Regional differences in muscle activation during hamstrings exercise. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2015;29(1):159-164. doi:10.1519/JSC.0000000000000598.
studies.relevance: Direct lying leg-curl EMG in resistance-trained men using an 8RM load; supports hamstring primary classification and regional-emphasis limitations.

studies.type: High-density prone leg-curl EMG
studies.shortCitation: Hegyi et al., Scand J Med Sci Sports, 2019
studies.finding: Prone leg curl was among the exercises with high hamstring activity, and high-density EMG showed exercise-dependent biceps femoris long-head and semitendinosus regional patterns.
studies.citation: Hegyi A, Csala D, Peter A, Finni T, Cronin NJ. High-density electromyography activity in various hamstring exercises. Scandinavian Journal of Medicine & Science in Sports. 2019;29(1):34-43. doi:10.1111/sms.13303.
studies.relevance: Directly included prone leg curl and measured biceps femoris long head and semitendinosus with 15-channel high-density EMG in amateur athletes.

studies.type: Lying leg curl hamstring-to-quadriceps EMG
studies.shortCitation: Veeck et al., Res Sports Med, 2024
studies.finding: Lying leg curl produced the greatest hamstring-to-quadriceps activation ratio among parallel squat, Romanian deadlift, hip thrust, lying leg curl, and seated knee extension, with relatively homogeneous lateral-to-medial hamstring activation.
studies.citation: Veeck F, de Vargas JS, Godinho RAT, Wilhelm EN, Daros Pinto M, Pinto RS. Hamstring-to-quadriceps activation ratio during lower-limb strengthening exercises. Research in Sports Medicine. 2024;32(5):843-856. doi:10.1080/15438627.2023.2286355.
studies.relevance: Directly studied lying leg curl among common lower-body exercises and supports its high hamstring targeting with low quadriceps contribution.

studies.type: Seated versus prone leg-curl MRI training study
studies.shortCitation: Maeo et al., Med Sci Sports Exerc, 2021
studies.finding: Both seated and prone leg-curl training increased hamstring muscle volume, but seated training produced greater hypertrophy in the biarticular hamstrings because they operated at longer muscle lengths.
studies.citation: Maeo S, Huang M, Wu Y, Sakurai H, Kusagawa Y, Sugiyama T, Kanehisa H, Isaka T. Greater Hamstrings Muscle Hypertrophy but Similar Damage Protection after Training at Long versus Short Muscle Lengths. Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise. 2021;53(4):825-837. doi:10.1249/MSS.0000000000002523.
studies.relevance: Direct prone leg-curl training comparison with MRI-measured individual hamstring muscle volume and T2; supports semimembranosus inclusion and seated-versus-prone limitations.

studies.type: Prone leg-curl EMG and EMG-rise study
studies.finding: Conventional prone leg curls at 8, 16, and 24RM produced substantial biceps femoris long-head and semitendinosus peak nEMG, while Nordic hamstring produced faster EMG rise.
studies.citation: Krommes K, Jakobsen MD, Bandholm T, Andersen LL, Zebis MK, Shield AJ, Holmich P, Thorborg K. Cross-sectional Study of EMG and EMG Rise During Fast and Slow Hamstring Exercises. International Journal of Sports Physical Therapy. 2021;16(4):1033-1042. doi:10.26603/001c.25364.
studies.relevance: Close prone knee-flexion evidence using an elastic-band leg-curl setup; useful for biceps femoris long-head and semitendinosus activation and fatigue interpretation.

studies.type: Prone leg-curl knee and ankle position EMG
studies.finding: In trained men, prone leg-curl maximal isometric contractions measured biceps femoris, gastrocnemius lateralis, and soleus lateralis activity, with force and activation affected by knee and ankle position.
studies.citation: Marchetti PH, Magalhaes RA, Gomes WA, da Silva JJ, Stecyk SD, Whiting WC. Different Knee and Ankle Positions Affect Force and Muscle Activation During Prone Leg Curl in Trained Subjects. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2021;35(12):3322-3326. doi:10.1519/JSC.0000000000003333.
studies.relevance: Direct prone leg-curl evidence measuring biceps femoris and gastrocnemius lateralis; supports gastrocnemius as a secondary knee-flexion assistant and ankle-position limitations.

movements.name: Machine Hack Squat
movements.variant: Angled hack squat machine with back and shoulder pads and a fixed sled path; treated separately from barbell hack squat, Smith squat, leg press, and free-weight squat variants.
movements.description: Set the shoulders and back firmly against the pads, place the feet on the platform at a repeatable height and width, unlock the sled, and descend under control while keeping the heels down and knees tracking over the feet. Drive through the platform to stand without slamming into lockout, then engage the safeties before stepping out.

hypertrophy.rationale: Excellent machine-supported squat stimulus, usually quad-biased with meaningful glute loading when depth and foot placement allow.

strength.rationale: Supports heavy bilateral lower-body loading, but strength expression is highly machine-specific and less self-stabilized than free squatting.

joint_resilience.rationale: Provides controlled knee and hip loading through useful range, with deductions because fixed sled geometry and deep knee flexion can be unforgiving if setup is mismatched.

athletic_transfer.rationale: Lower transfer than free squats because the pad and rails remove much of the balance, bracing, and whole-body coordination.

control.rationale: Low Motor Control demand because the back pad and guided sled path stabilize most of the movement.

fatigue_efficiency.rationale: Good local lower-body stimulus with less trunk fatigue than back squats, though heavy sled loading still creates major quad and systemic fatigue.

setup.rationale: Requires a specific machine, plate or stack loading, safety setup, and repeatable foot placement.

ease.rationale: Easier to stabilize than free squats, but foot placement, depth, heel contact, pelvic position, and safety handles still require attention.

progression.rationale: Load, reps, and range are easy to track, with deductions for large plate jumps and machine-to-machine path differences.

support.rationale: Very high external support from the shoulder pads, back pad, foot platform, rails, and safety catches.

primary.name: Quadriceps
primary.evidenceShort: Hack squat and close machine squat evidence support a quad-biased role.
primary.evidence: Hack squat variation EMG and close leg press/squat studies support high knee-extensor demand in guided lower-body pressing, with quadriceps classified as the main visible target.

secondary.name: Gluteus maximus
secondary.evidenceShort: Hip-extension contributor, foot-placement and depth sensitive.
secondary.evidence: Squat-variation and leg press evidence measures gluteus maximus involvement in related guided and free squat patterns; in the hack squat it is meaningful but typically secondary to the quad-biased sled path.

secondary.name: Hamstrings
secondary.evidenceShort: Measured assistant with reduced emphasis in hack squat comparisons.
secondary.evidence: Squat-variation and leg press studies measure hamstring activity, but hack squat support and knee-extension dominance keep hamstrings in a secondary role rather than a main target.

support.name: Trunk stabilizers
support.evidenceShort: Measured but lower than unsupported back squat.
support.evidence: A direct back-versus-hack squat study found trunk activation is load sensitive in both lifts but lower in the hack squat, supporting a small visible support role due to bracing against the machine.

evidence.verdict: Machine hack squat: quadriceps primary; gluteus maximus and hamstrings secondary; trunk stabilizers support.
evidence.clinicalShort: Exact hack squat EMG evidence is thinner than free squat and leg press evidence, so close guided-squat and leg-press studies are used conservatively.
evidence.limitsShort: Machine angle, back-pad angle, foot height, stance width, depth, heel lift, lockout, load, and sled friction can all change emphasis.
evidence.summary: The machine hack squat is classified as a guided machine squat with high external support. Direct hack squat trunk-activation evidence and squat-variant EMG, combined with close leg press and squat biomechanics, support quadriceps as the primary target, gluteus maximus and hamstrings as secondary contributors, and trunk stabilizers as a smaller support role.
evidence.clinicalInterpretation: Because commercial hack squat machines vary substantially, direct evidence from one machine path may not generalize perfectly. The classification emphasizes visible roles that are consistent across the available direct hack, squat-variation, leg press, and biomechanics evidence.
evidence.limitations: This entry assumes a conventional angled sled hack squat with the back supported. It is not a barbell hack squat, pendulum squat, Smith machine squat, or leg press. The local anatomy registry does not contain a broad adductor or adductor magnus mesh, so no visible adductor role was added.

studies.type: Squat variation EMG
studies.finding: Front, hack, and other squat variations were compared using EMG from lower-limb and trunk muscles.
studies.citation: Erdag D, Yavuz HU. Evaluation of Muscle Activities During Different Squat Variations Using Electromyography Signals. In: Ahram T, Karwowski W, Pickl S, Taiar R, editors. Human Systems Engineering and Design II. Advances in Intelligent Systems and Computing. 2019;1026:859-865. doi:10.1007/978-3-030-35249-3_114.
studies.relevance: Closest direct hack squat EMG source for lower-limb and trunk role classification.

studies.type: Back versus hack squat trunk EMG
studies.finding: Hack squats allowed higher absolute loads but produced lower trunk muscle activation than back squats at matched relative loads.
studies.citation: Clark DR, Lambert MI, Hunter AM. Trunk Muscle Activation in the Back and Hack Squat at the Same Relative Loads. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2019;33 Suppl 1:S60-S69. doi:10.1519/JSC.0000000000002144.
studies.relevance: Direct hack squat evidence for machine support, trunk stabilizer role, and support/control ratings.

studies.type: 45 degree leg press EMG variation study
studies.finding: Leg press foot placement and load changed quadriceps, hamstring, gastrocnemius, and gluteus maximus activation.
studies.citation: Da Silva EM, Brentano MA, Cadore EL, De Almeida AP, Kruel LF. Analysis of muscle activation during different leg press exercises at submaximum effort levels. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2008;22(4):1059-1065. doi:10.1519/JSC.0b013e3181739445.
studies.relevance: Close guided-machine lower-body press evidence for quadriceps, gluteus maximus, and hamstring role support when exact hack squat muscle data are limited.

studies.type: Squat and leg press biomechanics and EMG
studies.finding: Squat and leg press technique variations altered lower-body muscle activity and knee joint forces.
studies.citation: Escamilla RF, Fleisig GS, Zheng N, Lander JE, Barrentine SW, Andrews JR, Bergemann BW, Moorman CT 3rd. Effects of technique variations on knee biomechanics during the squat and leg press. Medicine and Science in Sports and Exercise. 2001;33(9):1552-1566. doi:10.1097/00005768-200109000-00020.
studies.relevance: Biomechanics and EMG source for guided lower-body press and squat comparisons, foot placement, stance, and knee-loading limitations.

studies.type: Free squat biomechanics and EMG comparison
studies.finding: Front and back squats produced similar overall muscle recruitment, helping anchor the expected lower-body extensor pattern for squat variants.
studies.citation: Gullett JC, Tillman MD, Gutierrez GM, Chow JW. A biomechanical comparison of back and front squats in healthy trained individuals. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2009;23(1):284-292. doi:10.1519/JSC.0b013e31818546bb.
studies.relevance: Close free-squat comparator used only to anchor the lower-body extensor demands of squat-family movement patterns.

studies.type: Parallel, full, and front squat EMG
studies.shortCitation: Contreras et al., J Appl Biomech, 2016
studies.finding: Squat variations measured gluteus maximus, biceps femoris, and vastus lateralis EMG amplitudes.
studies.citation: Contreras B, Vigotsky AD, Schoenfeld BJ, Beardsley C, McMaster DT, Reyneke JHT, Cronin JB. A Comparison of Gluteus Maximus, Biceps Femoris, and Vastus Lateralis Electromyography Amplitude in Parallel, Full, and Front Squat Variations in Resistance-Trained Females. Journal of Applied Biomechanics. 2016;32(1):16-22. doi:10.1123/jab.2015-0113.
studies.relevance: Close squat-variation EMG source for gluteus maximus, biceps femoris, and vastus lateralis role support.

movements.name: Machine Hip Thrust
movements.variant: Guided hip-thrust machine with a fixed pad or belt loading the hips and external support from the machine frame.
movements.description: Sit into the machine with the upper back and hips aligned to the pads, secure the hip pad or belt low across the pelvis, plant the feet evenly, brace the trunk, drive the hips up by squeezing the glutes until the hips reach full extension, then lower under control while keeping the ribs down and the pelvis stable.

hypertrophy.rationale: Excellent glute hypertrophy option because the machine stabilizes setup while direct comparison evidence reports gluteus maximus activation similar to barbell hip thrusts.

strength.rationale: Builds loaded hip-extension strength, but the guided machine path is less transferable to free-weight force expression.

joint_resilience.rationale: Provides controlled hip-extension loading with low knee demand, but the guided setup gives limited broad joint-capacity exposure.

athletic_transfer.rationale: The machine is highly constrained and supported, so transfer to upright or dynamic athletic movement is narrow despite strong glute loading.

control.rationale: Very low motor-control demand because the machine removes most balance, bar positioning, and path management.

fatigue_efficiency.rationale: Very efficient local glute stimulus with low setup leakage, low balance cost, and little unrelated systemic fatigue.

setup.rationale: Fast setup once the machine is available, with mainly seat, pad, belt, and load adjustments.

ease.rationale: Easier than free-weight hip thrusts because the machine simplifies loading, positioning, and repeated set execution.

progression.rationale: Machine loads and reps are easy to record and repeat, with deductions for machine-specific leverage and stack increments.

support.rationale: Very high external support from the frame, pads, foot platform, and guided loading path.

primary.name: Gluteus maximus
primary.evidenceShort: Direct machine comparison reports gluteus maximus activation similar to barbell hip thrusts.
primary.evidence: Machine-versus-barbell hip-thrust evidence reports similar gluteus maximus activation between the machine and free-weight versions. Broader hip-thrust research supports gluteus maximus as the dominant hip-extension target.

secondary.name: Hamstrings
secondary.evidenceShort: Machine comparison reports higher biceps femoris activation than the barbell version.
secondary.evidence: The direct machine-versus-barbell comparison measured greater biceps femoris activation in the machine condition, while broader hip-thrust evidence supports hamstrings as meaningful secondary hip extensors.

support.name: Gluteus medius
support.evidenceShort: Hip-thrust literature includes gluteus medius as a measured gluteal contributor.
support.evidence: Systematic review evidence includes gluteus medius among hip-thrust muscles evaluated. It is listed as support because the standard machine movement is bilateral and guided.

support.name: Quadriceps
support.evidenceShort: Vastus lateralis is measured at lower activation than barbell in the machine comparison.
support.evidence: The direct machine comparison measured vastus lateralis activity and reported lower mean activation than the free-weight version, supporting a small support classification rather than a target-muscle role.

evidence.verdict: Machine hip thrust: gluteus maximus primary; hamstrings secondary; gluteus medius and quadriceps support.
evidence.clinicalShort: EMG estimates acute excitation and should not be treated as a direct measure of hypertrophy, safety, or individual adaptation.
evidence.limitsShort: Machine brand, pad path, hip-belt position, foot platform, seat angle, and range of motion can materially change loading.
evidence.summary: The machine hip thrust is classified as a guided lower-body hip-extension movement. The direct comparison evidence supports a gluteus-maximus-dominant profile similar to barbell hip thrusts, with meaningful hamstring contribution and limited quadriceps involvement.
evidence.clinicalInterpretation: The machine version should be scored separately from the barbell version because external support, setup friction, path constraint, and ease of repeated loading are materially different even when glute activation is similar.
evidence.limitations: The available direct machine evidence is narrower than the barbell evidence base and may not generalize across all commercial hip-thrust machines.

studies.type: Machine versus barbell hip thrust EMG
studies.finding: Machine and free-weight hip thrusts showed similar gluteus maximus mean activation; the machine showed greater biceps femoris mean activation and lower vastus lateralis mean activation.
studies.citation: Petrizzo J, Lopez J, Gaeta A, Aquino M, Otto R, Wygand J. Machine Vs. Barbell Hip Thrust: Electromyographic, Biomechanical, And Ease Of Use Comparison: 2266. Medicine and Science in Sports and Exercise. 2023;55(9S):749. doi:10.1249/01.mss.0000986876.72568.fb.
studies.relevance: Direct machine hip-thrust evidence for gluteus maximus, biceps femoris, vastus lateralis, and ease-of-use comparison with free weight.

studies.type: Barbell hip thrust systematic review
studies.finding: The review concluded that hip-thrust mechanics favor hip-extensor activation, with an excitation sequence led by gluteus maximus followed by erector spinae, hamstrings, and quadriceps femoris.
studies.citation: Krause Neto W, Vieira TL, Gama EF. Barbell Hip Thrust, Muscular Activation and Performance: A Systematic Review. Journal of Sports Science and Medicine. 2019;18(2):198-206.
studies.relevance: Broader hip-thrust movement-family evidence for muscle hierarchy and role boundaries.

studies.type: Barbell hip thrust versus back squat EMG
studies.shortCitation: Contreras et al., J Appl Biomech, 2015
studies.finding: The barbell hip thrust produced greater upper/lower gluteus maximus and biceps femoris activity than the back squat in the tested condition, while vastus lateralis favored the squat.
studies.citation: Contreras B, Vigotsky AD, Schoenfeld BJ, Beardsley C, Cronin J. A Comparison of Gluteus Maximus, Biceps Femoris, and Vastus Lateralis Electromyographic Activity in the Back Squat and Barbell Hip Thrust Exercises. Journal of Applied Biomechanics. 2015;31(6):452-458. doi:10.1123/jab.2014-0301.
studies.relevance: Direct barbell hip-thrust EMG source used to anchor the general hip-thrust muscle profile.

studies.type: Barbell hip thrust biomechanics
studies.finding: Biomechanical analysis of trained lifters at 70% 1RM characterized hip and knee extensor demand across the barbell hip thrust.
studies.citation: Brazil A, Needham L, Palmer JL, Bezodis IN. A comprehensive biomechanical analysis of the barbell hip thrust. PLOS ONE. 2021;16(3):e0249307. doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0249307.
studies.relevance: Movement-family biomechanics source used for hip-extension loading and progression interpretation.

movements.name: One-Arm Dumbbell Row
movements.variant: One-arm dumbbell row with the opposite hand or knee supported on a bench and the dumbbell pulled toward the hip or lower ribs.
movements.description: Set one hand or one hand and knee on a bench, brace the torso, and let the dumbbell hang under the shoulder without rounding the back. Pull the elbow back toward the hip or lower ribs, pause briefly without twisting the torso, then lower until the arm is long and the shoulder blade can reach forward under control.

hypertrophy.rationale: Strong unilateral row stimulus for lats, mid-back, posterior shoulder, and elbow flexors, with target quality depending on torso discipline and elbow path.

strength.rationale: Builds meaningful one-arm pulling strength, but dumbbell size, bench support, grip, and trunk rotation limit clean force expression compared with barbell anchors.

joint_resilience.rationale: Provides controlled shoulder, elbow, scapular, and trunk exposure, but it is not primarily a joint-resilience drill.

athletic_transfer.rationale: The unilateral load and anti-rotation demand add some transfer, while bench support and a narrow pull path keep it less sport-like than standing pulls.

control.rationale: Requires scapular timing, elbow-path control, grip, and trunk anti-rotation while one side works independently.

fatigue_efficiency.rationale: Good back stimulus with modest systemic cost, but grip, biceps, and torso compensation can limit target loading.

setup.rationale: Needs an open bench and a suitable dumbbell, with some friction from stance, bench height, and heavy dumbbell handling.

ease.rationale: Conceptually simple, but consistent torso position, scapular motion, and avoiding rotation take practice.

progression.rationale: Load and reps are easy to log, but dumbbell jumps can be coarse and performance can change with bench and body position.

support.rationale: The bench supports part of the body, but the working arm follows a free path and the trunk must resist rotation.

primary.name: Latissimus dorsi
primary.evidenceShort: Row-family EMG supports lat emphasis with tucked-elbow paths.
primary.evidence: Direct row EMG shows greater latissimus dorsi excitation when shoulder abduction is closer to 0 degrees, and prone row data show latissimus dorsi as a measured prime mover. This one-arm dumbbell variant uses the same shoulder-extension and adduction pattern when the elbow tracks toward the hip.

secondary.name: Teres major
secondary.evidenceShort: Measured shoulder-extension assistant in rowing.
secondary.evidence: Seated row EMG directly measured teres major alongside latissimus dorsi during heavy rowing, supporting a shoulder-extension assistant role that carries to the one-arm dumbbell row when the elbow is driven back.

secondary.name: Middle trapezius
secondary.evidenceShort: Row EMG supports scapular-retraction contribution.
secondary.evidence: Seated cable and prone row EMG studies measured middle or transverse trapezius activity during rowing, especially as the shoulder moves into greater abduction or the row reaches the retracted finish.

secondary.name: Rhomboids
secondary.evidenceShort: Inferred from grouped middle trapezius/rhomboid EMG and scapular retraction.
secondary.evidence: This visible role is marked as inference: Lehman et al. grouped middle trapezius and rhomboid EMG during row tasks, and the one-arm dumbbell row requires scapular retraction as the dumbbell is pulled toward the torso.

secondary.name: Posterior deltoid
secondary.evidenceShort: Measured row contributor, especially with wider elbow paths.
secondary.evidence: Posterior deltoid or rear deltoid activity is directly measured in seated row and prone row EMG studies; it assists shoulder extension and horizontal abduction but remains path-sensitive and secondary to the back target.

secondary.name: Biceps brachii
secondary.evidenceShort: Measured elbow-flexion assistant in rows.
secondary.evidence: Row EMG studies repeatedly measure biceps brachii activity, and a unilateral dumbbell row training study found elbow-flexor hypertrophy lower than curls but still present after row training. This supports a secondary elbow-flexor role.

support.name: Rotator cuff
support.evidenceShort: Direction-specific shoulder stabilization during row.
support.evidence: Rotator cuff recruitment during row tasks is direction-specific and consistent with dynamic glenohumeral stabilization rather than a primary hypertrophy role.

support.name: Erector spinae
support.evidenceShort: Trunk-position support while rowing.
support.evidence: Row studies measuring trunk musculature show erector spinae involvement during free-weight and unilateral row tasks. Bench support reduces but does not remove the need to hold a stable torso during heavy one-arm dumbbell rows.

support.name: External oblique
support.evidenceShort: Unilateral row evidence supports anti-rotation control.
support.evidence: Saeterbakken et al. found unilateral row performance increased external oblique activity compared with bilateral conditions, supporting an anti-rotation support role in one-arm rowing.

evidence.verdict: One-arm dumbbell row: latissimus dorsi primary; teres major, middle trapezius, rhomboids, posterior deltoid, and biceps brachii secondary; rotator cuff, erector spinae, and external oblique support.
evidence.clinicalShort: EMG estimates acute excitation, not hypertrophy, mechanical tension, adaptation, or injury risk.
evidence.limitsShort: Bench setup, torso angle, elbow flare, grip, dumbbell size, range of motion, and trunk rotation can shift emphasis between lats, upper back, posterior shoulder, elbow flexors, and trunk support.
evidence.summary: The one-arm dumbbell row is classified as a unilateral, partly bench-supported horizontal pulling exercise. Direct evidence for the exact bench-supported dumbbell variant is limited, so the classification combines row-family EMG, unilateral dumbbell row training evidence for elbow flexors, rowing trunk EMG, and a peer-reviewed one-arm dumbbell row technique source. A tucked-elbow path supports latissimus dorsi as the primary target; teres major, middle trapezius, rhomboids, posterior deltoid, and biceps brachii assist the pull; rotator cuff, erector spinae, and external oblique are included as support for shoulder and trunk control.
evidence.clinicalInterpretation: Surface EMG and short-term hypertrophy studies should not be treated as direct proof of long-term adaptation for every row setup. Technique and load path matter because the same dumbbell can be pulled as a lat-biased row, a wider upper-back row, or a momentum-assisted torso rotation.
evidence.limitations: The evidence base includes seated cable row, prone barbell row, unilateral row trunk studies, and a unilateral dumbbell row training study. These are close but not identical to every bench-supported one-arm dumbbell row. Brachialis and brachioradialis were not added because they are not available as local visible anatomy entries.

studies.type: Seated cable row EMG and force study
studies.shortCitation: Vasconcelos et al., Int J Strength Cond, 2023
studies.finding: Rows closer to 0 degrees of shoulder abduction increased upper and lower latissimus activity, while greater abduction increased upper-back and posterior deltoid activity.
studies.citation: Vasconcelos CMWA, Lopes CR, Almeida VM, Neto WK, Soares EG. Effect Of Different Grip Position And Shoulder-Abduction Angle On Muscle Strength And Activation During The Seated Cable Row. International Journal of Strength and Conditioning. 2023;3(1):1-13. doi:10.47206/ijsc.v3i1.190.
studies.relevance: Direct row-family EMG of latissimus dorsi, trapezius, posterior deltoid, and biceps brachii across shoulder-abduction and grip conditions.

studies.type: Prone row range-of-motion EMG study
studies.shortCitation: Fischer et al., J Electromyogr Kinesiol, 2025
studies.finding: Prone barbell row EMG measured latissimus dorsi, transverse trapezius, rear deltoid, and biceps brachii across full, upper-half, and lower-half ranges of motion.
studies.citation: Fischer J, Burger C, Seguel JM, Rodoplu C, Paternoster FK, Tilp M, Konrad A. Impact of different ranges of motion in the prone barbell row on muscle excitation. Journal of Electromyography and Kinesiology. 2025;83:103025. doi:10.1016/j.jelekin.2025.103025.
studies.relevance: Close row variant with chest support and direct EMG of the main visible back, posterior shoulder, and elbow-flexor contributors.

studies.type: Latissimus dorsi exercise EMG study
studies.finding: Seated row produced a high latissimus-to-biceps activation ratio and high grouped middle trapezius/rhomboid activity among traditional latissimus exercises.
studies.citation: Lehman GJ, Buchan DD, Lundy A, Myers N, Nalborczyk A. Variations in muscle activation levels during traditional latissimus dorsi weight training exercises: An experimental study. Dynamic Medicine. 2004;3:4. doi:10.1186/1476-5918-3-4.
studies.relevance: Row-family EMG evidence for latissimus dorsi, biceps brachii, and grouped middle trapezius/rhomboid contribution.

studies.type: Seated row EMG and verbal-instruction study
studies.finding: At 70% 1RM, seated row produced substantial latissimus dorsi, teres major, posterior deltoid, and biceps brachii activity.
studies.citation: Fujita RA, De Marchi PU, Silva NRS, Gomes MM. Verbal instruction does not change myoelectric activity during seated row exercise in trained and untrained men. Motriz: Revista de Educacao Fisica. 2019;25(4):e10190100. doi:10.1590/s1980-6574201900040100.
studies.relevance: Direct seated row EMG including teres major and posterior deltoid, used as close row-family evidence.

studies.type: Unilateral dumbbell row training study
studies.finding: Eight weeks of unilateral dumbbell row training increased elbow-flexor thickness less than unilateral biceps curl training, supporting biceps as a secondary rather than primary target.
studies.citation: Mannarino P, Matta T, Lima J, Simao R, Freitas de Salles B. Single-Joint Exercise Results in Higher Hypertrophy of Elbow Flexors Than Multijoint Exercise. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2021;35(10):2677-2681. doi:10.1519/JSC.0000000000003234.
studies.relevance: Exact unilateral dumbbell row intervention evidence for elbow-flexor contribution and its secondary status.

studies.type: Rotator cuff recruitment study
studies.shortCitation: Wattanaprakornkul et al., J Electromyogr Kinesiol, 2011
studies.finding: Rotator cuff recruitment during bench press and row was direction-specific, consistent with dynamic shoulder stabilization.
studies.citation: Wattanaprakornkul D, Halaki M, Cathers I, Ginn KA. Direction-specific recruitment of rotator cuff muscles during bench press and row. Journal of Electromyography and Kinesiology. 2011;21(6):1041-1049. doi:10.1016/j.jelekin.2011.09.002.
studies.relevance: Directly supports rotator cuff involvement as shoulder stabilization during row tasks.

studies.type: Rowing exercise trunk EMG and lumbar-load study
studies.finding: Different rowing exercises produced different trunk muscle activation, lumbar motion, load, and stiffness demands.
studies.citation: Fenwick CMJ, Brown SHM, McGill SM. Comparison of different rowing exercises: trunk muscle activation and lumbar spine motion, load, and stiffness. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2009;23(2):350-358. doi:10.1519/JSC.0b013e3181942019.
studies.relevance: Row-family evidence for trunk support and fatigue costs during free-weight and unilateral row variants.

studies.type: Bi- and unilateral row core EMG study
studies.shortCitation: Saeterbakken et al., Int J Sports Med, 2015
studies.finding: Unilateral row performance activated the external oblique more than bilateral performance, while free-weight rows produced greater erector spinae or multifidus activity than machine rows.
studies.citation: Saeterbakken A, Andersen V, Brudeseth A, Lund H, Fimland MS. The Effect of Performing Bi- and Unilateral Row Exercises on Core Muscle Activation. International Journal of Sports Medicine. 2015;36(11):900-905. doi:10.1055/s-0034-1398646.
studies.relevance: Directly compares unilateral and bilateral row core activation and supports anti-rotation support in one-arm rowing.

studies.type: One-arm dumbbell row technique article
studies.finding: Describes the dumbbell one-arm row technique and setup as a supported unilateral pulling exercise.
studies.citation: Graham JF. Dumbbell One-Arm Row. Strength and Conditioning Journal. 2001;23(2):59. doi:10.1519/00126548-200104000-00014.
studies.relevance: Peer-reviewed technique source for the exact named movement and setup assumptions.

movements.name: Overhead Cable Triceps Extension
movements.variant: Cable elbow extension performed with the upper arm flexed overhead, commonly facing away from a pulley with a rope or handle and the elbows pointing forward or upward.
movements.description: Set a cable so the line of pull stays behind or below the hands, take the handle overhead, and brace with the ribs stacked over the pelvis. Keep the upper arms mostly fixed, bend the elbows until the triceps are stretched, extend the elbows until the arms are nearly straight, then return under control without letting the shoulders collapse or the low back arch.

hypertrophy.rationale: Excellent triceps hypertrophy accessory because cable overhead elbow-extension training produced large triceps growth, likely helped by loading the long head at a longer muscle length.

strength.rationale: Useful for elbow-extension strength, but the overhead isolation setup is not a major maximal-strength expression compared with compound presses.

joint_resilience.rationale: Can build tolerance to controlled overhead elbow-extension loading, but shoulder flexion and deep elbow flexion make it a narrow resilience tool.

athletic_transfer.rationale: Very low athletic-transfer signal because it is a stationary single-joint triceps exercise.

control.rationale: Requires more shoulder, rib, elbow-path, and cable-line control than a pushdown, but still has limited whole-body coordination demand.

fatigue_efficiency.rationale: High local triceps stimulus with modest systemic cost, though overhead setup and shoulder-position fatigue can reduce efficiency for some users.

setup.rationale: Requires a cable station, correct pulley height, handle selection, and careful body position, so setup is more involved than a standard pushdown.

ease.rationale: Learnable, but the overhead position, elbow tracking, cable angle, and trunk bracing are more sensitive than neutral-arm pushdowns.

progression.rationale: Cable stack loading is trackable, with deductions for friction, attachment differences, body-angle changes, and shoulder-position consistency.

support.rationale: The cable path is externally loaded and predictable, but the user must stabilize the overhead arm position and trunk without a bench or guided lever.

primary.name: Triceps brachii
primary.evidenceShort: Cable overhead training studies support the triceps as the target.
primary.evidence: Cable overhead-arm elbow extension studies directly trained and measured triceps brachii adaptations, with MRI evidence showing larger hypertrophy than neutral-arm cable extension. Shoulder-position EMG and biomechanics studies support head-level triceps involvement during elbow extension with the arm elevated.

evidence.verdict: Overhead cable triceps extension: triceps brachii primary; no visible secondary or support muscles added.
evidence.clinicalShort: EMG and imaging studies estimate excitation and adaptation under specific protocols, not pain or injury risk.
evidence.limitsShort: Pulley height, facing direction, rope versus bar, shoulder flexion angle, elbow range, trunk position, load, and fatigue can shift emphasis and tolerance.
evidence.summary: The overhead cable triceps extension is classified as a cable elbow-extension isolation movement performed with the arm elevated. Direct training studies using cable overhead-arm elbow extension support triceps brachii as the primary visible role. No secondary or support muscles are shown because the reviewed evidence centers on triceps adaptation and head-level triceps behavior, while shoulder and trunk muscles function mainly to hold position.
evidence.clinicalInterpretation: Surface electromyography and MRI muscle-volume changes help interpret muscle involvement and adaptation in a specific protocol. They should not be treated as direct measures of mechanical tension, individual hypertrophy response, pain risk, or injury risk.
evidence.limitations: The local anatomy dataset exposes triceps brachii as a whole muscle, not separate long, lateral, and medial heads. Direct training evidence often uses unilateral cable conditions and controlled elbow ranges rather than every gym version of the overhead rope extension. Dumbbell, EZ-bar, machine, seated, kneeling, one-arm, and cable-from-high versus cable-from-low overhead extensions should be separate variants if the app needs that detail.

studies.type: Direct cable overhead versus neutral-arm hypertrophy study
studies.shortCitation: Maeo et al., Eur J Sport Sci, 2023
studies.finding: Overhead-arm cable elbow extension produced greater triceps brachii hypertrophy than neutral-arm cable elbow extension despite lower absolute loads.
studies.citation: Maeo S, Wu Y, Huang M, Sakurai H, Kusagawa Y, Sugiyama T, Kanehisa H, Isaka T. Triceps brachii hypertrophy is substantially greater after elbow extension training performed in the overhead versus neutral arm position. European Journal of Sport Science. 2023;23(7):1240-1250. doi:10.1080/17461391.2022.2100279.
studies.relevance: Most direct source for the requested cable overhead triceps extension, using a cable machine, overhead arm position, 12 weeks of training, and MRI-measured triceps volume.

studies.type: Cable pushdown versus overhead extension training study
studies.shortCitation: Stasinaki et al., J Funct Morphol Kinesiol, 2018
studies.finding: Unilateral cable overhead extensions at long fascicle length and cable push-downs at short fascicle length both improved elbow-extension strength and triceps architecture over six weeks.
studies.citation: Stasinaki AN, Zaras N, Methenitis S, Tsitkanou S, Krase A, Kavvoura A, Terzis G. Triceps Brachii Muscle Strength and Architectural Adaptations with Resistance Training Exercises at Short or Long Fascicle Length. Journal of Functional Morphology and Kinesiology. 2018;3(2):28. doi:10.3390/jfmk3020028.
studies.relevance: Directly studied cable overhead extension as a long-fascicle-length triceps training condition, though the sample was small and novice female participants.

studies.type: Shoulder-position elbow-extension EMG
studies.shortCitation: Alves et al., J Sports Med Phys Fitness, 2018
studies.finding: Dumbbell elbow extension exercises showed shoulder-position-dependent triceps head activity.
studies.citation: Alves D, Matta T, Oliveira L. Effect of shoulder position on triceps brachii heads activity in dumbbell elbow extension exercises. Journal of Sports Medicine and Physical Fitness. 2018;58(9):1247-1252. doi:10.23736/S0022-4707.17.06849-9.
studies.relevance: Close elbow-extension EMG evidence for triceps head behavior at different shoulder positions; less direct because it used dumbbells rather than cables.

studies.type: Triceps head function by shoulder elevation
studies.shortCitation: Kholinne et al., Acta Orthop Traumatol Turc, 2018
studies.finding: Each triceps head showed different force and activity patterns across shoulder elevation angles during elbow-extension tasks.
studies.citation: Kholinne E, Zulkarnain RF, Sun YC, Lim S, Chun JM, Jeon IH. The different role of each head of the triceps brachii muscle in elbow extension. Acta Orthopaedica et Traumatologica Turcica. 2018;52(3):201-205. doi:10.1016/j.aott.2018.02.005.
studies.relevance: Biomechanics and EMG context for why overhead shoulder elevation changes triceps head behavior during elbow extension.

movements.name: Parallel Bar Dip
movements.variant: Bodyweight parallel-bar dip performed on fixed parallel or V-shaped dip bars without external load or machine assistance.
movements.description: Support the body on parallel bars with arms straight, shoulders controlled, and the torso slightly inclined as needed. Lower under control by bending the elbows and allowing the shoulders to extend until reaching a manageable depth, then press back up by extending the elbows and flexing the shoulders without collapsing into the bottom position or shrugging at the top.

hypertrophy.rationale: Strong bodyweight loading for pectoralis major and triceps brachii, but shoulder depth tolerance, relative strength, and technique can limit target-muscle volume.

strength.rationale: Useful upper-body pushing strength builder, especially once weighted, but bodyweight entry demands and loading setup make force expression less clean than barbell pressing.

joint_resilience.rationale: Can build controlled shoulder, elbow, and scapular tolerance, but loaded shoulder extension is a meaningful constraint and is not ideal for every shoulder.

athletic_transfer.rationale: Good upper-body support-strength transfer for calisthenics and obstacle-style tasks, though it remains bilateral and equipment-specific.

control.rationale: Requires meaningful scapular depression, shoulder position, elbow path, depth, and suspended-body control.

fatigue_efficiency.rationale: Delivers a lot of pressing stimulus with little setup, but high relative load, shoulder-range demands, and failure risk can leak fatigue.

setup.rationale: Needs only a stable dip station or parallel bars, but bar spacing, height, access, and weighted progression setup add friction.

ease.rationale: Simple to understand but hard to perform well because adequate relative strength, shoulder extension tolerance, and scapular control are required from the start.

progression.rationale: Progresses well with a belt, vest, bands, or assistance, but load changes are less granular and less standardized than a stack, dumbbells, or a barbell.

support.rationale: The bars are fixed, but the body is suspended and the user must stabilize the shoulders, scapulae, elbows, trunk, and depth.

primary.name: Pectoralis major
primary.evidenceShort: Direct bar-dip EMG supports strong pectoralis loading.
primary.evidence: Direct dip-variation EMG measured pectoralis major during bar dips and found higher peak activation than the bench dip; a separate bar-dip fatigue study found pectoralis major peak activation increased under fatigue and concluded the bar dip effectively targets pectoralis major.

primary.name: Triceps brachii
primary.evidenceShort: Direct bar-dip EMG supports high elbow-extension demand.
primary.evidence: Direct bar-dip EMG measured triceps brachii as a suspected elbow-extension agonist, with higher peak activation than the bench dip. The fatigue study reported increased triceps brachii peak activation when fatigued and concluded the bar dip effectively targets triceps brachii.

secondary.name: Anterior deltoid
secondary.evidenceShort: Measured shoulder-flexion assistant in bar dips.
secondary.evidence: The dip-variation EMG study measured anterior deltoid as a suspected shoulder-flexion agonist and found higher peak activation in the bar dip than in the bench dip. It is secondary because the strongest exact-variant conclusions emphasize pectoralis major and triceps brachii as the main targets.

support.name: Serratus anterior
support.evidenceShort: Measured scapular support demand during bar dips.
support.evidence: Direct dip EMG classified serratus anterior among active scapular stabilizers, with higher peak activation in the bar dip than the bench dip. In the fatigue study, serratus anterior peak activation increased, supporting a visible scapular-support role.

support.name: Latissimus dorsi
support.evidenceShort: Measured stabilizer/depressor contribution in bar dips.
support.evidence: The direct dip studies measured latissimus dorsi as a suspected glenohumeral stabilizer. Bar dips produced higher latissimus activation than bench dips, and the fatigue study reported increased latissimus dorsi peak amplitude among muscles associated with scapular depression.

evidence.verdict: Bodyweight parallel-bar dip: pectoralis major and triceps brachii primary; anterior deltoid secondary; serratus anterior and latissimus dorsi support.
evidence.clinicalShort: EMG estimates acute excitation, not hypertrophy, mechanical tension, adaptation, or injury risk.
evidence.limitsShort: Torso lean, bar spacing, shoulder depth, fatigue, added load, assistance, ring instability, and bench-dip substitutions can materially change muscle contribution and shoulder loading.
evidence.summary: The parallel bar dip is classified as a bodyweight upper-body pushing exercise using fixed bars. Direct dip EMG and kinematic evidence supports pectoralis major and triceps brachii as the clearest main targets for a neutral bar-dip entry. Anterior deltoid is included as a measured shoulder-flexion assistant. Serratus anterior and latissimus dorsi are included as support because the direct studies measured them as scapular or glenohumeral stabilizers and reported meaningful activation in the bar-dip condition, especially with fatigue.
evidence.clinicalInterpretation: Surface electromyography is useful for estimating acute muscle excitation under a specific technique, load, and normalization method. It should not be interpreted as a direct measure of hypertrophy, mechanical tension, long-term adaptation, or injury risk. The main direct studies used experienced healthy males and self-selected bar-dip technique.
evidence.limitations: The closest direct studies used a V-shaped bar and self-moderated depth rather than enforcing a single parallel-bar spacing or torso angle. Lower trapezius was measured and increased under fatigue, but it is not shown as a visible role because the local anatomy label groups middle and lower fibers and the concise app classification is clearer with serratus anterior and latissimus dorsi as support. Infraspinatus, biceps brachii, and upper trapezius were not included because their bar-dip evidence is weaker or less directly tied to the main classification. Weighted dips, assisted dips, ring dips, bench dips, and straight-bar dips should be separate movements.

studies.type: Bench, bar, and ring dip EMG and kinematics
studies.finding: Experienced males performed bench, bar, and ring dips; bar dips showed higher peak activation than bench dips for pectoralis major, anterior deltoid, triceps brachii, serratus anterior, and latissimus dorsi.
studies.citation: McKenzie A, Crowley-McHattan Z, Meir R, Whitting J, Volschenk W. Bench, Bar, and Ring Dips: Do Kinematics and Muscle Activity Differ? International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. 2022;19(20):13211. doi:10.3390/ijerph192013211.
studies.relevance: Directly studied the closest variant: bodyweight bar dips on a fixed V-shaped dip bar, with 3D kinematics and surface EMG of nine upper-limb and trunk muscles.

studies.type: Bar dip fatigue EMG and kinematics
studies.finding: During one set of bar dips to exhaustion, fatigue increased peak pectoralis major, triceps brachii, serratus anterior, lower trapezius, and latissimus dorsi activation while peak joint angles did not materially change.
studies.citation: McKenzie A, Crowley-McHattan Z, Meir R, Whitting J, Volschenk W. Fatigue Increases Muscle Activations but Does Not Change Maximal Joint Angles during the Bar Dip. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. 2022;19(21):14390. doi:10.3390/ijerph192114390.
studies.relevance: Direct bar-dip study using experienced males, 3D kinematics, and surface EMG across non-fatigued and fatigued repetitions.

studies.type: Dip shoulder-extension biomechanics review
studies.shortCitation: McKenzie et al., Strength Cond J, 2021
studies.finding: Discussed loaded glenohumeral extension in the dip and practical constraints for managing shoulder range, load, and progression.
studies.citation: McKenzie AK, Crowley-McHattan ZJ, Meir R, Whitting JW, Volschenk W. Glenohumeral Extension and the Dip: Considerations for the Strength and Conditioning Professional. Strength and Conditioning Journal. 2021;43(1):93-100. doi:10.1519/SSC.0000000000000579.
studies.relevance: Close shoulder-extension and prescription context for the dip; used for interpretation of depth, progression, and joint-resilience constraints rather than for assigning prime movers.

studies.type: Parallel bar dip pectoralis major rupture case report
studies.finding: Case report and review describing pectoralis major rupture during parallel bar dips.
studies.citation: Carek PJ, Hawkins A. Rupture of pectoralis major during parallel bar dips: case report and review. Medicine and Science in Sports and Exercise. 1998;30(3):335-338. doi:10.1097/00005768-199803000-00001.
studies.relevance: Directly involves the parallel bar dip and informs caution around loaded shoulder extension and pectoralis major stress, but it is not used to infer normal activation magnitude.

movements.name: Pull-Up
movements.variant: Pronated bodyweight pull-up from a fixed overhead bar, performed without assistance, kipping, or added external load.
movements.description: Hang from a fixed overhead bar with a pronated grip and arms long, then set the shoulders down without swinging. Pull the chest toward the bar by driving the elbows down and back until the chin clears the bar, then lower under control to the starting hang while keeping the torso organized.

hypertrophy.rationale: Strong bodyweight stimulus for lats, elbow flexors, posterior shoulder, and scapular stabilizers, with the main tradeoff that relative strength can cap usable volume.

strength.rationale: High-force closed-chain vertical pulling builds meaningful upper-body strength, but the bodyweight-only variant has less precise loading than weighted or machine options.

joint_resilience.rationale: Full-range shoulder, elbow, and grip loading can build tolerance, but the hanging position and high relative load make it less forgiving than supported progressions.

athletic_transfer.rationale: Bodyweight vertical pulling transfers well to climbing, obstacle, and self-movement tasks, though it remains bilateral and bar-constrained.

control.rationale: Requires scapular timing, body-line control, grip organization, and swing management without external torso support.

fatigue_efficiency.rationale: Setup cost is low and the stimulus is focused, but grip, elbow flexors, shoulders, and failed reps can add recovery cost before enough target volume is accumulated.

setup.rationale: Needs only a fixed overhead bar and bodyweight, but bar availability, height, and grip surface still matter.

ease.rationale: The pattern is simple to understand but difficult to perform well because it requires substantial relative strength and controlled scapular mechanics.

progression.rationale: Reps are easy to track, but bodyweight-only overload is coarse unless the user changes assistance, tempo, range, or adds weight as a separate variant.

support.rationale: The hands are fixed to the bar, but the body is otherwise suspended and must stabilize itself through the pull.

primary.name: Latissimus dorsi
primary.evidenceShort: Direct pull-up EMG supports the main vertical-pull role.
primary.evidence: Pull-up and grip-variation EMG studies report high latissimus dorsi activation during conventional and pronated pull-ups, and shoulder-modeling work supports latissimus dorsi as a major contributor across pull-up techniques.

secondary.name: Biceps brachii
secondary.evidenceShort: Measured elbow-flexion contributor in pull-up EMG.
secondary.evidence: Biceps brachii is repeatedly measured during pull-up and chin-up EMG, with Youdas et al. reporting substantial activation and Dickie et al. showing higher biceps activity in the concentric phase across pull-up variations; it assists the pull but is not the main back target.

secondary.name: Posterior deltoid
secondary.evidenceShort: Measured shoulder-extension assistant in traditional pull-ups.
secondary.evidence: Traditional pull-up EMG directly measured posterior deltoid along with latissimus dorsi, middle trapezius, and biceps brachii, supporting a meaningful shoulder-extension assistant role rather than a primary target.

secondary.name: Pectoralis major
secondary.evidenceShort: Measured shoulder-adduction assistant, not the main target.
secondary.evidence: Youdas et al. measured pectoralis major activity during conventional pull-ups, and Dickie et al. found greater pectoralis major activity in the concentric phase across pull-up variations; it is included as a secondary shoulder-adduction contributor, not as a chest-focused target.

support.name: Trapezius (middle and lower fibers)
support.evidenceShort: Middle and lower trapezius activity supports scapular control.
support.evidence: Youdas et al. reported lower trapezius activity and a sequential activation pattern during pull-ups, while Dickie et al. and Snarr et al. measured middle trapezius during pronated or traditional pull-up variations; these fibers are classified as scapular support.

support.name: Rotator cuff
support.evidenceShort: Infraspinatus EMG and shoulder modeling support stabilization.
support.evidence: Youdas et al. directly measured substantial infraspinatus activity during pull-ups, and Urbanczyk et al. modeled rotator-cuff and scapular-stabilizer loading across pull-up techniques; the broader rotator cuff role is treated as glenohumeral support.

evidence.verdict: Pronated bodyweight pull-up: latissimus dorsi primary; biceps brachii, posterior deltoid, and pectoralis major secondary; middle/lower trapezius and rotator cuff support.
evidence.clinicalShort: EMG estimates acute excitation, not hypertrophy, mechanical tension, adaptation, or injury risk.
evidence.limitsShort: Grip width, grip orientation, bar path, range of motion, swing, fatigue, and relative body mass can shift muscle contribution and performance.
evidence.summary: The pull-up is classified as an unsupported bodyweight vertical pull from a fixed bar with a pronated grip. Direct pull-up EMG supports latissimus dorsi as the primary visible target, with biceps brachii, posterior deltoid, and pectoralis major as meaningful secondary contributors. Middle/lower trapezius and rotator cuff involvement are included as support because the evidence points to scapular and glenohumeral control demands rather than primary hypertrophy targeting.
evidence.clinicalInterpretation: Surface EMG and shoulder modeling are useful for estimating acute excitation and loading in specific pull-up setups, but they should not be treated as direct measures of hypertrophy, long-term adaptation, or injury risk. A bodyweight pull-up also mixes target-muscle capacity with relative body mass and technique quality.
evidence.limitations: The entry applies only to a strict pronated bodyweight pull-up from a fixed bar. Chin-ups, neutral-grip pull-ups, towel pull-ups, suspension pull-ups, assisted pull-ups, kipping pull-ups, and weighted pull-ups should be treated as separate variants. Brachioradialis and brachialis were not added as visible roles because the current local anatomy map does not expose those muscles; biceps brachii is the mapped elbow-flexor role retained for the app card.

studies.type: Pull-up, chin-up, and rotating-handle EMG
studies.finding: Conventional pull-ups showed high latissimus dorsi, biceps brachii, infraspinatus, lower trapezius, pectoralis major, erector spinae, and external oblique activation, with lower trapezius more active in the pull-up than chin-up.
studies.citation: Youdas JW, Amundson CL, Cicero KS, Hahn JJ, Harezlak DT, Hollman JH. Surface electromyographic activation patterns and elbow joint motion during a pull-up, chin-up, or Perfect-Pullup rotational exercise. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2010;24(12):3404-3414. doi:10.1519/JSC.0b013e3181f1598c.
studies.relevance: Directly studied conventional pull-ups and chin-ups in healthy adults using surface EMG of latissimus dorsi, biceps brachii, infraspinatus, lower trapezius, pectoralis major, erector spinae, and external oblique.

studies.type: Pull-up grip-variation EMG
studies.shortCitation: Dickie et al., J Electromyogr Kinesiol, 2017
studies.finding: Pronated, supinated, neutral, and rope pull-ups produced broadly similar shoulder-arm-forearm activation across full repetitions, with pronated grip increasing middle trapezius activity versus neutral grip.
studies.citation: Dickie JA, Faulkner JA, Barnes MJ, Lark SD. Electromyographic analysis of muscle activation during pull-up variations. Journal of Electromyography and Kinesiology. 2017;32:30-36. doi:10.1016/j.jelekin.2016.11.004.
studies.relevance: Directly includes the chosen pronated pull-up condition in strength-trained men and compares it with supinated, neutral, and rope pull-up variations.

studies.type: Traditional, suspension, and towel pull-up EMG
studies.shortCitation: Snarr et al., J Hum Kinet, 2017
studies.finding: Traditional pronated pull-ups at 1.5 times bi-acromial grip width produced meaningful latissimus dorsi, posterior deltoid, middle trapezius, and biceps brachii activity.
studies.citation: Snarr RL, Hallmark AV, Casey JC, Esco MR. Electromyographical Comparison of a Traditional, Suspension Device, and Towel Pull-Up. Journal of Human Kinetics. 2017;58:5-13. doi:10.1515/hukin-2017-0068.
studies.relevance: Very close to the selected variant: traditional pull-ups from a secure overhead bar with pronated hands at 1.5 times bi-acromial width, performed by resistance-trained adults.

studies.type: Pull-up technique article
studies.shortCitation: Ronai and Scibek, Strength Cond J, 2014
studies.finding: Described pull-up setup, phases, technique, progressions, and common variation boundaries.
studies.citation: Ronai P, Scibek E. The Pull-up. Strength & Conditioning Journal. 2014;36(3):88-90. doi:10.1519/SSC.0000000000000052.
studies.relevance: Peer-reviewed technique context for defining the fixed-bar bodyweight pull-up variant and rating setup, ease, progression, and support.

studies.type: Pull-up shoulder muscle-force modeling
studies.shortCitation: Urbanczyk et al., Scand J Med Sci Sports, 2020
studies.finding: Kinematic, kinetic, and shoulder-modeling analysis found variant-specific muscle-force patterns and emphasized rotator cuff, scapular stabilizer, and shoulder-girdle loading during pull-ups.
studies.citation: Urbanczyk CA, Prinold JAI, Reilly P, Bull AMJ. Avoiding high-risk rotator cuff loading: Muscle force during three pull-up techniques. Scandinavian Journal of Medicine & Science in Sports. 2020;30(11):2205-2214. doi:10.1111/sms.13780.
studies.relevance: Direct pull-up biomechanics and modeled muscle-force evidence for pronated front grip, pronated wide grip, and supinated reverse grip pull-ups.

studies.type: Pull-up kinematic characterization
studies.shortCitation: Garavaglia et al., Sport Sci Health, 2023
studies.finding: Motion-capture analysis of pull-ups in climbers and active subjects characterized execution quality, compensations, and segmental kinematics across repetitions.
studies.citation: Garavaglia L, Romano J, Lazzari F, Pittaccio S. Biomechanical characterisation of the pull-up exercise. Sport Sciences for Health. 2024;20(1):221-234. doi:10.1007/s11332-023-01097-1.
studies.relevance: Biomechanics source for motor-control, athletic-transfer, and technique-quality interpretation during repeated pull-ups.

studies.type: Body-mass prone-grip pull-up training study
studies.finding: Eight weeks of velocity-based body-mass prone-grip pull-up training improved pull-up strength and endurance, with lower velocity loss outperforming higher velocity loss on most outcomes.
studies.citation: Sanchez-Moreno M, Cornejo-Daza PJ, Gonzalez-Badillo JJ, Pareja-Blanco F. Effects of Velocity Loss During Body Mass Prone-Grip Pull-up Training on Strength and Endurance Performance. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2020;34(4):911-917. doi:10.1519/JSC.0000000000003500.
studies.relevance: Direct body-mass prone-grip pull-up training evidence in strength-trained men, supporting strength, progression, fatigue, and programming interpretation.

movements.name: Push-Up
movements.variant: Standard floor push-up with hands near shoulder width, feet on the floor, and bodyweight loading.
movements.description: Start in a straight-body plank with hands near shoulder width, wrists under or slightly outside the shoulders, feet on the floor, and the torso braced. Lower under control by bending the elbows until the chest approaches the floor without losing body position, then press the floor away until the elbows are extended and the body remains aligned.

hypertrophy.rationale: Useful chest, triceps, and anterior-deltoid stimulus, but target loading is limited by bodyweight, high reps, and relative-strength constraints.

strength.rationale: Builds early pressing strength, but loading is indirect and quickly becomes less precise for maximal force development.

joint_resilience.rationale: Can build wrist, elbow, shoulder, and scapular tolerance, but the fixed hand position and bodyweight load are not ideal for every user.

athletic_transfer.rationale: Good body-control transfer for a simple floor press, though it is still a fixed closed-chain pattern without locomotion or external load handling.

control.rationale: Meaningful plank, scapular, wrist, and whole-body line control demand.

fatigue_efficiency.rationale: Efficient setup and moderate systemic cost, but high-rep sets can become endurance-limited before target muscles receive enough overload.

setup.rationale: Nearly frictionless: needs only floor space and repeatable hand and foot placement.

ease.rationale: Familiar and simple to start, but good reps require enough relative strength, wrist tolerance, depth control, and trunk stiffness.

progression.rationale: Overload is noisy because load changes require angle, tempo, external weight, bands, or variation changes rather than simple increments.

support.rationale: Hands and feet contact the floor, but the torso and shoulders are not externally supported.

primary.name: Pectoralis major
primary.evidenceShort: High activation in standard and shoulder-width push-up EMG.
primary.evidence: Conventional and shoulder-width floor push-up EMG studies consistently report meaningful pectoralis major activation; Freeman et al. measured the standard shoulder-width variant and Youdas et al. reported high pectoralis major activation across conventional hand positions.

secondary.name: Triceps brachii
secondary.evidenceShort: High elbow-extension activation; hand width sensitive.
secondary.evidence: Multiple direct push-up EMG studies measured triceps brachii activation during conventional, normal, or shoulder-width floor push-ups. The triceps is classified as secondary because it is a major elbow-extension contributor but not the main chest-press target in this entry.

secondary.name: Anterior deltoid
secondary.evidenceShort: Measured shoulder-flexion assist in the standard push-up.
secondary.evidence: Freeman et al. directly measured anterior deltoid during a standard shoulder-width floor push-up and reported moderate activation, supporting a secondary pressing role rather than a primary target classification.

support.name: Serratus anterior
support.evidenceShort: Scapulothoracic support measured in conventional push-ups.
support.evidence: Youdas et al. measured considerable serratus anterior activation during conventional floor push-ups, and Lear and Gross showed serratus anterior involvement across push-up progressions. It is classified as scapulothoracic support rather than the primary hypertrophy target.

evidence.verdict: Standard floor push-up: pectoralis major primary; triceps brachii and anterior deltoid secondary; serratus anterior support.
evidence.clinicalShort: EMG estimates acute excitation, not hypertrophy, mechanical tension, adaptation, or injury risk.
evidence.limitsShort: Hand width, body angle, range of motion, tempo, fatigue, wrist position, and relative body mass can shift load and muscle contribution.
evidence.summary: The standard floor push-up is classified as a bodyweight horizontal pressing exercise. Direct EMG evidence supports pectoralis major as the primary app target, with triceps brachii and anterior deltoid as meaningful secondary movers. Serratus anterior is included as a support muscle because conventional push-up studies directly measure substantial scapulothoracic activity, but it is not treated as the primary hypertrophy target.
evidence.clinicalInterpretation: Surface electromyography is useful for estimating acute muscle excitation under a specific technique, hand position, tempo, and normalization method. It should not be interpreted as a direct measure of hypertrophy, long-term adaptation, mechanical tension, or injury risk.
evidence.limitations: Most direct studies used small samples of healthy young adults, and definitions of normal or shoulder-width hand placement vary. Biceps brachii was not included as a visible role because Freeman et al. reported very low activation in the standard variant. Rotator cuff and trunk muscles were not included as visible roles because the strongest exact-variant evidence in this record does not directly support a concise app classification for the available anatomy set.

studies.type: Push-up hand-position EMG
studies.finding: Shoulder-width, wide, and narrow push-ups measured pectoralis major and triceps brachii activation.
studies.citation: Cogley RM, Archambault TA, Fibeger JF, Koverman MM, Youdas JW, Hollman JH. Comparison of Muscle Activation Using Various Hand Positions During the Push-Up Exercise. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2005;19(3):628-633. doi:10.1519/15094.1.
studies.relevance: Directly studied floor push-ups using shoulder-width, wide-base, and narrow-base hand positions and measured pectoralis major and triceps brachii.

studies.type: Push-up variant EMG and kinetics
studies.finding: Normal push-up loaded about two-thirds of body weight initially and measured pectoralis major and triceps activity across variants.
studies.citation: Gouvali MK, Boudolos K. Dynamic and Electromyographical Analysis in Variants of Push-Up Exercise. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2005;19(1):146-151. doi:10.1519/14733.1.
studies.relevance: Direct push-up study including a normal variant, surface EMG of pectoralis major and triceps brachii, and bodyweight-relative loading.

studies.type: Standard push-up EMG and spine load
studies.finding: Standard shoulder-width push-up measured pectoralis major, anterior deltoid, triceps brachii, biceps brachii, trunk EMG, and spine compression.
studies.citation: Freeman S, Karpowicz A, Gray J, McGill S. Quantifying Muscle Patterns and Spine Load during Various Forms of the Push-Up. Medicine and Science in Sports and Exercise. 2006;38(3):570-577. doi:10.1249/01.mss.0000189317.08635.1b.
studies.relevance: Directly matches the standard floor push-up assumption: hands and toes on the floor, hands shoulder width apart, straight body position, and bodyweight loading.

studies.type: Conventional push-up EMG
studies.finding: Conventional push-ups required high pectoralis major, triceps brachii, and serratus anterior activation across hand positions.
studies.citation: Youdas JW, Budach BD, Ellerbusch JV, Stucky CM, Wait KR, Hollman JH. Comparison of Muscle-Activation Patterns During the Conventional Push-Up and Perfect Pushup Exercises. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2010;24(12):3352-3362. doi:10.1519/JSC.0b013e3181cc23b0.
studies.relevance: Direct conventional floor push-up study measuring pectoralis major, triceps brachii, serratus anterior, and posterior deltoid at shoulder-width, wide-base, and narrow-base positions.

studies.type: Scapular stabilizer EMG during push-up progression
studies.finding: Push-up progressions facilitated serratus anterior and upper trapezius activation as scapular stabilizers.
studies.citation: Lear LJ, Gross MT. An Electromyographical Analysis of the Scapular Stabilizing Synergists During a Push-Up Progression. Journal of Orthopaedic and Sports Physical Therapy. 1998;28(3):146-157. doi:10.2519/jospt.1998.28.3.146.
studies.relevance: Supports serratus anterior as a scapular stabilizing/support contributor during push-up progressions, not as the primary chest-press target.

studies.type: Traditional push-up body-mass support
studies.finding: Traditional push-ups support less body mass at the top than bottom position, informing bodyweight loading and progression limits.
studies.citation: Suprak DN, Dawes J, Stephenson MD. The Effect of Position on the Percentage of Body Mass Supported During Traditional and Modified Push-Up Variants. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2011;25(2):497-503. doi:10.1519/JSC.0b013e3181bde2cf.
studies.relevance: Quantifies traditional push-up body-mass support across top and bottom positions, supporting progression and fatigue scoring.

studies.type: Push-up variant force-plate analysis
studies.finding: Regular, knee, feet-elevated, and hands-elevated push-ups produced different vertical ground-reaction forces.
studies.citation: Ebben WP, Wurm B, VanderZanden TL, Spadavecchia ML, Durocher JJ, Bickham CT, Petushek EJ. Kinetic Analysis of Several Variations of Push-Ups. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2011;25(10):2891-2894. doi:10.1519/JSC.0b013e31820c8587.
studies.relevance: Supports the rating interpretation that push-up intensity can be progressed by body angle, but with less precision than external loading.

movements.name: Reverse Crunch
movements.variant: Bodyweight floor reverse crunch emphasizing posterior pelvic tilt and trunk flexion from the pelvis toward the ribs.
movements.description: Lie on the floor with the hips and knees bent, brace lightly, then curl the pelvis off the floor by pulling the knees toward the chest without swinging. Pause with the low back rounded slightly, then lower under control until the pelvis returns to the floor while keeping the movement compact.

hypertrophy.rationale: Useful local abdominal stimulus, but bodyweight loading and short range limit hypertrophy progression.

strength.rationale: Builds low-load trunk-flexion strength, but it is not a high-force strength anchor.

joint_resilience.rationale: Limited broad resilience value because it is repeated spinal flexion and hip flexion rather than a progressive joint-loading drill.

athletic_transfer.rationale: Low direct transfer because it lacks standing bracing, anti-rotation, gait, or loaded force-transfer demands.

control.rationale: Requires pelvic curl control and swing suppression, but the floor makes balance and stabilization demands low.

fatigue_efficiency.rationale: Quick abdominal stimulus with low systemic fatigue, though the training ceiling is modest.

setup.rationale: Requires only floor space.

ease.rationale: Easy to understand, but users often swing the legs or turn it into mostly hip flexion.

progression.rationale: Progression is mostly reps, tempo, incline, or leverage; external loading is awkward.

support.rationale: The floor supports the trunk and removes balance demand.

primary.name: Rectus abdominis
primary.evidenceShort: Reverse-crunch EMG supports high rectus activation.
primary.evidence: Reverse-crunch and reverse-curl-up EMG evidence directly measures upper and lower rectus abdominis activity, with inclined reverse crunches among the higher abdominal-activation tasks in traditional and nontraditional abdominal exercise research.

secondary.name: Internal oblique
secondary.evidenceShort: Reverse-crunch evidence supports oblique contribution.
secondary.evidence: Escamilla et al. measured internal oblique activity during reverse-crunch-family abdominal work, supporting a secondary trunk-flexion and pelvic-control role.

secondary.name: External oblique
secondary.evidenceShort: Exact reverse-crunch report supports oblique activity.
secondary.evidence: The San Diego State/ACE abdominal EMG report ranked the reverse crunch highly for grouped oblique activity, supporting a secondary external-oblique role alongside the primary rectus abdominis target.

evidence.verdict: Floor reverse crunch: rectus abdominis primary; internal and external oblique secondary; no separate support muscles listed.
evidence.clinicalShort: EMG estimates acute excitation, not hypertrophy, mechanical tension, adaptation, or injury risk.
evidence.limitsShort: Incline angle, knee bend, pelvis curl, speed, and swinging can change abdominal versus hip-flexor emphasis.
evidence.summary: The reverse crunch is classified as a floor trunk-flexion exercise biased toward posterior pelvic tilt. Direct reverse-crunch and reverse-curl-up evidence supports rectus abdominis as the primary visible target. Obliques are included as secondary contributors because exact and close abdominal EMG sources show meaningful oblique activity during reverse-crunch and crunch-family tasks.
evidence.clinicalInterpretation: A controlled pelvic curl makes this more abdominal; swinging the legs increases hip-flexor and thigh contribution. The exercise is best treated as a low-setup accessory rather than a heavy abdominal progression.
evidence.limitations: Escamilla et al. used an inclined 30-degree reverse crunch, which is harder than a flat floor variant. The exact ACE report groups obliques rather than separating internal and external oblique. Rectus femoris was not listed because it is not the intended target and this project does not expose a standalone rectus femoris anatomy label. Weighted reverse crunches, decline reverse crunches, hanging knee raises, and captain's-chair knee raises should be separate entries.

studies.type: Traditional and nontraditional abdominal exercise EMG
studies.finding: Reverse crunch inclined 30 degrees was among the highest exercises for upper and lower rectus abdominis and internal oblique activity, and it also produced high rectus femoris activity.
studies.citation: Escamilla RF, Babb E, DeWitt R, Jew P, Kelleher P, Burnham T, Busch J, D'Anna K, Mowbray R, Imamura RT. Electromyographic analysis of traditional and nontraditional abdominal exercises: implications for rehabilitation and training. Physical Therapy. 2006;86(5):656-671.
studies.relevance: Direct reverse-crunch-family EMG evidence for rectus abdominis and internal oblique activity.

studies.type: Upper and lower rectus abdominis exercise EMG
studies.finding: Compared upper and lower rectus abdominis activity during several abdominal exercises including the reverse curl-up.
studies.citation: Clark KM, Holt LE, Sinyard J. Electromyographic comparison of the upper and lower rectus abdominis during abdominal exercises. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2003;17(3):475-483. doi:10.1519/1533-4287(2003)017<0475:ECOTUA>2.0.CO;2.
studies.relevance: Direct reverse-curl-up evidence for rectus abdominis interpretation and limits around upper/lower abdominal selectivity.

studies.type: San Diego State/ACE abdominal EMG report
studies.finding: The reverse crunch ranked above traditional crunch for rectus abdominis and grouped oblique EMG activity in a 13-exercise comparison.
studies.citation: Francis P, Davis J. New Study Puts the Crunch on Ineffective Ab Exercises. ACE FitnessMatters. May/June 2001. San Diego State University Biomechanics Lab and American Council on Exercise.
studies.relevance: Exact flat reverse-crunch EMG report for rectus abdominis and grouped oblique activation; interpreted cautiously because it was a research report rather than a peer-reviewed journal article.

studies.type: Commercial and common abdominal exercise EMG
studies.finding: Common abdominal exercise EMG measured rectus abdominis and oblique activation across crunch-family tasks.
studies.citation: Escamilla RF, McTaggart MSC, Fricklas EJ, et al. An electromyographic analysis of commercial and common abdominal exercises: implications for rehabilitation and training. Journal of Orthopaedic and Sports Physical Therapy. 2006;36(2):45-57. doi:10.2519/jospt.2006.36.2.45.
studies.relevance: Close abdominal exercise source for external-oblique contribution and crunch-family interpretation.

movements.name: Seated Cable Lat Pulldown
movements.variant: Seated overhead cable lat pulldown with thigh pad support, pulled in front of the head toward the upper to mid chest.
movements.description: Sit at a lat pulldown station with the thighs secured under the pad, take the handle overhead with arms long, and set a tall torso with the ribs and pelvis controlled. Pull the elbows down and slightly back until the handle reaches the upper to mid chest, then return the handle overhead under control without shrugging or losing the seated position.

hypertrophy.rationale: Strong vertical-pull hypertrophy stimulus for lats and elbow flexors, with grip and path changing emphasis.

strength.rationale: Builds vertical pulling force, but the seated cable setup transfers imperfectly to bodyweight pulling strength.

joint_resilience.rationale: Some controlled shoulder and elbow exposure, but it is not primarily a joint-resilience movement.

athletic_transfer.rationale: Limited transfer because the seated thigh-padded setup removes most whole-body pulling and bodyweight coordination.

control.rationale: Requires scapular timing and torso discipline, but the seat and thigh pad remove most balance and whole-body control demand.

fatigue_efficiency.rationale: Good back stimulus with manageable systemic cost, though grip, elbow flexors, and shoulder irritation can leak fatigue.

setup.rationale: Usually available and repeatable, but handle choice, thigh-pad height, seat position, and station geometry add setup friction.

ease.rationale: Approachable guided pattern, with technique limits from grip, torso lean, scapular control, and bottom-position consistency.

progression.rationale: Cable stacks make load and reps easy to track, with deductions for pulley friction, attachments, and machine geometry.

support.rationale: The seated base and thigh pad provide substantial support, though the arms and scapulae still guide a free cable path.

primary.name: Latissimus dorsi
primary.evidenceShort: Direct front pulldown EMG supports primary lat role.
primary.evidence: Seated lat pulldown EMG studies consistently measure latissimus dorsi activity during front-to-chest pulldowns; newer multi-grip and high-density EMG work supports latissimus dorsi as the stable primary target across common front pulldown variations.

secondary.name: Teres major
