secondary.evidenceShort: Measured shoulder-adduction assistant.
secondary.evidence: Direct lat pulldown EMG measured teres major during common hand positions, and instruction research grouped teres major with latissimus dorsi as a back-muscle target that can increase with cueing; it is classified as secondary because the latissimus dorsi remains the intended main target.

secondary.name: Biceps brachii
secondary.evidenceShort: Directly measured elbow-flexion contributor.
secondary.evidence: Lat pulldown EMG studies repeatedly measure biceps brachii activity, with activation changing by grip and phase; it assists the vertical pull through elbow flexion but is not the intended main back target.

secondary.name: Posterior deltoid
secondary.evidenceShort: Measured shoulder-extension/adduction assistant.
secondary.evidence: Posterior deltoid activity is directly recorded in front, behind-neck, and multi-grip lat pulldown studies; its role varies with trunk angle and bar path, making it a secondary shoulder contributor rather than the main target.

secondary.name: Pectoralis major
secondary.evidenceShort: Directly measured shoulder-adduction assistant.
secondary.evidence: Pectoralis major is measured during front lat pulldown variants and can assist shoulder adduction, especially with anterior/front trajectories and closer grips; it is included as a secondary contributor, not as a chest-focused target.

support.name: Trapezius (middle and lower fibers)
support.evidenceShort: Scapular control role measured in pulldown studies.
support.evidence: Middle and lower trapezius activity has been measured during lat pulldown and isometric pulldown tasks; these fibers are best classified as scapular support because rows and angle-specific conditions can emphasize them more than the standard seated pulldown.

support.name: Rotator cuff
support.evidenceShort: Infraspinatus measured as shoulder stabilizer.
support.evidence: A recent multi-grip lat pulldown EMG study directly measured infraspinatus, a rotator cuff muscle, and interpreted it as a stabilizing and accessory contributor affected by grip and trunk position; the broader rotator cuff support role is an anatomical inference from that direct infraspinatus evidence.

evidence.verdict: Front seated cable lat pulldown: latissimus dorsi primary; teres major, biceps brachii, posterior deltoid, and pectoralis major secondary; middle/lower trapezius and rotator cuff support.
evidence.clinicalShort: EMG estimates acute muscle excitation, not hypertrophy, mechanical tension, long-term adaptation, or injury risk.
evidence.limitsShort: Grip width, forearm orientation, handle type, torso lean, front vs behind-neck path, load, and cueing can shift activation; separate grip-specific pulldowns should be separate movements.
evidence.summary: The seated cable lat pulldown is classified as a supported vertical pulling exercise performed from an overhead cable with thigh pad support and a front-to-chest bar path. Direct EMG evidence supports latissimus dorsi as the main target across common front pulldown variations. Teres major, biceps brachii, posterior deltoid, and pectoralis major have direct activation evidence and are classified as secondary contributors. Middle/lower trapezius and rotator cuff involvement is classified as support for scapular and glenohumeral control.
evidence.clinicalInterpretation: Surface and high-density EMG are useful for estimating acute excitation in the tested setup, but they should not be treated as direct measures of hypertrophy, mechanical tension, adaptation, or safety. Technique, load prescription, normalization method, and participant training status affect interpretation.
evidence.limitations: The evidence base includes front pulldowns, behind-neck pulldowns, V-bar pulldowns, wide and narrow grips, neutral and supinated grips, isometric pulldowns, and machine-constraint comparisons. This entry applies those data only to a generic seated front cable pulldown with thigh pad support. Deep scapular muscles, grip/forearm muscles, and individual latissimus dorsi regions remain under-described for this app classification.

studies.type: Lat pulldown hand-position EMG
studies.finding: Wide-grip anterior pulldown produced the greatest latissimus dorsi activity among tested hand positions.
studies.citation: Signorile JF, Zink AJ, Szwed SP. A comparative electromyographical investigation of muscle utilization patterns using various hand positions during the lat pull-down. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2002;16(4):539-546. doi:10.1519/1533-4287(2002)016<0539:ACEIOM>2.0.CO;2.
studies.relevance: Direct seated lat pulldown EMG on a cable system using close, supinated, wide-grip anterior, and wide-grip posterior conditions; measured latissimus dorsi, teres major, posterior deltoid, pectoralis major, and long head of triceps.

studies.type: Front, behind-neck, and V-bar pulldown EMG
studies.finding: Compared front-of-neck, behind-neck, and V-bar pulldowns at 80% 1RM and supported front pulldown as the preferred general technique.
studies.citation: Sperandei S, Barros MAP, Silveira-Junior PCS, Oliveira CG. Electromyographic analysis of three different types of lat pull-down. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2009;23(7):2033-2038. doi:10.1519/JSC.0b013e3181b8d30a.
studies.relevance: Directly tested the front pulldown family and measured pectoralis major, latissimus dorsi, posterior deltoid, and biceps brachii in trained adult men.

studies.type: Lat pulldown instruction EMG
studies.finding: Specific instruction could increase latissimus dorsi and teres major activity during front wide-grip lat pulldown in novices.
studies.citation: Snyder BJ, Leech JR. Voluntary increase in latissimus dorsi muscle activity during the lat pull-down following expert instruction. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2009;23(8):2204-2209. doi:10.1519/JSC.0b013e3181bb7213.
studies.relevance: Direct lat pulldown EMG evidence for cue-sensitive latissimus dorsi and teres major recruitment; useful for technique and targeting interpretation.

studies.type: Grip width and forearm orientation pulldown EMG
studies.finding: Pronated grips elicited greater latissimus dorsi activity than supinated grips, while middle trapezius and biceps brachii were not affected by grip type.
studies.citation: Lusk SJ, Hale BD, Russell DM. Grip width and forearm orientation effects on muscle activity during the lat pull-down. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2010;24(7):1895-1900. doi:10.1519/JSC.0b013e3181ddb0ab.
studies.relevance: Directly tested lat pulldown grip width and forearm orientation with EMG of latissimus dorsi, middle trapezius, and biceps brachii.

studies.type: Lat pulldown and row EMG
studies.finding: Wide and reverse-grip pulldowns produced similar latissimus dorsi and biceps patterns, while rows emphasized middle trapezius/rhomboids more.
studies.citation: Lehman GJ, Buchan DD, Lundy A, Myers N, Nalborczyk A. Variations in muscle activation levels during traditional latissimus dorsi weight training exercises: an experimental study. Dynamic Medicine. 2004;3:4. doi:10.1186/1476-5918-3-4.
studies.relevance: Pulldown-family EMG evidence for latissimus dorsi, biceps brachii, and middle trapezius/rhomboid contribution, with limitations around grip-specific claims.

studies.type: Lat pulldown machine-constraint kinematics and EMG
studies.shortCitation: Koyama et al., Eur J Appl Physiol, 2010
studies.finding: Lat pulldown kinematics and EMG changed across machines with different movement constraints.
studies.citation: Koyama Y, Kobayashi H, Suzuki S, Enoka RM. Enhancing the weight training experience: a comparison of limb kinematics and EMG activity on three machines. European Journal of Applied Physiology. 2010;109(5):789-801. doi:10.1007/s00421-010-1421-y.
studies.relevance: Supports rating interpretation that machine/cable constraints affect repeatability, stability, and muscle activation during lat pulldown tasks.

studies.type: Chin-up vs lat pulldown kinematics and EMG
studies.finding: Lat pulldown and chin-up both engaged latissimus dorsi and biceps brachii; chin-up produced greater biceps and erector spinae activity in the concentric phase.
studies.citation: Doma K, Deakin GB, Ness KF. Kinematic and electromyographic comparisons between chin-ups and lat-pull down exercises. Sports Biomechanics. 2013;12(3):302-313. doi:10.1080/14763141.2012.760204.
studies.relevance: Close vertical-pull comparison with a lat pulldown condition; helps distinguish supported cable pulldown demands from bodyweight vertical pulling.

studies.type: Isometric pulldown latissimus and lower trapezius EMG
studies.shortCitation: Park and Yoo, J Electromyogr Kinesiol, 2013
studies.finding: Latissimus dorsi activity decreased and inferior trapezius activity increased as shoulder elevation angle increased during isometric pulldown exertions.
studies.citation: Park SY, Yoo WG. Selective activation of the latissimus dorsi and the inferior fibers of trapezius at various shoulder angles during isometric pull-down exertion. Journal of Electromyography and Kinesiology. 2013;23(6):1350-1355. doi:10.1016/j.jelekin.2013.08.006.
studies.relevance: Isometric pulldown evidence supporting lower trapezius as an angle-sensitive scapular support contributor rather than the primary target in standard pulldowns.

studies.type: Pronated grip-width pulldown EMG and strength
studies.finding: Narrow and medium pronated grips allowed slightly greater 6RM load than wide grip, while grip width produced broadly similar activation across 1-2 times biacromial distance.
studies.citation: Andersen V, Fimland MS, Wiik E, Skoglund A, Saeterbakken AH. Effects of grip width on muscle strength and activation in the lat pull-down. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2014;28(4):1135-1142. doi:10.1097/JSC.0000000000000232.
studies.relevance: Direct lat pulldown evidence for grip-width effects on load and activation in the common pronated front-pulldown family.

studies.type: High-density front vs back lat pulldown EMG
studies.shortCitation: Padovan et al., J Hum Kinet, 2024
studies.finding: Front lat pulldown with thighs blocked showed greater prime-mover excitation than behind-neck pulldown in several muscles and distinct spatial excitation patterns.
studies.citation: Padovan R, Toninelli N, Longo S, Tornatore G, Esposito F, Ce E, Coratella G. High-Density Electromyography Excitation in Front vs. Back Lat Pull-Down Prime Movers. Journal of Human Kinetics. 2024;91:47-60. doi:10.5114/jhk/185211.
studies.relevance: Very close to the chosen variant: seated front lat pulldown on a machine with thighs blocked by padding, pronated grip at 1.5 times inter-acromion distance, and pull to the middle chest.

studies.type: Multi-grip lat pulldown EMG
studies.finding: Across seven pulldown variations, latissimus dorsi remained the primary target and grip variations did not significantly change activation of the main muscles.
studies.citation: Buonsenso A, Di Fonza D, Di Claudio G, Carangelo M, Centorbi M, di Cagno A, Calcagno G, Fiorilli G. Electromyographic Analysis of Back Muscle Activation During Lat Pulldown Exercise: Effects of Grip Variations and Forearm Orientation. Journal of Functional Morphology and Kinesiology. 2025;10(3):345. doi:10.3390/jfmk10030345.
studies.relevance: Recent direct lat pulldown EMG with trained men, 70% repetition maximum, seven grip/trunk variants, and measurements of latissimus dorsi, posterior deltoid, biceps brachii, middle and lower trapezius, and infraspinatus.

movements.name: Seated Cable Row
movements.variant: Bilateral seated cable row with feet braced on foot plates, torso upright, and a cable handle pulled toward the lower ribs or upper abdomen.
movements.description: Sit facing a low cable with the feet pressed into the foot plates, knees slightly bent, torso tall, and arms extended without rounding the low back; pull the handle toward the lower ribs or upper abdomen by driving the elbows back, keep the cable path controlled, pause briefly with the shoulder blades drawn back, then return until the arms are long without letting the weight stack pull the torso out of position.

hypertrophy.rationale: Strong horizontal-pull hypertrophy stimulus for lats, mid-back, posterior shoulder, and elbow flexors, but path and torso movement shift emphasis.

strength.rationale: Builds pulling strength, but cable friction, handle choice, and torso motion make force expression less clean than stricter anchors.

joint_resilience.rationale: Some shoulder, scapular, and elbow tolerance benefit, but it is not mainly a resilience exercise.

athletic_transfer.rationale: More transferable than a fixed machine row, but seated support and a cable path still constrain whole-body transfer.

control.rationale: Meaningful scapular, torso, elbow-path, and grip control, though external support keeps balance demands moderate-low.

fatigue_efficiency.rationale: Good upper-back stimulus with moderate fatigue and low axial loading, but grip and biceps fatigue can limit the target stimulus.

setup.rationale: Cable row setup is usually manageable but depends on station, handle, stack increments, foot position, and seat distance.

ease.rationale: Relatively learnable, but consistent torso angle, scapular timing, elbow path, and avoiding momentum require attention.

progression.rationale: Progresses well on a cable stack, with deductions for cable friction, handle changes, torso movement, and station geometry.

support.rationale: Feet and pelvis are supported, but the cable path is not fixed and the trunk and shoulders must stabilize the pull.

primary.name: Latissimus dorsi
primary.evidenceShort: Direct seated cable row EMG supports highest emphasis with close elbow paths.
primary.evidence: Seated cable row studies measuring upper and lower latissimus dorsi show greater lat activation when shoulder abduction is closer to 0 degrees, and high-density EMG found the narrow seated row better suited to prioritizing latissimus dorsi.

secondary.name: Teres major
secondary.evidenceShort: Measured shoulder-extension assistant in seated row.
secondary.evidence: Fujita et al. measured teres major during the seated row at 70% 1RM and treated it with latissimus dorsi as a shoulder-extension target, supporting a meaningful assistant role rather than the primary visible target.

secondary.name: Middle trapezius
secondary.evidenceShort: Direct row EMG supports scapular-retraction contribution.
secondary.evidence: Lehman et al. reported the highest middle trapezius/rhomboid activity during seated row conditions, while seated cable row EMG shows middle trapezius activation rises as shoulder abduction increases.

secondary.name: Rhomboids
secondary.evidenceShort: Inferred from grouped middle trapezius/rhomboid EMG and scapular retraction.
secondary.evidence: This role is marked as inference: direct surface EMG in Lehman et al. grouped the middle trapezius and rhomboids rather than isolating rhomboid activity, and the row variant requires scapular retraction as the handle is pulled toward the torso.

secondary.name: Posterior deltoid
secondary.evidenceShort: Measured row contributor; increases with wider or higher-abduction paths.
secondary.evidence: Seated row studies record posterior deltoid activation, with greater posterior deltoid and upper-back activation as shoulder abduction approaches wider row positions; this makes it a meaningful but path-sensitive secondary mover.

secondary.name: Biceps brachii
secondary.evidenceShort: Measured elbow-flexion assistant, lower than curl-specific work.
secondary.evidence: Multiple seated row EMG studies measured biceps brachii during rowing; Vasconcelos et al. found cable preacher curl produced greater biceps activation than all row conditions, supporting biceps as a secondary elbow-flexion assistant rather than a primary target.

support.name: Rotator cuff
support.evidenceShort: Direction-specific shoulder stabilization during row.
support.evidence: Wattanaprakornkul et al. directly studied rotator cuff recruitment during bench press and row tasks, supporting a glenohumeral stabilization role during loaded shoulder extension rather than a primary hypertrophy role.

support.name: Erector spinae
support.evidenceShort: Trunk-position support, not the intended target.
support.evidence: High-density seated row EMG recorded erector spinae activity, and the foot-supported seated cable row still requires the trunk to resist the cable pull; this is classified as support rather than a back-extension target.

evidence.verdict: Seated cable row: latissimus dorsi primary; teres major, middle trapezius, rhomboids, posterior deltoid, and biceps brachii secondary; rotator cuff and erector spinae support.
evidence.clinicalShort: EMG estimates acute excitation, not hypertrophy, mechanical tension, adaptation, or injury risk.
evidence.limitsShort: Grip, handle width, shoulder abduction, torso lean, chest support, and pull target can shift emphasis between lats, trapezius, posterior deltoid, and elbow flexors.
evidence.summary: The seated cable row is classified as a supported horizontal pulling exercise. Direct seated cable row evidence supports latissimus dorsi as the primary target when the elbows stay close to the torso. Teres major assists shoulder extension, middle trapezius and rhomboids contribute to scapular retraction, posterior deltoid assists shoulder extension or horizontal abduction depending on path, and biceps brachii assists elbow flexion. Rotator cuff and erector spinae roles are included as support because they stabilize the shoulder and trunk rather than define the intended training target.
evidence.clinicalInterpretation: Surface electromyography is useful for estimating acute muscle excitation under a specific setup. It should not be interpreted as a direct measure of hypertrophy, mechanical tension, long-term adaptation, or injury risk.
evidence.limitations: The strongest exact evidence compares seated cable row grip and shoulder-abduction variants rather than every commercial cable station and handle. Rhomboids are not isolated by fine-wire EMG here and are included by explicit inference from grouped middle trapezius/rhomboid EMG plus the scapular retraction demand. Chest-supported seated row, machine row, inverted row, bent-over row, and unilateral cable row should be treated as separate variants.

studies.type: Seated cable row EMG and force study
studies.shortCitation: Vasconcelos et al., Int J Strength Cond, 2023
studies.finding: Close-to-0-degree shoulder-abduction rows increased upper/lower latissimus activity and peak force, while wider/higher-abduction rows increased upper trapezius, middle trapezius, and posterior deltoid activity.
studies.citation: Vasconcelos CMWA, Lopes CR, Almeida VM, Neto WK, Soares EG. Effect Of Different Grip Position And Shoulder-Abduction Angle On Muscle Strength And Activation During The Seated Cable Row. International Journal of Strength and Conditioning. 2023;3(1):1-13. doi:10.47206/ijsc.v3i1.190.
studies.relevance: Directly studied seated cable row variations with surface EMG of upper trapezius, middle trapezius, upper latissimus, lower latissimus, posterior deltoid, and biceps brachii in recreationally trained participants.

studies.type: High-density seated row EMG study
studies.shortCitation: Padovan et al., J Hum Kinet, 2025
studies.finding: Narrow seated row showed greater latissimus dorsi EMG amplitude, while wide seated row emphasized trapezius, lateral deltoid, and erector spinae in specific phases.
studies.citation: Padovan R, Ce E, Longo S, Tornatore G, Trentin C, Esposito F, Coratella G. High-Density Surface Electromyography Excitation of Prime Movers in the Narrow vs. Wide Grip Seated Row Exercise. Journal of Human Kinetics. 2025;Advanced Online Publication:1-16. doi:10.5114/jhk/209550.
studies.relevance: Directly compared narrow and wide seated row using high-density EMG of latissimus dorsi, trapezius regions, deltoids, biceps brachii, triceps brachii, and erector spinae in resistance-trained men.

studies.type: Latissimus dorsi exercise EMG study
studies.finding: Seated row produced a high latissimus-to-biceps activation ratio and the highest middle trapezius/rhomboid activity among the tested latissimus dorsi exercises.
studies.citation: Lehman GJ, Buchan DD, Lundy A, Myers N, Nalborczyk A. Variations in muscle activation levels during traditional latissimus dorsi weight training exercises: An experimental study. Dynamic Medicine. 2004;3:4. doi:10.1186/1476-5918-3-4.
studies.relevance: Includes seated row with retracted and non-retracted scapulae and measured latissimus dorsi, biceps brachii, and a grouped middle trapezius/rhomboid signal.

studies.type: Seated row EMG and verbal-instruction study
studies.finding: At 70% 1RM, seated row produced substantial latissimus dorsi, teres major, posterior deltoid, and biceps brachii activity, and verbal instruction did not materially change the average EMG response.
studies.citation: Fujita RA, De Marchi PU, Silva NRS, Gomes MM. Verbal instruction does not change myoelectric activity during seated row exercise in trained and untrained men. Motriz: Revista de Educacao Fisica. 2019;25(4):e10190100. doi:10.1590/s1980-6574201900040100.
studies.relevance: Direct seated row EMG study measuring latissimus dorsi, teres major, posterior deltoid, triceps brachii long head, and biceps brachii in trained and untrained men.

studies.type: Rotator cuff recruitment study
studies.shortCitation: Wattanaprakornkul et al., J Electromyogr Kinesiol, 2011
studies.finding: Rotator cuff recruitment during bench press and row was direction-specific, consistent with dynamic shoulder stabilization.
studies.citation: Wattanaprakornkul D, Halaki M, Cathers I, Ginn KA. Direction-specific recruitment of rotator cuff muscles during bench press and row. Journal of Electromyography and Kinesiology. 2011;21(6):1041-1049. doi:10.1016/j.jelekin.2011.09.002.
studies.relevance: Directly supports rotator cuff involvement as shoulder stabilization during row tasks.

studies.type: Seated cable row technique review
studies.finding: Describes the seated cable row setup, coaching constraints, and three-point base of support from both feet on plates plus the pelvis on the bench.
studies.citation: Ronai P. Do it right: The seated cable row exercise. ACSM's Health & Fitness Journal. 2019;23(4):32-37. doi:10.1249/FIT.0000000000000492.
studies.relevance: Provides peer-reviewed technique and setup context for the exact foot-supported seated cable row variant.

movements.name: Seated Machine Calf Raise
movements.variant: Seated calf-raise machine with the knees flexed around 90 degrees and resistance applied through a thigh pad; treated separately from standing, donkey, leg-press, and bodyweight calf raises.
movements.description: Sit with the balls of the feet on the platform, the knees bent and held under the thigh pad, and the ankles free to move. Lower the heels under control until the calves are stretched, press through the forefoot to raise the heels as high as controlled, pause briefly, then return without bouncing or letting the knees lift into the pad.

hypertrophy.rationale: Strong direct soleus stimulus with low unrelated fatigue, but seated knee flexion makes it less complete for gastrocnemius growth than a knee-extended calf raise.

strength.rationale: Loads plantar-flexion force directly, but the single-joint seated setup has limited carryover to whole-body strength expression.

joint_resilience.rationale: Provides controlled ankle and Achilles tendon exposure through useful range, with less knee-extended gastrocnemius length than standing options.

athletic_transfer.rationale: The ankle action is relevant to gait and jumping, but the seated supported setup removes posture, ground reaction, and coordination demands.

control.rationale: Very low Motor Control demand beyond ankle range, tempo, and keeping the knees settled under the pad.

fatigue_efficiency.rationale: High local calf stimulus with very low systemic fatigue, balance cost, or unrelated recovery demand.

setup.rationale: Requires a specific machine plus pad height and load setup, but the setup is quick and repeatable once adjusted.

ease.rationale: Simple guided movement with minimal skill demand; the main technique constraints are full range, controlled tempo, and pad placement.

progression.rationale: Load, reps, pauses, and range are easy to track, with minor limitations from machine increments and individual machine geometry.

support.rationale: Very high external support from the seat, thigh pad, foot platform, and guided resistance path.

primary.name: Soleus
primary.evidenceShort: Bent-knee calf raises preferentially emphasize soleus.
primary.evidence: Bent-knee calf-raise evidence shows greater acute soleus swelling than straight-leg calf raises, and seated knee-flexed training produced soleus hypertrophy comparable to standing training while limiting gastrocnemius growth.

secondary.name: Gastrocnemius
secondary.evidenceShort: Still contributes to plantar flexion, but knee flexion reduces its emphasis.
secondary.evidence: The gastrocnemius is part of the triceps surae and contributes during calf-raise tasks, but seated knee-flexed training produced much smaller or nonsignificant gastrocnemius hypertrophy than standing knee-extended training.

evidence.verdict: Seated machine calf raise: soleus primary; gastrocnemius secondary; no separate support muscles listed.
evidence.clinicalShort: Acute swelling, EMG, and MRI hypertrophy answer different questions and do not directly determine tendon tolerance or long-term programming by themselves.
evidence.limitsShort: Knee angle, foot platform height, dorsiflexion depth, pause duration, machine cam path, load, and bouncing change the training stress.
evidence.summary: The seated machine calf raise is classified as a supported bent-knee plantar-flexion exercise. Direct straight-leg versus bent-leg calf-raise evidence supports a soleus-biased classification, while gastrocnemius remains a secondary plantar-flexion contributor because knee flexion shortens the gastrocnemius and reduces its growth response relative to standing calf raises.
evidence.clinicalInterpretation: Ultrasound swelling and EMG studies estimate acute local use under specific exercise conditions, while MRI hypertrophy studies reflect training adaptation across weeks. These measures should be interpreted with knee angle, ankle range of motion, and loading method rather than treated as universal muscle-growth rankings.
evidence.limitations: This entry assumes a conventional seated calf-raise machine with the knees flexed near 90 degrees. Straight-knee standing, donkey, leg-press calf-raise, single-leg, and bodyweight variants should be classified separately because gastrocnemius and soleus emphasis changes with knee angle and setup.

studies.type: Straight-leg versus bent-leg calf-raise swelling study
studies.finding: Bent-leg calf raises produced greater soleus swelling, while straight-leg calf raises produced greater gastrocnemius swelling.
studies.citation: Kassiano W, Costa B, Kunevaliki G, Soares D, Stavinski N, Francsuel J, Carneiro MAS, Tricoli I, Nunes JP, Ribeiro AS, Cyrino ES. Muscle Swelling of the Triceps Surae in Response to Straight-Leg and Bent-Leg Calf Raise Exercises in Young Women. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2023;37(7):e438-e443. doi:10.1519/JSC.0000000000004491.
studies.relevance: Direct knee-angle calf-raise comparison measuring medial gastrocnemius, lateral gastrocnemius, and soleus thickness before and after exercise.

studies.type: Standing versus seated calf-raise hypertrophy study
studies.finding: Seated knee-flexed calf-raise training increased soleus volume similarly to standing training but did not significantly increase gastrocnemius volume.
studies.citation: Kinoshita M, Maeo S, Kobayashi Y, Eihara Y, Ono M, Sato M, Sugiyama T, Kanehisa H. Triceps surae muscle hypertrophy is greater after standing versus seated calf-raise training. Frontiers in Physiology. 2023;14:1272106. doi:10.3389/fphys.2023.1272106.
studies.relevance: Direct seated versus standing calf-raise training comparison using MRI muscle volume outcomes for soleus and gastrocnemius heads.

studies.type: Triceps surae fMRI and EMG
studies.finding: Functional MRI and EMG characterized distinct gastrocnemius and soleus involvement in triceps-surae activation.
studies.citation: Kinugasa R, Akima H. Neuromuscular activation of triceps surae using muscle functional MRI and EMG. Medicine and Science in Sports and Exercise. 2005;37(4):593-598. doi:10.1249/01.mss.0000159026.99792.76.
studies.relevance: Supports separating soleus and gastrocnemius rather than using one generic calf label.

movements.name: Seated Machine Chest Fly
movements.variant: Seated pec-deck or machine chest fly with guided arms, pads, or handles, treated separately from dumbbell fly, cable fly, and chest press variations.
movements.description: Sit with the back against the pad, feet flat, and the seat adjusted so the handles or pads travel around mid-chest height. Set the start position so the chest is stretched without forcing the shoulders forward, keep a small consistent elbow bend, bring the arms together along the guided path, then return slowly until the chest is loaded again.

hypertrophy.rationale: Strong chest hypertrophy option because direct pec-deck evidence shows high pectoralis activation and the guided path lets most effort stay local to the chest.

strength.rationale: Useful for shoulder-adduction force in a narrow pattern, but it is a single-joint isolation movement with lower absolute loading and little transfer to pressing strength.

joint_resilience.rationale: Can provide controlled shoulder horizontal-adduction exposure, but the long-arm stretched position and fixed path make it a limited general joint-resilience tool.

athletic_transfer.rationale: Very little athletic-transfer signal because the task is seated, bilateral, guided, and isolated from whole-body force production.

control.rationale: Very low motor-control demand because the machine constrains the path and removes most balance and free-arm stabilization.

fatigue_efficiency.rationale: High local chest stimulus with low systemic cost and little triceps fatigue leakage compared with pressing.

setup.rationale: Low-friction once the machine is available, with deductions for seat height, start-range, arm-pad or handle, and load-stack adjustments.

ease.rationale: Easy to learn and repeat because the path is guided, though shoulder range and start position still need sensible adjustment.

progression.rationale: Load, reps, and range are simple to record, with deductions for coarse stack jumps, machine-specific friction, and differing cam paths.

support.rationale: Very high external support from the seat, back pad, guided arms, and constrained path.

primary.name: Pectoralis major
primary.evidenceShort: Direct pec-deck EMG supports the pec as the main target.
primary.evidence: Machine pec-deck and chest-exercise EMG studies measured pectoralis major activity directly and found pec-deck activation similar to bench press or among the highest tested chest exercises. The movement is a guided horizontal shoulder-adduction pattern, matching the intended pectoralis major target.

secondary.name: Anterior deltoid
secondary.evidenceShort: Direct pec-deck EMG shows meaningful shoulder-flexion/adduction assistance.
secondary.evidence: Pec-deck studies directly measured anterior deltoid activity and found meaningful recruitment during the exercise. It is classified as secondary because the movement is programmed as a chest fly, machine geometry and arm rotation can shift deltoid contribution, and pectoralis major remains the intended target.

evidence.verdict: Seated machine chest fly: pectoralis major primary; anterior deltoid secondary; no visible support muscles added.
evidence.clinicalShort: EMG estimates acute excitation, not hypertrophy, mechanical tension, adaptation, pain, or injury risk.
evidence.limitsShort: Pec-deck pad versus handle design, seat height, arm path, start range, elbow angle, load, tempo, and shoulder rotation can shift emphasis.
evidence.summary: The seated machine chest fly is classified as a guided horizontal shoulder-adduction isolation movement. Direct pec-deck EMG supports pectoralis major as the primary visible target and anterior deltoid as a meaningful secondary contributor. Triceps brachii is not shown because direct pec-deck evidence reports it as much less relevant than in pressing. Biceps brachii is not shown because stronger biceps evidence comes from free-weight dumbbell flyes, where independent dumbbells and elbow-angle stabilization are not the same demand as a guided machine.
evidence.clinicalInterpretation: Surface electromyography is useful for estimating muscle excitation in a specific machine setup, load, and range of motion. It should not be treated as a direct measure of long-term hypertrophy, mechanical tension, joint stress, pain risk, or injury risk.
evidence.limitations: The evidence base mixes exact machine pec-deck studies, a university thesis on multiple chest exercises, and close dumbbell-fly or bench-press-family evidence. Direct studies used small samples, mostly young trained men, and differed in load prescription, cadence, normalization, exercise order, and whether the pec deck used forearm pads or handles. Commercial machines differ in cam design, seat geometry, start-range stops, handle height, and whether the elbows are flexed near 90 degrees or held slightly bent.

studies.type: Direct machine pec-deck EMG
studies.shortCitation: Rocha Junior et al., Rev Bras Med Esporte, 2007
studies.finding: Machine pec deck and bench press showed similar pectoralis major and anterior deltoid RMS activity, while triceps brachii was much less relevant in the pec deck.
studies.citation: Rocha Junior VA, Gentil P, Oliveira E, do Carmo J. Comparison among the EMG activity of the pectoralis major, anterior deltoidis and triceps brachii during the bench press and peck deck exercises. Revista Brasileira de Medicina do Esporte. 2007;13(1):43e-46e. doi:10.1590/S1517-86922007000100012.
studies.relevance: Directly studied a machine pec deck in 13 trained men at 10RM load and measured pectoralis major, anterior deltoid, and triceps brachii.

studies.type: Direct pec-deck pectoralis major EMG thesis
studies.shortCitation: Schanke, University of Wisconsin-La Crosse thesis, 2012
studies.finding: The pec-deck machine was not significantly different from barbell bench press for pectoralis major activation and was among the highest tested chest exercises.
studies.citation: Schanke W. Electromyographical analysis of the pectoralis major muscle during various chest exercises. Master's thesis. University of Wisconsin-La Crosse; 2012.
studies.relevance: Directly included the pec-deck machine and pectoralis major EMG in healthy resistance-trained men; useful for the primary chest-target classification, with lower evidentiary weight than peer-reviewed journal studies.

studies.type: Direct pec-deck deltoid EMG
studies.finding: Anterior deltoid activation during peck deck was about 50% MVIC and similar to bench press in trained men.
studies.citation: Botton CE, Wilhelm EN, Ughini CC, Pinto RS, Lima CS. Electromyographical analysis of the deltoid between different strength training exercises. Medicina Sportiva. 2013;17(2):67-71. doi:10.5604/17342260.1055261.
studies.relevance: Directly measured anterior, medial, and posterior deltoid activity during a peck-deck exercise at 10RM load; used to classify anterior deltoid as a visible secondary contributor.

studies.type: Close dumbbell fly EMG comparison
studies.shortCitation: Solstad et al., J Sports Sci Med, 2020
studies.finding: Dumbbell flyes involved pectoralis major and anterior deltoid but showed lower agonist activation than barbell bench press overall; biceps brachii was higher in flyes, likely from elbow and arm stabilization.
studies.citation: Solstad TE, Andersen V, Shaw M, Hoel EM, Vonheim A, Saeterbakken AH. A Comparison of Muscle Activation between Barbell Bench Press and Dumbbell Flyes in Resistance-Trained Males. Journal of Sports Science and Medicine. 2020;19(4):645-651.
studies.relevance: Not a machine pec-deck study; used as close fly-pattern evidence for free-weight fly mechanics, biceps exclusion boundaries, and rating limits.

studies.type: Systematic review of bench-press EMG with pec-deck context
studies.finding: Bench-press EMG literature supports pectoralis major as a dominant horizontal-press muscle and notes that pec deck preferentially stimulates pectoralis major and anterior deltoid over triceps brachii.
studies.citation: Stastny P, Golas A, Blazek D, Maszczyk A, Wilk M, Pietraszewski P, Petr M, Uhlir P, Zajac A. A systematic review of surface electromyography analyses of the bench press movement task. PLOS ONE. 2017;12(2):e0171632. doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0171632.
studies.relevance: Provides review context for horizontal pressing and pec-deck comparisons, plus interpretation limits for EMG-based classifications.

movements.name: Seated Machine Chest Press
movements.variant: Seated machine chest press with guided handles or a guided lever path, treated separately from Smith machine, cable, dumbbell, and barbell pressing.
movements.description: Sit with the back against the pad, feet flat, and the handles set near mid-chest height. Brace lightly, keep the shoulders down and controlled against the pad, press the handles forward along the machine path until the elbows are nearly straight, then return under control until the chest and shoulders are loaded without losing position.

hypertrophy.rationale: Excellent chest hypertrophy option because the machine supplies a stable path and allows high local effort with low coordination cost.

strength.rationale: Builds pressing force in a constrained path, but it is less representative of free-weight strength expression.

joint_resilience.rationale: Can provide controlled exposure, but the fixed path is not a broad joint-resilience tool and may not match every shoulder.

athletic_transfer.rationale: Almost no athletic-transfer signal because the task is seated, guided, bilateral, and externally stabilized.

control.rationale: Very low control demand; the machine removes most balance, path, and stabilization requirements.

fatigue_efficiency.rationale: Very efficient local pressing stimulus with low systemic fatigue and little setup leakage once adjusted.

setup.rationale: Low-friction once the machine is available, with only seat, handle, and load adjustments.

ease.rationale: One of the easiest pressing patterns to learn and repeat because path and body position are highly constrained.

progression.rationale: Machine load and reps are easy to record, with deductions for stack increments and machine-specific path differences.

support.rationale: Extremely high external support from the seat, back pad, and guided pressing path.

primary.name: Pectoralis major
primary.evidenceShort: Direct seated machine EMG supports the pec as the main target.
primary.evidence: Seated chest press and chest press machine EMG studies measured multiple pectoralis major regions and found substantial activation during the guided press pattern; movement-family review evidence also identifies pectoralis major as a dominant horizontal-press contributor.

secondary.name: Anterior deltoid
secondary.evidenceShort: Measured machine-press assistant; path and angle sensitive.
secondary.evidence: Anterior deltoid activity was directly measured during seated chest press and chest press machine variants. It contributes meaningfully to pressing but is classified as secondary because the exercise is primarily a chest press and anterior-deltoid demand changes with path, grip, and press angle.

secondary.name: Triceps brachii
secondary.evidenceShort: Measured elbow-extension contributor in chest press EMG.
secondary.evidence: Direct seated chest press and chest press machine EMG studies measured triceps brachii activity, supporting its role as an elbow-extension contributor rather than the primary target of the movement.

support.name: Serratus anterior
support.evidenceShort: Measured scapulothoracic support in lever-machine pressing.
support.evidence: A chest press lever-machine study measured serratus anterior activity alongside scapular kinematics. Because the movement is guided and the serratus role is scapulothoracic control, it is classified as support rather than a prime chest target.

support.name: Rotator cuff
support.evidenceShort: Pressing-family inference for shoulder stabilization.
support.evidence: This role is marked as an inference from close bench-press evidence: rotator cuff EMG during bench press shows direction-specific recruitment consistent with glenohumeral stabilization. Direct seated machine chest press rotator cuff data were not found in the reviewed sources.

evidence.verdict: Guided seated chest press: pectoralis major primary; anterior deltoid and triceps brachii secondary; serratus anterior and rotator cuff support.
evidence.clinicalShort: EMG estimates acute excitation, not hypertrophy, mechanical tension, adaptation, or injury risk.
evidence.limitsShort: Machine design, seat height, handle path, grip, load, range of motion, and training status can shift muscle emphasis.
evidence.summary: The seated machine chest press is classified as a supported guided horizontal pressing movement. Direct seated chest press and chest press machine studies support pectoralis major as the primary visible target, with anterior deltoid and triceps brachii as meaningful secondary contributors. Serratus anterior is included as support from direct lever-machine EMG and scapular kinematic evidence. Rotator cuff support is included only as a clearly marked inference from close bench-press stabilization evidence.
evidence.clinicalInterpretation: Surface electromyography is useful for estimating acute muscle excitation under a specific load, grip, and machine setup. It should not be treated as a direct measure of hypertrophy, mechanical tension, long-term adaptation, or injury risk.
evidence.limitations: The reviewed evidence includes selectorized seated chest press, chest press machine, and lever-machine chest press variants rather than every commercial guided-handle design. Most direct samples were small and male or physically active/trained, and studies differed in load prescription, normalization, grip, range of motion, and whether concentric and eccentric phases were separated.

studies.type: Direct seated chest press EMG
studies.shortCitation: Muyor et al., J Hum Kinet, 2023
studies.finding: Seated chest press variants produced similar pectoralis, anterior deltoid, and triceps activity to common horizontal bench press conditions, with grip-specific differences.
studies.citation: Muyor JM, Rodriguez-Ridao D, Oliva-Lozano JM. Comparison of Muscle Activity between the Horizontal Bench Press and the Seated Chest Press Exercises Using Several Grips. Journal of Human Kinetics. 2023;87:23-34. doi:10.5114/jhk/161468.
studies.relevance: Directly studied seated machine chest press with prone and neutral grips in trained adults and measured pectoralis major regions, anterior deltoid, and triceps brachii.

studies.type: Direct chest press machine EMG
studies.shortCitation: Coratella et al., Eur J Sport Sci, 2020
studies.finding: A selectorized seated chest press produced substantial sternocostal pectoralis and anterior deltoid excitation; free-weight press variations showed greater triceps and lateral deltoid excitation in competitive bodybuilders.
studies.citation: Coratella G, Tornatore G, Longo S, Esposito F, Ce E. Specific prime movers' excitation during free-weight bench press variations and chest press machine in competitive bodybuilders. European Journal of Sport Science. 2020;20(5):571-579. doi:10.1080/17461391.2019.1655101.
studies.relevance: Directly tested a selectorized seated chest press machine at 80% 1RM and measured pectoralis major heads, anterior deltoid, lateral deltoid, and triceps brachii during concentric and eccentric phases.

studies.type: Chest press lever machine EMG and scapular kinematics
studies.finding: A chest press lever machine showed similar activation to barbell bench press at 10RM load and included serratus anterior and scapular motion data.
studies.citation: Borges E, Dalla H, Mastandrea L, Nunes S, Santarem J. Comparative evaluation of muscular activation and scapular kinematics in a chest press lever machine and a barbell bench press. Journal of Physical Education and Sport. 2019;19:912-916. doi:10.7752/jpes.2019.s3131.
studies.relevance: Directly compared a guided chest press lever machine with barbell bench press while measuring pectoralis major heads, anterior deltoid, serratus anterior, and scapular kinematics.

studies.type: Systematic review of bench press EMG
studies.finding: Bench press EMG literature supports pectoralis major and triceps brachii as dominant contributors, with anterior deltoid also involved and stability conditions affecting interpretation.
studies.citation: Stastny P, Golas A, Blazek D, Maszczyk A, Wilk M, Pietraszewski P, Petr M, Uhlir P, Zajac A. A systematic review of surface electromyography analyses of the bench press movement task. PLOS ONE. 2017;12(2):e0171632. doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0171632.
studies.relevance: Provides movement-family context for horizontal pressing and interpretation limits when direct seated-machine data are compared with free-weight evidence.

studies.type: Rotator cuff recruitment study
studies.shortCitation: Wattanaprakornkul et al., J Electromyogr Kinesiol, 2011
studies.finding: Rotator cuff muscles were recruited in a direction-specific manner during bench press and row tasks, consistent with dynamic shoulder stabilization.
studies.citation: Wattanaprakornkul D, Halaki M, Cathers I, Ginn KA. Direction-specific recruitment of rotator cuff muscles during bench press and row. Journal of Electromyography and Kinesiology. 2011;21(6):1041-1049. doi:10.1016/j.jelekin.2011.09.002.
studies.relevance: Not a seated machine chest press study; used only to infer glenohumeral stabilization by the rotator cuff in close pressing tasks.

movements.name: Seated Machine Hamstring Curl
movements.variant: Seated hamstring curl machine with a thigh restraint and lower-leg pad resistance, treated separately from prone, standing, cable, band, slider, and Nordic curl variants.
movements.description: Sit with the knees aligned to the machine pivot, the thighs secured under the pad, and the lower-leg pad set just above the heels. Hold the handles or seat, keep the hips and thighs fixed, curl the pad down and back by flexing the knees, then return under control until the knees are nearly straight without letting the stack rest.

hypertrophy.rationale: Excellent direct hamstring hypertrophy movement, especially because the seated position loads biarticular hamstrings at longer muscle lengths.

strength.rationale: Builds isolated knee-flexion force, but does not represent integrated lower-body strength.

joint_resilience.rationale: Strong posterior-knee and hamstring-tendon capacity signal under controlled lengthened-position loading.

athletic_transfer.rationale: Very low transfer to athletic movement because the task is seated, supported, and isolated.

control.rationale: Very low control demand beyond machine setup, tempo, and avoiding hip movement.

fatigue_efficiency.rationale: High local hamstring stimulus with low systemic fatigue and minimal unrelated recovery cost.

setup.rationale: Requires machine availability and several repeatable pad or range adjustments, but no complex loading once set.

ease.rationale: Simple guided single-joint movement with low balance and coordination demand.

progression.rationale: Load, reps, and range are easy to track, with deductions for stack increments, friction, and machine geometry.

support.rationale: Very high external support from the seat, back pad, thigh restraint, handles, and guided lever path.

primary.name: Hamstrings
primary.evidenceShort: Direct seated leg curl MRI and leg-curl EMG support the hamstrings as the main target.
primary.evidence: Seated leg curl training studies using MRI show increases in whole-hamstring and individual hamstring muscle volume, while leg-curl and knee-flexion EMG evidence supports the hamstrings as the dominant knee-flexion target.

secondary.name: Gastrocnemius
secondary.evidenceShort: Biarticular knee-flexion assistant; ankle-position dependent.
secondary.evidence: Gastrocnemius crosses the knee and can contribute to knee-flexion torque during leg-curl-like tasks; experimental and modeling work shows a greater knee-flexion moment when the ankle is dorsiflexed than plantar-flexed.

evidence.verdict: Seated machine leg curl: hamstrings primary; gastrocnemius secondary; no visible support muscles added.
evidence.clinicalShort: EMG estimates acute excitation; MRI muscle volume reflects training adaptation, not a direct single-session hypertrophy signal.
evidence.limitsShort: Commercial machine geometry, hip angle, knee-pivot alignment, ankle position, pad placement, load, tempo, and range of motion can shift emphasis.
evidence.summary: The seated machine leg curl is classified as a supported knee-flexion isolation exercise. Direct seated leg curl training evidence supports the hamstrings as the primary target, with particular relevance for the biarticular hamstrings because the seated hip-flexed position trains them at longer lengths. Gastrocnemius is included as a secondary visible role because it is a biarticular knee flexor and leg-curl biomechanics show ankle-position-dependent contribution to knee-flexion torque. No support muscles are shown because the reviewed evidence did not justify a specific stabilizer role for the card.
evidence.clinicalInterpretation: Surface and fine-wire EMG are useful for estimating muscle excitation under specific joint angles, loads, and contraction modes. MRI volume studies support that repeated seated leg curl training can enlarge hamstring muscles, but they do not identify the exact acute stimulus from a single repetition. Neither EMG nor MRI adaptation evidence should be read as a direct injury-risk or pain prediction.
evidence.limitations: Exact commercial seated leg curl EMG evidence is limited. The strongest exact evidence uses MRI training outcomes from seated or modified seated leg-curl machines, while supporting EMG and biomechanics sources include prone or generic leg curl, maximum knee flexion, and isokinetic knee-flexion tasks. Participants were mostly healthy young adults or weight-trained men, not all age groups or clinical populations. Sartorius, gracilis, popliteus, and individual hamstring heads were not added as separate visible roles because the available evidence was not strong enough to classify them clearly for a generic seated machine card.

studies.type: Direct seated versus prone leg curl MRI training study
studies.shortCitation: Maeo et al., Med Sci Sports Exerc, 2021
studies.finding: Seated leg curl training increased whole hamstrings and biarticular hamstring muscle volume more than prone leg curl training.
studies.citation: Maeo S, Huang M, Wu Y, Sakurai H, Kusagawa Y, Sugiyama T, Kanehisa H, Isaka T. Greater Hamstrings Muscle Hypertrophy but Similar Damage Protection after Training at Long versus Short Muscle Lengths. Medicine and Science in Sports and Exercise. 2021;53(4):825-837. doi:10.1249/MSS.0000000000002523.
studies.relevance: Directly studied seated leg curl training on a modified seated machine with hip flexion, knee-flexion pad resistance, fixed setup, MRI-measured individual hamstring volumes, and 1RM-based loading.

studies.type: Modified seated leg curl lengthened-state eccentric training
studies.shortCitation: Maeo et al., Med Sci Sports Exerc, 2024
studies.finding: Lengthened-state eccentric training using isoinertial weight-stack resistance in an accentuated hip-flexed seated-curl setup increased hamstrings and biceps femoris long head volume more than Nordic hamstring training.
studies.citation: Maeo S, Balshaw TG, Nin DZ, Mc Dermott EJ, Osborne T, Cooper NB, Massey GJ, Kong PUIW, Pain MTG, Folland JP. Hamstrings Hypertrophy Is Specific to the Training Exercise: Nordic Hamstring versus Lengthened State Eccentric Training. Medicine and Science in Sports and Exercise. 2024;56(10):1893-1905. doi:10.1249/MSS.0000000000003490.
studies.relevance: Close direct evidence for a seated leg-curl-style weight-stack setup in a hip-flexed lengthened hamstring position, with MRI muscle-volume outcomes and knee-flexion strength testing.

studies.type: Leg curl hamstring EMG comparison
studies.finding: Weight-trained men performed leg curl, stiff-leg deadlift, and back squat at 75% 1RM; leg curl was used as a high hamstring-activation resistance exercise comparison.
studies.citation: Wright GA, Delong TH, Gehlsen G. Electromyographic Activity of the Hamstrings During Performance of the Leg Curl, Stiff-Leg Deadlift, and Back Squat Movements. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 1999;13(2):168-174. doi:10.1519/00124278-199905000-00012.
studies.relevance: Leg-curl movement-family EMG evidence supporting hamstring involvement during loaded knee-flexion resistance exercise, though not specific to a seated machine.

studies.type: Fine-wire EMG of hamstrings during maximum knee flexion
studies.shortCitation: Onishi et al., J Electromyogr Kinesiol, 2002
studies.finding: Fine-wire EMG showed individual hamstring activity during maximum knee flexion and demonstrated that activation changes with knee angle and differs among hamstring muscles.
studies.citation: Onishi H, Yagi R, Oyama M, Akasaka K, Ihashi K, Handa Y. EMG-angle relationship of the hamstring muscles during maximum knee flexion. Journal of Electromyography and Kinesiology. 2002;12(5):399-406. doi:10.1016/S1050-6411(02)00033-0.
studies.relevance: Supports the knee-flexion role of individual hamstring muscles and the limitation that hamstring-head emphasis changes with joint angle rather than remaining uniform across the curl.

studies.type: Gastrocnemius contribution during leg-curl-like knee flexion
studies.shortCitation: Gallucci and Challis, J Appl Biomech, 2002
studies.finding: Isokinetic knee-flexion torque was higher with the ankle dorsiflexed than plantar-flexed, supporting an ankle-position-dependent gastrocnemius contribution during leg curls.
studies.citation: Gallucci JG, Challis JH. Examining the role of the gastrocnemius during the leg curl exercise. Journal of Applied Biomechanics. 2002;18(1):15-27. doi:10.1123/jab.18.1.15.
studies.relevance: Directly addresses gastrocnemius contribution to knee-flexion torque in leg-curl-relevant tasks and informs secondary-role and ankle-position limitations.

movements.name: Seated Machine Leg Extension
movements.variant: Seated knee-extension machine with shin pad resistance, treated separately from cable, band, bodyweight, sissy squat, recumbent, and hip-angle-specific leg-extension variants.
movements.description: Sit with the knees aligned to the machine pivot, the back and hips fixed against the pads, and the shin pad set just above the ankles. Hold the handles or seat, straighten the knees to lift the pad without letting the hips rise, pause near full extension without slamming the stack, then lower under control until the knees are flexed again.

hypertrophy.rationale: Excellent direct quadriceps stimulus with strong isolation and repeatable loading, supported by leg-extension EMG and hypertrophy studies.

strength.rationale: Builds isolated knee-extension force well, but it does not express integrated lower-body strength through the hip, ankle, trunk, or ground contact.

joint_resilience.rationale: Useful controlled loading for the knee extensors and patellofemoral tolerance, with deductions because open-chain terminal extension can be sensitive to knee status, pad placement, and range selection.

athletic_transfer.rationale: Very low direct transfer because the task is seated, guided, bilateral by default, and lacks gait, landing, balance, hip extension, or whole-body force transfer.

control.rationale: Very low Motor Control demand beyond alignment, tempo, range control, and keeping the hips seated.

fatigue_efficiency.rationale: High local quad stimulus with low systemic fatigue and little unrelated recovery cost when knee tolerance is good.

setup.rationale: Requires a specific machine plus repeatable seat, pivot, pad, and range adjustments, but loading is quick once the machine is set.

ease.rationale: Simple guided single-joint movement with minimal balance or coordination demand, though pad and knee-pivot setup still matter.

progression.rationale: Load, reps, tempo, side-to-side work, and range are easy to track, with minor deductions for stack increments and machine geometry.

support.rationale: Very high external support from the seat, back pad, handles, shin pad, and guided lever path.

primary.name: Quadriceps
primary.evidenceShort: Direct leg-extension EMG and hypertrophy studies support the quadriceps as the main target.
primary.evidence: Leg-extension studies directly measure high activity in superficial quadriceps heads, knee-extension comparisons show rectus femoris, vastus lateralis, and vastus medialis involvement, and longitudinal leg-extension training studies report hypertrophy in rectus femoris, vastus lateralis, or whole quadriceps measures.

evidence.verdict: Seated machine leg extension: quadriceps primary; no visible secondary or support muscles added.
evidence.clinicalShort: EMG estimates acute excitation; ultrasound or MRI hypertrophy studies reflect training adaptation, not single-session muscle growth or knee safety.
evidence.limitsShort: Machine cam path, hip angle, knee-pivot alignment, shin-pad position, range of motion, load, tempo, terminal extension, and knee symptoms can all change the training stress.
evidence.summary: The seated machine leg extension is classified as a supported open-chain knee-extension isolation exercise. Direct leg-extension EMG evidence supports the quadriceps as the visible primary role, and longitudinal knee-extension or leg-extension training studies show that the movement can increase quadriceps size and knee-extension strength. Secondary and support roles are intentionally empty because the reviewed evidence did not justify adding a specific non-quadriceps visible muscle to a generic seated machine card.
evidence.clinicalInterpretation: Surface EMG and MRI T2 are useful for estimating acute excitation or regional use under specific joint angles, loads, and range conditions. Ultrasound and MRI training studies support longer-term quadriceps adaptation, but they do not directly predict pain, injury risk, or whether a specific knee should tolerate terminal open-chain loading.
evidence.limitations: Exact commercial-machine geometry varies across selectorized, plate-loaded, unilateral, bilateral, upright, and recumbent designs. Most EMG studies measure superficial quadriceps heads rather than every quadriceps component, and most training studies use young healthy or trained participants. The available evidence supports the quadriceps aggregate, but not a separate visible role for rectus femoris, vastus lateralis, vastus medialis, vastus intermedius, hip flexors, hamstrings, calves, or trunk stabilizers in this generic card.

studies.type: Direct leg-extension EMG range and rotation study
studies.finding: In 24 participants performing 8RM leg extensions, vastus medialis oblique, rectus femoris, and vastus lateralis EMG varied by repetition, range segment, and limb rotation.
studies.citation: Signorile JF, Lew KM, Stoutenberg M, Pluchino A, Lewis JE, Gao J. Range of motion and leg rotation affect electromyography activation levels of the superficial quadriceps muscles during leg extension. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2014;28(9):2536-2545. doi:10.1519/JSC.0000000000000582.
studies.relevance: Direct leg-extension EMG evidence for superficial quadriceps activation during loaded repetitions, with practical limitations for range of motion and limb rotation.

studies.type: Direct leg-extension foot-position EMG study
studies.finding: Leg-extension EMG showed quadriceps-head activation across foot positions, with medial rotation emphasizing vastus lateralis and vastus medialis and lateral rotation emphasizing rectus femoris.
studies.citation: Stoutenberg M, Pluchino AP, Ma F, Hoctor JE, Signorile JF. The impact of foot position on electromyographical activity of the superficial quadriceps muscles during leg extension. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2005;19(4):931-938. doi:10.1519/R-16364.1.
studies.relevance: Direct leg-extension movement-family EMG evidence measuring superficial quadriceps heads and showing that foot or limb position can shift emphasis.

studies.type: Knee extension versus leg press quadriceps EMG study
studies.shortCitation: Ema et al., Eur J Appl Physiol, 2016
studies.finding: Rectus femoris activation was higher during knee extension than during leg press, while vasti activation did not differ between the exercises in the same way.
studies.citation: Ema R, Sakaguchi M, Akagi R, Kawakami Y. Unique activation of the quadriceps femoris during single- and multi-joint exercises. European Journal of Applied Physiology. 2016;116(5):1031-1041. doi:10.1007/s00421-016-3363-5.
studies.relevance: Supports knee extension as a quadriceps exercise with distinctive rectus femoris activation compared with a multi-joint lower-body press.

studies.type: Leg-extension hip-angle hypertrophy study
studies.shortCitation: Larsen et al., J Sports Sci, 2025
studies.finding: Twenty-two untrained men completed 10 weeks of unilateral leg-extension training; both 90 degree and 40 degree hip-flexion conditions trained rectus femoris and vastus lateralis, with greater rectus femoris hypertrophy in the lower hip-flexion condition.
studies.citation: Larsen S, Sandvik Kristiansen BS, Swinton PA, Wolf M, Fredriksen AB, Falch HN, van den Tillaar R, Sandberg NO. The effects of hip flexion angle on quadriceps femoris muscle hypertrophy in the leg extension exercise. Journal of Sports Sciences. 2025;43(2):210-221. doi:10.1080/02640414.2024.2444713.
studies.relevance: Direct leg-extension training evidence including an upright seated 90 degree hip-flexion condition, with ultrasound outcomes for rectus femoris and vastus lateralis.

studies.type: Unilateral seated leg-extension hypertrophy study
studies.finding: Eight weeks of unilateral seated leg-extension training increased rectus femoris and vastus lateralis muscle thickness and knee-extension strength in recreationally active young men.
studies.citation: Varovic D, Zganjer K, Vuk S, Schoenfeld BJ. Drop-Set Training Elicits Differential Increases in Non-Uniform Hypertrophy of the Quadriceps in Leg Extension Exercise. Sports. 2021;9(9):119. doi:10.3390/sports9090119.
studies.relevance: Direct seated leg-extension training evidence for quadriceps hypertrophy and knee-extension strength adaptation.

studies.type: Open-chain knee-extension versus squat hypertrophy study
studies.finding: Eight weeks of unilateral open-chain knee-extension training increased quadriceps volume similarly to closed-chain squat training but produced a different, more distal hypertrophy pattern.
studies.citation: Earp JE, Angelino D, Hatfield DL, Colantuono V, Jackson ER, Morgan KD, Adami A, Melanson KJ, Blazevich AJ. Differing hypertrophy patterns from open and closed kinetic chain training affect quadriceps femoris center of mass and moment of inertia. Frontiers in Physiology. 2023;14:1074705. doi:10.3389/fphys.2023.1074705.
studies.relevance: Direct open-chain knee-extension training evidence for quadriceps volume adaptation and regional hypertrophy pattern.

studies.type: Open-chain knee-extension biomechanics study
studies.shortCitation: Escamilla et al., Med Sci Sports Exerc, 1998
studies.finding: Open-chain knee extension produced distinct knee extensor torque, muscle activity, and knee joint force patterns compared with squat and leg press tasks.
studies.citation: Escamilla RF, Fleisig GS, Zheng N, Barrentine SW, Wilk KE, Andrews JR. Biomechanics of the knee during closed kinetic chain and open kinetic chain exercises. Medicine and Science in Sports and Exercise. 1998;30(4):556-569. doi:10.1097/00005768-199804000-00014.
studies.relevance: Biomechanics source for open-chain knee-extension joint loading, rehabilitation/training limits, and joint-resilience scoring.

movements.name: Seated Machine Reverse Fly
movements.variant: Seated reverse pec-deck or rear-delt fly machine with a guided horizontal-abduction path.
movements.description: Sit facing the pad or in the machine's reverse-fly position with the handles near shoulder height and the chest supported if the machine provides a pad. Keep the ribs controlled and elbows softly bent, sweep the arms out and back along the guided path, pause without shrugging, then return until the posterior shoulders are stretched without losing shoulder position.

hypertrophy.rationale: Good posterior-shoulder hypertrophy accessory with direct reverse-fly-machine EMG support, but total load and target area are narrow.

strength.rationale: Builds horizontal-abduction strength in a small range, but it is not a meaningful global strength anchor.

joint_resilience.rationale: Can train controlled posterior-shoulder and scapular tolerance, but machine path and small loads keep resilience impact limited.

athletic_transfer.rationale: Low transfer because the exercise is seated, guided, bilateral, and isolated from whole-body force production.

control.rationale: Requires some scapular and humeral-position awareness, but the machine removes most path and balance demands.

fatigue_efficiency.rationale: Efficient posterior-shoulder stimulus with low systemic fatigue and little unrelated loading when the machine fits well.

setup.rationale: Low friction once the machine is available, with seat height, handle orientation, and start range as the main adjustments.

ease.rationale: Easy to learn because the machine guides the path, though grip and range need adjustment to avoid shrugging or shoulder irritation.

progression.rationale: Machine load and reps are easy to track, with deductions for stack increments, machine geometry, and range-stop differences.

support.rationale: Very high external support from the seat, pads, and guided arms, even though the shoulder still stabilizes the motion.

primary.name: Posterior deltoid
primary.evidenceShort: Direct reverse-fly-machine EMG supports primary posterior deltoid role.
primary.evidence: A direct reverse-fly-machine EMG study measured posterior deltoid activity and found hand position can significantly change posterior deltoid activation, supporting it as the primary target of the machine reverse fly.

support.name: Rotator cuff
support.evidenceShort: Infraspinatus EMG supports shoulder-stabilizing support.
support.evidence: The reverse-fly-machine study directly measured infraspinatus and found greater activity with a neutral hand position, supporting rotator cuff involvement as glenohumeral support rather than the main visible target.

support.name: Trapezius (middle and lower fibers)
support.evidenceShort: Scapular-retraction and horizontal-abduction evidence supports support role.
support.evidence: Scapular-retraction EMG and prone horizontal-abduction evidence show meaningful middle and lower trapezius involvement when the shoulders abduct or retract. In the guided reverse fly, these fibers are classified as scapular support.

evidence.verdict: Seated machine reverse fly: posterior deltoid primary; rotator cuff and middle/lower trapezius support.
evidence.clinicalShort: EMG estimates acute excitation, not hypertrophy, mechanical tension, adaptation, pain, or injury risk.
evidence.limitsShort: Handle orientation, seat height, chest-pad support, start range, elbow bend, load, shrugging, and machine arm path can shift posterior deltoid, infraspinatus, and trapezius contribution.
evidence.summary: The seated machine reverse fly is classified as a guided horizontal-abduction accessory. Direct reverse-fly-machine EMG supports posterior deltoid as the primary target and infraspinatus, represented by the local rotator cuff entry, as shoulder support. Middle/lower trapezius are included as support from scapular-retraction and prone horizontal-abduction evidence rather than as the main target.
evidence.clinicalInterpretation: The exact reverse-fly-machine evidence studied hand position in trained men and measured posterior deltoid, middle deltoid, and infraspinatus, not every commercial machine path or all scapular muscles. EMG should not be read as direct long-term hypertrophy or injury-risk evidence.
evidence.limitations: Rhomboids were not added because the best exact machine evidence did not isolate them and the concise visible classification is clearer without extrapolating every scapular retractor. A bent-over dumbbell reverse fly should be treated as a separate variant because the trunk and free-weight stability demands differ.

studies.type: Reverse-fly-machine hand-position EMG study
studies.finding: Neutral hand position on the reverse fly machine significantly increased posterior deltoid and infraspinatus mean EMG activity compared with pronated hand position.
studies.citation: Schoenfeld B, Sonmez RGT, Kolber MJ, Contreras B, Harris R, Ozen S. Effect of hand position on EMG activity of the posterior shoulder musculature during a horizontal abduction exercise. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2013;27(10):2644-2649. doi:10.1519/JSC.0b013e318281e1e9.
studies.relevance: Directly studied the reverse fly machine in resistance-trained men and measured posterior deltoid, middle deltoid, and infraspinatus.

studies.type: Scapular-retraction trapezius EMG study
studies.shortCitation: Kara et al., J Athl Train, 2021
studies.finding: Scapular retraction at different shoulder-abduction angles produced meaningful upper, middle, and lower trapezius activity, with 90 degrees activating all trapezius parts.
studies.citation: Kara D, Harput G, Duzgun I. Shoulder-Abduction Angle and Trapezius Muscle Activity During Scapular-Retraction Exercise. Journal of Athletic Training. 2021;56(12):1327-1333. doi:10.4085/1062-6050-0053.21.
studies.relevance: Close scapular-retraction evidence for middle and lower trapezius support during horizontal-abduction style shoulder work.

studies.type: Trapezius and serratus anterior exercise EMG study
studies.finding: Shoulder horizontal extension with external rotation and prone arm raises produced high middle or lower trapezius EMG activity.
studies.citation: Ekstrom RA, Donatelli RA, Soderberg GL. Surface electromyographic analysis of exercises for the trapezius and serratus anterior muscles. Journal of Orthopaedic and Sports Physical Therapy. 2003;33(5):247-258. doi:10.2519/jospt.2003.33.5.247.
studies.relevance: Close shoulder horizontal-abduction and scapular-control evidence for middle and lower trapezius support.

movements.name: Seated Machine Shoulder Press
movements.variant: Seated guided machine shoulder press from shoulder height to overhead, usually with neutral or semi-neutral handles in front of the body.
movements.description: Sit with the back against the pad, feet flat, and the seat adjusted so the handles start near shoulder height. Brace lightly, keep the ribs down and shoulders controlled, press the handles overhead along the guided path until the elbows are nearly straight, then lower under control until the shoulders are loaded without forcing an uncomfortable bottom range.

hypertrophy.rationale: Strong shoulder and triceps hypertrophy option because machine evidence supports deltoid and triceps excitation while the guided path reduces coordination cost.

strength.rationale: Builds vertical pressing force in a repeatable path, but fixed machine mechanics transfer less cleanly to free-weight or sport strength expression.

joint_resilience.rationale: Can provide controlled overhead exposure, but the fixed path and user-specific shoulder mobility make it a limited general joint-resilience tool.

athletic_transfer.rationale: Very low transfer because the lift is seated, bilateral, back-supported, and externally guided.

control.rationale: Low motor-control demand because the machine constrains the path and removes most balance and free-load stabilization.

fatigue_efficiency.rationale: Good local shoulder and triceps stimulus with low systemic fatigue, though overhead joint tolerance and triceps fatigue can still limit volume.

setup.rationale: Low-friction once the machine is available, with only seat, handle, and stack adjustments.

ease.rationale: Easy to learn and repeat because the path, seat, and back pad constrain most of the movement.

progression.rationale: Machine load and reps are simple to record, with deductions for stack jumps and machine-specific lever paths.

support.rationale: Very high external support from the seat, back pad, handles, and guided overhead path.

primary.name: Anterior deltoid
primary.evidenceShort: Direct machine shoulder-press EMG supports major deltoid involvement.
primary.evidence: Front machine shoulder press EMG directly measured anterior deltoid activity, and close Smith-machine shoulder press evidence also found high anterior deltoid activation. Medial deltoid is important in the literature but is not available as a local visible anatomy entry in this dataset.

secondary.name: Triceps brachii
secondary.evidenceShort: Measured elbow-extension contributor in shoulder-press EMG.
secondary.evidence: Front machine shoulder press and seated/standing shoulder press studies measured triceps brachii activity during overhead pressing. It is classified as secondary because it extends the elbows while the movement is primarily selected for shoulder pressing.

secondary.name: Pectoralis major
secondary.evidenceShort: Front machine press evidence shows initial-phase assistance.
secondary.evidence: Front machine shoulder press EMG measured pectoralis major and found greater excitation in front-machine pressing than behind-neck machine pressing. It is included as a secondary assistant because front overhead press mechanics can involve the clavicular pectoralis major, especially near the start.

support.name: Serratus anterior
support.evidenceShort: Overhead-press and shoulder-elevation evidence supports scapular upward-rotation support.
support.evidence: Military-press EMG reports serratus anterior involvement, and shoulder-elevation review evidence identifies serratus anterior as a key scapular upward-rotation and stabilization muscle. In this seated machine variant it is classified as support because the machine guides the press path.

support.name: Rotator cuff
support.evidenceShort: Biomechanical inference for glenohumeral stabilization during overhead elevation.
support.evidence: This support role is an explicit biomechanics inference: shoulder exercise review evidence describes the rotator cuff as stabilizing the glenohumeral joint and controlling humeral head translation during elevation. Direct seated machine shoulder press rotator-cuff EMG was not found.

evidence.verdict: Seated machine shoulder press: anterior deltoid primary; triceps brachii and pectoralis major secondary; serratus anterior and rotator cuff support.
evidence.clinicalShort: EMG estimates acute excitation, not hypertrophy, mechanical tension, adaptation, pain, or injury risk.
evidence.limitsShort: Machine path, front versus behind-neck setup, grip, seat height, back pad angle, load, range of motion, and shoulder mobility can shift emphasis.
evidence.summary: The seated machine shoulder press is classified as a guided vertical pressing exercise. Direct front machine shoulder press evidence supports anterior deltoid, triceps brachii, and pectoralis major involvement. Serratus anterior is included as scapular support from military-press and shoulder-elevation evidence, while rotator cuff support is an explicit biomechanics inference. Medial deltoid and upper trapezius are important in the literature but are not separate visible anatomy entries in this dataset, so they are documented here rather than added as unmapped roles.
evidence.clinicalInterpretation: Surface electromyography is useful for estimating acute muscle excitation under a specific machine path, load, grip, and range of motion. It should not be interpreted as a direct measure of hypertrophy, mechanical tension, long-term adaptation, pain risk, or injury risk.
evidence.limitations: Direct machine data come from competitive bodybuilders using a specific Technogym shoulder press, and the front-machine condition used a forward neutral grip. Close evidence includes seated and standing barbell or dumbbell shoulder presses and Smith-machine shoulder press. Commercial shoulder-press machines vary in seat angle, lever path, grip orientation, converging path, starting depth, and whether the handles travel in front of or beside the head.

studies.type: Direct front/back barbell and machine overhead press EMG
studies.finding: Front and back machine shoulder press variants were compared with barbell military press; anterior, medial, and posterior deltoid, upper trapezius, pectoralis major, and triceps brachii were measured.
studies.citation: Coratella G, Tornatore G, Longo S, Esposito F, Ce E. Front vs Back and Barbell vs Machine Overhead Press: An Electromyographic Analysis and Implications For Resistance Training. Frontiers in Physiology. 2022;13:825880. doi:10.3389/fphys.2022.825880.
studies.relevance: Most direct source for the front machine shoulder press variant, including measured anterior deltoid, pectoralis major, and triceps brachii activity plus machine-vs-barbell stability implications.

studies.type: Seated and standing shoulder press EMG and 1RM comparison
studies.finding: Compared seated and standing barbell and dumbbell shoulder presses and measured anterior, medial, and posterior deltoids plus biceps and triceps brachii.
studies.citation: Saeterbakken AH, Fimland MS. Effects of Body Position and Loading Modality on Muscle Activity and Strength in Shoulder Presses. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2013;27(7):1824-1831. doi:10.1519/JSC.0b013e318276b873.
studies.relevance: Close seated shoulder-press evidence for deltoid and triceps roles and for stability, support, and progression ratings.

studies.type: Close Smith-machine shoulder press deltoid EMG
studies.finding: Smith-machine shoulder press produced high anterior deltoid activation compared with several other shoulder or chest exercises.
studies.citation: Botton CE, Wilhelm EN, Ughini CC, Pinto RS, Lima CS. Electromyographical analysis of the deltoid between different strength training exercises. Medicina Sportiva. 2013;17(2):67-71. doi:10.5604/17342260.1055261.
studies.relevance: Close guided shoulder press evidence for anterior deltoid activation; less direct because it used Smith-machine pressing rather than a seated lever shoulder press.

studies.type: Military press serratus and trapezius EMG
studies.shortCitation: Bull et al., Electromyogr Clin Neurophysiol, 2001
studies.finding: Military press variants with open and middle grip showed high to very high trapezius and serratus anterior activity.
