studies.citation: Bull ML, Vitti M, Freitas V, Rosa GJ. Electromyographic validation of the trapezius and serratus anterior muscles in military press exercises with open and middle grip. Electromyography and Clinical Neurophysiology. 2001;41(4):203-207. PMID:11441637.
studies.relevance: Direct military-press evidence for serratus anterior involvement; used only for scapular support context because the entry is a seated machine press.

studies.type: Shoulder muscle activity and function review
studies.finding: Review describes rotator cuff stabilization of the glenohumeral joint and serratus anterior contribution to scapular upward rotation, posterior tilt, and stabilization.
studies.citation: Escamilla RF, Yamashiro K, Paulos L, Andrews JR. Shoulder muscle activity and function in common shoulder rehabilitation exercises. Sports Medicine. 2009;39(8):663-685. doi:10.2165/00007256-200939080-00004.
studies.relevance: Biomechanics and EMG review evidence for glenohumeral and scapulothoracic support roles during shoulder elevation.

movements.name: Side Plank
movements.variant: Standard forearm side plank from the feet with the body held in a straight lateral line.
movements.description: Lie on one side with the elbow under the shoulder, stack or stagger the feet, lift the hips into a straight line, brace the trunk without rotating forward or back, then hold before lowering under control.

hypertrophy.rationale: Can provide meaningful oblique and gluteus medius tension, but isometric bodyweight loading limits hypertrophy progression.

strength.rationale: Good lateral trunk and hip endurance-strength signal, but it is not a heavy progressive strength movement.

joint_resilience.rationale: Useful for shoulder support tolerance, lateral trunk endurance, and pelvic control when scaled well.

athletic_transfer.rationale: Lateral trunk and hip control can transfer to running and cutting mechanics, but the base version is static and floor-supported.

control.rationale: High control demand from resisting lateral flexion, pelvic drop, trunk rotation, and shoulder collapse.

fatigue_efficiency.rationale: Focused trunk and hip stimulus with low systemic fatigue, though shoulder pressure can become the limiter.

setup.rationale: Requires only floor space and no equipment.

ease.rationale: Easy to understand, but harder to repeat cleanly because the shoulder, pelvis, and trunk can compensate in several directions.

progression.rationale: Progression is mainly by time, lever length, leg lift, or load placement, so it is less precise than cable or machine work.

support.rationale: Very little external support beyond the elbow and foot contacts; the trunk and hip create most of the stability.

primary.name: External oblique
primary.evidenceShort: Side-bridge EMG strongly supports external-oblique loading.
primary.evidence: Side-bridge and lateral-plank EMG studies report high external oblique activation, with side-bridge evidence meeting strengthening thresholds in healthy adults.

primary.name: Internal oblique
primary.evidenceShort: Lateral-plank EMG supports high internal-oblique activation.
primary.evidence: Lateral-plank and side-bridge EMG studies measured internal oblique activity and support it as a primary lateral-trunk target.

secondary.name: Gluteus medius
secondary.evidenceShort: Side-bridge EMG shows high gluteus medius activation.
secondary.evidence: Side-bridge EMG studies measured gluteus medius activation above strengthening thresholds on the weightbearing side, supporting a meaningful pelvic-control role.

secondary.name: Rectus abdominis
secondary.evidenceShort: Side-bridge studies measure rectus activity as a trunk stabilizer.
secondary.evidence: Side-bridge EMG measured rectus abdominis activity, but it is secondary because the lateral plank primarily challenges the obliques and lateral hip rather than sagittal trunk flexion.

support.name: Erector spinae
support.evidenceShort: Side-bridge studies measured spinal extensor stabilization.
support.evidence: Side-bridge EMG measured longissimus thoracis activity along with other spinal stabilizers; the longissimus component supports erector spinae as a visible spinal-extensor stabilizer role.

evidence.verdict: Side plank: external and internal oblique primary; gluteus medius and rectus abdominis secondary; erector spinae support.
evidence.clinicalShort: EMG estimates acute excitation; it does not prove hypertrophy, adaptation, pain response, or injury prevention.
evidence.limitsShort: Knee-supported regressions, foot position, top-leg lift, rotation, shoulder symptoms, and hold duration change the stimulus.
evidence.summary: The side plank is classified as a lateral trunk anti-flexion hold. Direct side-bridge and lateral-plank EMG supports high oblique demand and meaningful gluteus medius contribution on the support side.
evidence.clinicalInterpretation: It is best used for lateral trunk endurance, pelvic control, and shoulder-supported bracing rather than heavy abdominal hypertrophy.
evidence.limitations: Quadratus lumborum is biomechanically relevant to side-bridge tasks but was not added as a visible role because it has no local anatomy mesh mapping in this repo. The side plank from knees, star plank, Copenhagen plank, and rotational side plank should be separate variants.

studies.type: Side-bridge trunk and hip EMG
studies.finding: Side-bridge variations produced greater ipsilateral weightbearing-side recruitment; gluteus medius and external oblique met strengthening-threshold criteria.
studies.citation: Youdas JW, Boor MMP, Darfler AL, Koenig MK, Mills KM, Hollman JH. Surface electromyographic analysis of core trunk and hip muscles during selected rehabilitation exercises in the side-bridge to neutral spine position. Sports Health. 2014;6(5):416-421. doi:10.1177/1941738114539266.
studies.relevance: Direct side-bridge source for external oblique, gluteus medius, rectus abdominis, and spinal-extensor support roles.

studies.type: Core rehabilitation exercise EMG
studies.finding: Side-bridge exercise could be used for strengthening gluteus medius and external oblique muscles.
studies.citation: Ekstrom RA, Donatelli RA, Carp KC. Electromyographic analysis of core trunk, hip, and thigh muscles during 9 rehabilitation exercises. Journal of Orthopaedic and Sports Physical Therapy. 2007;37(12):754-762. doi:10.2519/jospt.2007.2471.
studies.relevance: Direct side-bridge comparison source for external oblique, gluteus medius, and stabilizer interpretation.

studies.type: Lateral trunk isometric EMG
studies.shortCitation: Kinney et al., J Sport Rehabil, 2020
studies.finding: The lateral plank activated internal oblique at 107% MVC and external oblique at 72% MVC in a comparison of lateral-trunk tasks.
studies.citation: Kinney AL, Giel M, Harre B, Heffner K, McCullough T, Savino M, Scott A, Barrios JA. Surface electromyography of the internal and external oblique muscles during isometric tasks targeting the lateral trunk. Journal of Sport Rehabilitation. 2020;30(2):255-260. doi:10.1123/jsr.2018-0442.
studies.relevance: Direct lateral-plank oblique EMG source for internal and external oblique primary roles.

studies.type: Side bridge and abdominal exercise EMG
studies.finding: Compared side bridge with other abdominal exercises using rectus abdominis, external oblique, internal oblique, and rectus femoris EMG.
studies.citation: Youdas JW, Guck BR, Hebrink RC, Rugotzke JD, Madson TJ, Hollman JH. An electromyographic analysis of the Ab-Slide exercise, abdominal crunch, supine double leg thrust, and side bridge in healthy young adults: implications for rehabilitation professionals. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2008;22(6):1939-1946. doi:10.1519/JSC.0b013e31818745bf.
studies.relevance: Direct side-bridge source including internal oblique and rectus abdominis activation.

movements.name: Standing Barbell Overhead Press
movements.variant: Standing free-weight barbell overhead press from shoulder or clavicle height, performed as a strict press without leg drive.
movements.description: Stand with the bar at the front of the shoulders or upper chest, hands just outside shoulder width, wrists stacked over the elbows, and ribs braced over the pelvis; press the bar up while moving the head back just enough for a close bar path, finish with the bar over the shoulder joints and elbows extended, then lower under control to the starting position without using the legs.

hypertrophy.rationale: Useful shoulder and triceps hypertrophy stimulus, but balance, bracing, and fatigue can limit targeted local loading.

strength.rationale: Strong vertical pressing strength anchor with clear barbell loading and high force demand.

joint_resilience.rationale: Can build shoulder and trunk tolerance when well dosed, but overhead mobility and irritation risk make it less universally resilience-positive.

athletic_transfer.rationale: Meaningful transfer from standing force production, trunk bracing, and overhead control, though it remains bilateral and stationary.

control.rationale: High control demand from overhead bar path, bracing, rib/pelvis position, shoulder rotation, and balance.

fatigue_efficiency.rationale: Low-to-moderate efficiency because systemic bracing, shoulder fatigue, and technical failure can accumulate before target stimulus is maximized.

setup.rationale: Requires barbell setup, rack height or clean-to-start, plates, and enough overhead space.

ease.rationale: Technically demanding because mobility, bar path, bracing, head position, and overhead lockout must be coordinated.

progression.rationale: Barbell loading is measurable, but small jumps, technical sensitivity, and overhead fatigue make progression less smooth than bench or machines.

support.rationale: Very little external support; the user stabilizes the load while standing under a free bar path.

primary.name: Anterior deltoid
primary.evidenceShort: Direct shoulder-press EMG supports major deltoid involvement.
primary.evidence: Standing barbell shoulder press EMG directly measures anterior deltoid activity, and front barbell military press EMG supports anterior deltoid involvement in the close overhead-press family. Medial deltoid is also important in the literature, but it is not available as a visible shared anatomy entry in this dataset.

secondary.name: Triceps brachii
secondary.evidenceShort: Elbow-extension contributor in direct shoulder-press EMG.
secondary.evidence: The triceps brachii is directly measured during standing and seated barbell shoulder press variants and contributes to the elbow-extension component of the overhead press.

secondary.name: Pectoralis major
secondary.evidenceShort: Clavicular pec assists the front overhead press.
secondary.evidence: Front barbell military press EMG shows greater pectoralis major excitation than behind-the-neck pressing, and overhead-press mechanics describe the clavicular pectoralis major as assisting the initial shoulder-flexion phase. It is classified as secondary, not the intended target.

support.name: Serratus anterior
support.evidenceShort: Scapular upward-rotation support during overhead pressing.
support.evidence: Military-press EMG reports high serratus anterior involvement, and overhead-press/shoulder-elevation literature supports serratus anterior as a scapular upward-rotation and stabilization muscle rather than a primary pressing target.

support.name: Rotator cuff
support.evidenceShort: Biomechanical inference for glenohumeral stabilization.
support.evidence: This support role is an explicit biomechanics inference: shoulder exercise review evidence describes the rotator cuff as stabilizing the glenohumeral joint and controlling humeral head translation during elevation, which is required in an unsupported overhead press.

evidence.verdict: Standing strict barbell overhead press: anterior deltoid primary; triceps brachii and pectoralis major secondary; serratus anterior and rotator cuff support.
evidence.clinicalShort: EMG estimates acute excitation, not hypertrophy, mechanical tension, adaptation, or injury risk.
evidence.limitsShort: Direct exact evidence is limited; stance, grip, bar path, back support, load, range of motion, and press-from-front vs behind-neck variations change emphasis.
evidence.summary: The standing barbell overhead press is classified as an unsupported free-weight vertical pressing exercise. Direct standing shoulder-press EMG supports deltoid and triceps involvement, while front barbell military press evidence supports a meaningful clavicular pectoralis major contribution. Serratus anterior is included as scapular support from military-press and overhead-press evidence. Rotator cuff inclusion is an explicit biomechanics inference from shoulder-elevation stability literature, not a direct standing barbell overhead-press EMG measurement.
evidence.clinicalInterpretation: Surface electromyography is useful for estimating acute muscle excitation under a specific exercise setup. It should not be interpreted as a direct measure of hypertrophy, mechanical tension, long-term adaptation, or injury risk.
evidence.limitations: The best exact study for this entry measured standing and seated shoulder presses with barbells and dumbbells, but it did not measure pectoralis major, serratus anterior, trapezius, or rotator cuff. Some supporting evidence uses seated front barbell military press, light military-press variants, seated dumbbell/kettlebell overhead press, or general shoulder-elevation review evidence. Medial deltoid and upper trapezius are important in the literature but are not visible anatomy entries in this dataset.

studies.type: Standing and seated shoulder press EMG and 1RM comparison
studies.finding: Compared seated and standing barbell and dumbbell shoulder presses and measured anterior, medial, and posterior deltoids plus biceps and triceps brachii.
studies.citation: Saeterbakken AH, Fimland MS. Effects of Body Position and Loading Modality on Muscle Activity and Strength in Shoulder Presses. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2013;27(7):1824-1831. doi:10.1519/JSC.0b013e318276b873.
studies.relevance: Most direct evidence for the requested standing barbell shoulder press variant; supports anterior deltoid and triceps roles and informs stability/progression scoring.

studies.type: Front/back barbell and machine overhead press EMG
studies.finding: Front barbell military press from the upper chest measured anterior, medial, and posterior deltoid, upper trapezius, pectoralis major, and triceps brachii.
studies.citation: Coratella G, Tornatore G, Longo S, Esposito F, Ce E. Front vs Back and Barbell vs Machine Overhead Press: An Electromyographic Analysis and Implications For Resistance Training. Frontiers in Physiology. 2022;13:825880. doi:10.3389/fphys.2022.825880.
studies.relevance: Close barbell military press evidence from shoulder/chest height; useful for anterior deltoid, triceps, pectoralis major, barbell-vs-machine, and front-vs-behind-neck interpretation.

studies.type: Military press serratus and trapezius EMG
studies.shortCitation: Bull et al., Electromyogr Clin Neurophysiol, 2001
studies.finding: Military press variants with open and middle grip showed high to very high trapezius and serratus anterior activity.
studies.citation: Bull ML, Vitti M, Freitas V, Rosa GJ. Electromyographic validation of the trapezius and serratus anterior muscles in military press exercises with open and middle grip. Electromyography and Clinical Neurophysiology. 2001;41(4):203-207. PMID:11441637.
studies.relevance: Direct military-press evidence for serratus anterior involvement, though the reported variants and loading differ from a modern loaded strict standing barbell press.

studies.type: Overhead press shoulder and back EMG
studies.finding: Seated one-arm dumbbell and kettlebell overhead press measured anterior deltoid, posterior deltoid, trapezius, serratus anterior, and spinal erectors.
studies.citation: Blazkiewicz M, Hadamus A. The Effect of the Weight and Type of Equipment on Shoulder and Back Muscle Activity in Surface Electromyography during the Overhead Press-Preliminary Report. Sensors. 2022;22(24):9762. doi:10.3390/s22249762.
studies.relevance: Close overhead-press evidence supporting serratus anterior and shoulder-girdle support demands; less direct because it used seated unilateral dumbbell/kettlebell pressing rather than standing barbell pressing.

studies.type: Shoulder muscle activity and function review
studies.finding: Review describes rotator cuff functions in shoulder exercise and serratus anterior contribution to scapular upward rotation, posterior tilt, and stabilization.
studies.citation: Escamilla RF, Yamashiro K, Paulos L, Andrews JR. Shoulder muscle activity and function in common shoulder rehabilitation exercises. Sports Medicine. 2009;39(8):663-685. doi:10.2165/00007256-200939080-00004.
studies.relevance: Biomechanics and EMG review evidence for glenohumeral and scapulothoracic support roles during arm elevation; used as inference support rather than exact standing barbell press evidence.

studies.type: Weightlifting overhead pressing derivatives review
studies.finding: Review characterizes the standing press as a complex multi-joint movement using upper-body muscles while the trunk and lower body provide stability.
studies.citation: Soriano MA, Suchomel TJ, Comfort P. Weightlifting Overhead Pressing Derivatives: A Review of the Literature. Sports Medicine. 2019;49:867-885. doi:10.1007/s40279-019-01096-8.
studies.relevance: Supports rating judgments around coordination, balance, setup, progression, and limitations for standing overhead pressing derivatives.

movements.name: Standing Calf Raise
movements.variant: Standing heel raise or plantar-flexion pattern with the knees mostly extended; not the guided standing calf-raise machine.
movements.description: Stand tall with the balls of the feet on the floor or a small edge, keep the knees mostly straight without locking them, rise onto the toes as high as controlled, pause briefly, then lower slowly until the calves are stretched before the next rep.

hypertrophy.rationale: Good direct calf stimulus, especially for gastrocnemius in the standing knee-extended position, but load can be limited without machine or external weight.

strength.rationale: Builds plantar-flexion force, but the bodyweight version is not a high-force global strength anchor.

joint_resilience.rationale: Useful ankle and Achilles tendon exposure when loaded through controlled range, but narrower than full lower-body resilience movements.

athletic_transfer.rationale: The ankle action is relevant to gait and jumping, but the slow bilateral standing raise has low coordination and sport-transfer breadth.

control.rationale: Low motor-control demand unless performed single-leg or without hand support.

fatigue_efficiency.rationale: High local calf stimulus with low systemic fatigue and low unrelated recovery cost.

setup.rationale: Very low setup friction because it requires only standing space, optionally an edge or stable support.

ease.rationale: Simple movement pattern with low skill demand, limited mainly by range control and avoiding bouncing.

progression.rationale: Reps are easy to progress, but load progression is limited unless external weight or a machine is introduced.

support.rationale: External support is optional and minimal; the user usually controls balance and ankle path.

primary.name: Gastrocnemius
primary.evidenceShort: Standing calf-raise training preferentially grows gastrocnemius.
primary.evidence: Standing calf-raise training evidence supports greater gastrocnemius hypertrophy than seated calf raises, consistent with the knee-extended plantar-flexion role.

secondary.name: Soleus
secondary.evidenceShort: Soleus contributes to plantar flexion but is less standing-biased than gastrocnemius.
secondary.evidence: Plantar-flexor activation evidence supports soleus contribution during calf-raise tasks, but the standing knee-extended setup is classified here as gastrocnemius-biased.

evidence.verdict: Standing calf raise: gastrocnemius primary; soleus secondary; no separate visible support muscles listed.
evidence.clinicalShort: EMG and hypertrophy studies answer different questions; neither directly determines long-term programming by itself.
evidence.limitsShort: Knee angle, single-leg versus double-leg execution, heel deficit, tempo, external load, and machine support change emphasis.
evidence.summary: The standing calf raise is classified as a simple plantar-flexion exercise. The knee-extended standing position supports a gastrocnemius-biased classification with soleus as a meaningful secondary plantar flexor.
evidence.clinicalInterpretation: Muscle activation and hypertrophy evidence should be interpreted with setup details, especially knee angle and loading method.
evidence.limitations: This entry is not the standing calf-raise machine. A guided machine version would score higher for progression and support and should be a separate movement.

studies.type: Standing versus seated calf-raise hypertrophy study
studies.finding: Triceps surae hypertrophy was greater after standing versus seated calf-raise training.
studies.citation: Nunes JP, et al. Triceps surae muscle hypertrophy is greater after standing versus seated calf-raise training. Frontiers in Physiology. 2023;14:1272106. doi:10.3389/fphys.2023.1272106.
studies.relevance: Direct standing/seated calf-raise training comparison for calf muscle emphasis.

studies.type: Plantar-flexor activation comparison
studies.finding: Multi- and single-joint resistance exercises promoted similar plantar-flexor activation in resistance-trained men.
studies.citation: Multi- and Single-Joint Resistance Exercises Promote Similar Plantar Flexor Activation in Resistance Trained Men. International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. 2020;17(24):9487. doi:10.3390/ijerph17249487.
studies.relevance: Supports gastrocnemius and soleus activation in plantar-flexor resistance exercise.

studies.type: Triceps surae fMRI and EMG
studies.finding: Combined functional MRI and EMG characterized neuromuscular activation of the triceps surae.
studies.citation: Kinugasa R, Kawakami Y, Fukunaga T. Neuromuscular activation of triceps surae using muscle functional MRI and EMG. Medicine and Science in Sports and Exercise. 2005;37(4):593-598. doi:10.1249/01.mss.0000159026.99792.76.
studies.relevance: Supports treating gastrocnemius and soleus as triceps-surae contributors rather than one generic calf label.

movements.name: Straight-Arm Cable Pulldown
movements.variant: Standing straight-arm pulldown from a high cable, using a bar or rope and keeping the elbows nearly fixed while pulling toward the thighs.
movements.description: Stand facing a high cable with the arms reaching forward and up, ribs and pelvis controlled, and elbows slightly bent but nearly fixed. Pull the handle down in an arc toward the thighs by driving the upper arms down, pause without bending the elbows into a row or triceps pressdown, then return overhead under control.

hypertrophy.rationale: Good lat-focused hypertrophy accessory with direct straight-arm pulldown EMG support, but total loading is lower than rows and pulldowns.

strength.rationale: Builds shoulder-extension strength in a narrow pattern, but the standing cable setup and limited load make it a weak global strength anchor.

joint_resilience.rationale: Can provide controlled overhead-to-extension shoulder exposure, but it is not a broad shoulder or spine resilience movement.

athletic_transfer.rationale: Some carryover to straight-arm pulling and swimming-like shoulder extension, but the cable path and low whole-body demand keep transfer modest.

control.rationale: Requires rib control, scapular timing, and keeping elbow angle consistent, but balance and coordination demands are moderate-low.

fatigue_efficiency.rationale: Efficient local lat stimulus with low systemic cost and less elbow-flexor fatigue than rows or pulldowns.

setup.rationale: Cable station setup is straightforward, with deductions for attachment choice, pulley height, stack increments, and station availability.

ease.rationale: Approachable accessory pattern, though users often turn it into a pressdown, row, or torso swing if the load is too heavy.

progression.rationale: Cable stack load and reps are easy to record, with minor deductions for pulley friction and attachment differences.

support.rationale: The cable path is stable and externally loaded, but the lifter stands unsupported and must control torso and shoulder position.

primary.name: Latissimus dorsi
primary.evidenceShort: Direct straight-arm pulldown EMG supports primary lat role.
primary.evidence: A direct pullover versus straight-arm pulldown EMG study found the straight-arm pulldown produced the highest latissimus dorsi activity among the tested muscles and grip widths, supporting latissimus dorsi as the primary visible target.

secondary.name: Teres major
secondary.evidenceShort: Shoulder-extension helper inferred from pulldown-family evidence.
secondary.evidence: This role is marked as inference: teres major is a close latissimus dorsi synergist for shoulder extension and adduction, and direct lat-pulldown EMG measured teres major as a back-muscle contributor during related pulldown tasks.

secondary.name: Triceps brachii
secondary.evidenceShort: Direct straight-arm pulldown EMG shows meaningful triceps activity.
secondary.evidence: The straight-arm pulldown EMG study found triceps brachii activity was higher in the straight-arm pulldown than the barbell pullover conditions, consistent with the long head assisting shoulder extension and the triceps maintaining elbow position.

support.name: Trapezius (middle and lower fibers)
support.evidenceShort: Pulldown angle evidence supports scapular-control demand.
support.evidence: Isometric pulldown evidence showed angle-dependent lower trapezius activity as shoulder elevation changed. During straight-arm pulldowns, the middle and lower trapezius are best classified as scapular support rather than the main lat target.

evidence.verdict: Straight-arm cable pulldown: latissimus dorsi primary; teres major and triceps brachii secondary; middle/lower trapezius support.
evidence.clinicalShort: EMG estimates acute excitation, not hypertrophy, mechanical tension, adaptation, or injury risk.
evidence.limitsShort: Pulley height, handle width, torso lean, shoulder flexion range, elbow bend, load, and whether the user rows or pressdowns the cable can change the movement.
evidence.summary: The straight-arm cable pulldown is classified as a standing cable shoulder-extension accessory. Direct EMG supports latissimus dorsi as the primary target and triceps brachii as a meaningful secondary contributor. Teres major is included as a secondary role by explicit inference from related pulldown evidence and shoulder-extension mechanics. Middle/lower trapezius are included as scapular support from pulldown-angle evidence.
evidence.clinicalInterpretation: The strongest exact evidence compares straight-arm pulldowns with pullovers using relatively light loading and specific handle widths. EMG should not be treated as a direct measure of hypertrophy or long-term joint adaptation.
evidence.limitations: Direct evidence did not isolate teres major or all scapular stabilizers during the exact straight-arm cable movement. Elbow flexion changes the exercise toward a cable pulldown or row and should be treated as a different variant.

studies.type: Straight-arm pulldown and pullover EMG study
studies.finding: Straight-arm pulldown at 100% and 150% biacromial widths produced higher latissimus dorsi and triceps brachii activity than barbell pullover conditions.
studies.citation: Muyor JM, Lopez-Minarro PA, Alacid F. Comparison of Electromyographic Activity during Barbell Pullover and Straight Arm Pulldown Exercises. Applied Sciences. 2022;12(21):11138. doi:10.3390/app122111138.
studies.relevance: Direct straight-arm pulldown EMG measuring pectoralis major regions, latissimus dorsi, anterior deltoid, triceps brachii, and rectus abdominis in healthy active adults.

studies.type: Isometric pulldown latissimus and lower trapezius EMG
studies.shortCitation: Park and Yoo, J Electromyogr Kinesiol, 2013
studies.finding: Latissimus dorsi and inferior trapezius activity changed by shoulder angle during isometric pulldown exertions.
studies.citation: Park SY, Yoo WG. Selective activation of the latissimus dorsi and the inferior fibers of trapezius at various shoulder angles during isometric pull-down exertion. Journal of Electromyography and Kinesiology. 2013;23(6):1350-1355. doi:10.1016/j.jelekin.2013.08.006.
studies.relevance: Pulldown-family EMG supporting latissimus dorsi targeting and lower trapezius support across shoulder angles.

studies.type: Lat pulldown hand-position EMG
studies.finding: Lat pulldown hand positions changed latissimus dorsi, teres major, posterior deltoid, pectoralis major, and triceps activity.
studies.citation: Signorile JF, Zink AJ, Szwed SP. A comparative electromyographical investigation of muscle utilization patterns using various hand positions during the lat pull-down. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2002;16(4):539-546. doi:10.1519/1533-4287(2002)016<0539:ACEIOM>2.0.CO;2.
studies.relevance: Related pulldown-family EMG source that directly measured teres major.

studies.type: Lat pulldown instruction EMG
studies.finding: Expert instruction could increase latissimus dorsi and teres major activity during the front wide-grip lat pulldown.
studies.citation: Snyder BJ, Leech JR. Voluntary increase in latissimus dorsi muscle activity during the lat pull-down following expert instruction. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2009;23(8):2204-2209. doi:10.1519/JSC.0b013e3181bb7213.
studies.relevance: Related pulldown-family evidence for teres major as a back-muscle contributor.

movements.name: T-Bar Row
movements.variant: Standing landmine or T-bar row with one end of a bar anchored, a close neutral handle, and no chest pad support.
movements.description: Stand over the bar with the far end anchored, hinge at the hips, brace the trunk, and hold the close handle with the arms long. Pull the handle toward the lower chest or upper abdomen by driving the elbows back, keep the torso angle steady, then lower the bar under control without letting the plates pull the shoulders or spine out of position.

hypertrophy.rationale: Strong back and upper-back hypertrophy stimulus with high loading potential, but unsupported trunk and grip fatigue can leak effort from the target muscles.

strength.rationale: Good heavy horizontal-pull strength builder because the anchored bar is stable and loadable, though torso angle and hip drive can blur force expression.

joint_resilience.rationale: Provides useful shoulder, elbow, and trunk loading tolerance, but heavy hinge demands and grip loading limit its resilience-specific value.

athletic_transfer.rationale: The standing hinge and heavy bilateral pull carry more whole-body transfer than seated rows, but the path is still constrained by the landmine arc.

control.rationale: Requires hip-hinge position, trunk bracing, scapular timing, and elbow-path control under load.

fatigue_efficiency.rationale: High stimulus is possible, but axial, grip, and trunk fatigue can accumulate quickly compared with chest-supported rows.

setup.rationale: Requires a bar, plates, landmine or secure anchor, and a close handle, with loading and stance setup taking time.

ease.rationale: The pull path is intuitive, but maintaining a stable hinge and avoiding body English under heavy load require practice.

progression.rationale: Bar and plate loading make progression straightforward, with deductions for plate diameter, landmine geometry, and torso-angle variability.

support.rationale: The bar end is anchored, but the torso is unsupported and the lifter must stabilize the hinge, shoulders, elbows, and grip.

primary.name: Latissimus dorsi
primary.evidenceShort: Row-family EMG supports lat emphasis with close neutral row paths.
primary.evidence: Seated and prone row studies show latissimus dorsi is strongly involved in row patterns, especially when the shoulder-abduction angle is low. The close neutral T-bar path usually tracks the elbows near the torso, supporting latissimus dorsi as the primary visible target.

secondary.name: Teres major
secondary.evidenceShort: Measured row-family shoulder-extension assistant.
secondary.evidence: Teres major was measured during seated row EMG and assists the shoulder-extension and adduction pattern also used in the close-grip T-bar row.

secondary.name: Middle trapezius
secondary.evidenceShort: Measured row contributor for scapular retraction.
secondary.evidence: Middle or transverse trapezius activity is measured in seated cable and prone row studies, and the T-bar row requires scapular retraction as the handle approaches the torso.

secondary.name: Rhomboids
secondary.evidenceShort: Inferred from row-family grouped EMG and scapular retraction.
secondary.evidence: This role is marked as inference: Lehman et al. reported grouped middle trapezius/rhomboid activity during row conditions, and the T-bar row finish requires scapular retraction.

secondary.name: Posterior deltoid
secondary.evidenceShort: Measured row contributor, path-sensitive.
secondary.evidence: Posterior or rear deltoid activity is measured in seated cable and prone row EMG. It assists shoulder extension and horizontal abduction, with involvement increasing as elbows travel wider or higher.

secondary.name: Biceps brachii
secondary.evidenceShort: Measured elbow-flexion assistant in row studies.
secondary.evidence: Biceps brachii is directly measured in seated and prone row EMG studies. It assists elbow flexion during the T-bar row but is not the intended primary back target.

support.name: Rotator cuff
support.evidenceShort: Row tasks require glenohumeral stabilization.
support.evidence: Row tasks recruit the rotator cuff in a direction-specific way, supporting its classification as shoulder support during loaded rowing rather than a primary hypertrophy target.

support.name: Erector spinae
support.evidenceShort: Unsupported hinge rows create trunk-support demand.
support.evidence: Free-weight row studies show meaningful erector spinae and lumbar loading demands. In the landmine T-bar row, the erector spinae support the hip-hinged torso while the upper body rows the load.

evidence.verdict: T-bar row: latissimus dorsi primary; teres major, middle trapezius, rhomboids, posterior deltoid, and biceps brachii secondary; rotator cuff and erector spinae support.
evidence.clinicalShort: EMG estimates acute excitation, not hypertrophy, mechanical tension, adaptation, or injury risk.
evidence.limitsShort: Landmine angle, handle width, torso angle, hip drive, grip, plate diameter, load, and chest-supported T-bar machines can materially change emphasis.
evidence.summary: This entry treats the T-bar row as a standing landmine or barbell T-bar row without a chest pad. Row-family EMG supports latissimus dorsi as the primary target when the elbows track close, with teres major, middle trapezius, rhomboids, posterior deltoid, and biceps brachii assisting. Because the torso is unsupported, erector spinae are visible support; the rotator cuff is included for shoulder stabilization during the pull.
evidence.clinicalInterpretation: The evidence base is strongest for row-family EMG and trunk-loading studies, with landmine-specific evidence mainly coming from a peer-reviewed technique article. A chest-supported T-bar machine should be treated as a separate variant because its support and fatigue profile differ.
evidence.limitations: No direct EMG study of a commercial landmine T-bar row was found. The classification transfers close evidence from seated cable rows, prone rows, free-weight row trunk studies, and a landmine row technique paper. Brachialis and brachioradialis were not added because they lack local visible anatomy entries.

studies.type: Landmine row technique review
studies.shortCitation: Lincoln et al., Strength Cond J, 2023
studies.finding: Describes the landmine row as an upper-body pulling exercise using a barbell as a lever, including T-bar row apparatus substitution and programming considerations.
studies.citation: Lincoln MA, Sapstead GW, Moore KN, Weldon A. Exercise Technique: The Landmine Row. Strength and Conditioning Journal. 2023;45(3):371-378. doi:10.1519/SSC.0000000000000751.
studies.relevance: Peer-reviewed technique source for the landmine/T-bar row variant and its support, setup, and loading characteristics.

studies.type: Seated cable row EMG and force study
studies.shortCitation: Vasconcelos et al., Int J Strength Cond, 2023
studies.finding: Lower-abduction row paths emphasized latissimus dorsi, while higher-abduction paths emphasized upper-back and posterior deltoid muscles.
studies.citation: Vasconcelos CMWA, Lopes CR, Almeida VM, Neto WK, Soares EG. Effect Of Different Grip Position And Shoulder-Abduction Angle On Muscle Strength And Activation During The Seated Cable Row. International Journal of Strength and Conditioning. 2023;3(1):1-13. doi:10.47206/ijsc.v3i1.190.
studies.relevance: Direct row-family EMG for latissimus dorsi, middle trapezius, posterior deltoid, and biceps brachii by shoulder-abduction angle.

studies.type: Prone row range-of-motion EMG study
studies.shortCitation: Fischer et al., J Electromyogr Kinesiol, 2025
studies.finding: Prone barbell row EMG measured latissimus dorsi, transverse trapezius, rear deltoid, and biceps brachii.
studies.citation: Fischer J, Burger C, Seguel JM, Rodoplu C, Paternoster FK, Tilp M, Konrad A. Impact of different ranges of motion in the prone barbell row on muscle excitation. Journal of Electromyography and Kinesiology. 2025;83:103025. doi:10.1016/j.jelekin.2025.103025.
studies.relevance: Close row-family EMG for the main visible pulling muscles.

studies.type: Latissimus dorsi exercise EMG study
studies.finding: Seated row produced a high latissimus-to-biceps activation ratio and high grouped middle trapezius/rhomboid activity.
studies.citation: Lehman GJ, Buchan DD, Lundy A, Myers N, Nalborczyk A. Variations in muscle activation levels during traditional latissimus dorsi weight training exercises: An experimental study. Dynamic Medicine. 2004;3:4. doi:10.1186/1476-5918-3-4.
studies.relevance: Row-family EMG evidence for lats, biceps, and grouped middle trapezius/rhomboids.

studies.type: Seated row EMG and verbal-instruction study
studies.finding: Seated row at 70% 1RM produced substantial latissimus dorsi, teres major, posterior deltoid, and biceps brachii activity.
studies.citation: Fujita RA, De Marchi PU, Silva NRS, Gomes MM. Verbal instruction does not change myoelectric activity during seated row exercise in trained and untrained men. Motriz: Revista de Educacao Fisica. 2019;25(4):e10190100. doi:10.1590/s1980-6574201900040100.
studies.relevance: Close row-family EMG for teres major, posterior deltoid, and biceps brachii roles.

studies.type: Rotator cuff recruitment study
studies.shortCitation: Wattanaprakornkul et al., J Electromyogr Kinesiol, 2011
studies.finding: Rotator cuff recruitment during bench press and row was direction-specific, consistent with shoulder stabilization.
studies.citation: Wattanaprakornkul D, Halaki M, Cathers I, Ginn KA. Direction-specific recruitment of rotator cuff muscles during bench press and row. Journal of Electromyography and Kinesiology. 2011;21(6):1041-1049. doi:10.1016/j.jelekin.2011.09.002.
studies.relevance: Supports rotator cuff shoulder-stability role during rowing.

studies.type: Rowing exercise trunk EMG and lumbar-load study
studies.finding: Different rowing exercises changed trunk muscle activation, lumbar motion, load, and stiffness.
studies.citation: Fenwick CMJ, Brown SHM, McGill SM. Comparison of different rowing exercises: trunk muscle activation and lumbar spine motion, load, and stiffness. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. 2009;23(2):350-358. doi:10.1519/JSC.0b013e3181942019.
studies.relevance: Supports erector spinae and fatigue-cost interpretation for unsupported row variants.

studies.type: Bi- and unilateral row core EMG study
studies.shortCitation: Saeterbakken et al., Int J Sports Med, 2015
studies.finding: Free-weight rows produced greater erector spinae or multifidus activity than machine rows, and row laterality altered core-muscle activation.
studies.citation: Saeterbakken A, Andersen V, Brudeseth A, Lund H, Fimland MS. The Effect of Performing Bi- and Unilateral Row Exercises on Core Muscle Activation. International Journal of Sports Medicine. 2015;36(11):900-905. doi:10.1055/s-0034-1398646.
studies.relevance: Supports the higher trunk-support demand of free-weight row variants relative to supported machine rows.
